Naymote described the development as an indication of growing institutional openness and recognition of citizens’ right to access and monitor local development plans and spending.

“The change is not only that citizens can access these documents. They can understand and use them to engage local authorities and advocate public resources to address priorities agreed upon by their communities,” said Eddie D. Jarwolo, Executive Director of Naymote Partners for Democratic Development.

The initiative has also received support from UNDP, which said stronger citizen participation in county budgeting could contribute to broader governance reforms.

“I am pleased that this initiative not only strengthens citizen participation in local development but also reinforces UNDP’s broader support to governance reforms,” said Trokon Bryant, UNDP Project Manager.

“By promoting transparency and accountability in county budgeting, the project contributes directly to advancing the rule of law and strengthening efforts to combat corruption,” Bryant added.

He said the partnership with the Government of Liberia supports implementation of the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID), particularly Pillar Four, which focuses on governance and anti-corruption.

Bryant said the collaboration is intended to ensure that county development funds are managed transparently, aligned with citizens’ priorities and protected against misuse.

“I extend sincere appreciation to Naymote for its strong partnership with UNDP and the Peacebuilding Fund in implementing the Social Accountability Monitoring Project. This collaboration is vital to empowering citizens, strengthening responsive governance, and building sustainable peace,” he said.

Despite the progress recorded, Naymote’s findings suggest that the central challenge is no longer simply whether counties are spending money on development, but whether those investments correspond to the priorities citizens have identified and whether counties have sufficient resources and time to implement them.

Naymote Partners for Democratic Development is a Liberian civil society organization focused on accountable democratic governance, political accountability, civic participation and inclusive development.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai’s Twin Test — Cocaine, a Contested Border, and a Presidency Under Pressure
World.content:
MONROVIA — Six weeks apart, two crises have converged on the desk of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, each testing a different pillar of his authority. One is a sprawling narcotics investigation that has reached into his own security services and, uncomfortably, his own family. The other is a border standoff with Guinea that has simmered, flared, and simmered again since March without a final resolution. Neither crisis threatens to topple the administration on its own. Together, they are shaping how Liberians — and Liberia’s neighbors — read the strength of a presidency now roughly halfway into its term.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

The Narcotics Reckoning

The drug investigation has moved with unusual speed for Liberian institutions. It began building in June, when authorities intercepted roughly 238 kilograms of cocaine disguised as seasoning-cube cargo at Roberts International Airport, then escalated dramatically in July with the seizure of nearly four metric tons of suspected cocaine — one of the largest drug busts in the country’s history, with an estimated street value north of $300 million.

What has followed looks less like a single case and more like a slow excavation of how deeply trafficking networks had embedded themselves in state institutions. Boakai has dismissed and suspended more than a dozen officials since late July, including senior figures at Roberts International Airport, a police commissioner overseeing criminal investigations and Interpol liaison work, and a deputy director at the National Security Agency. Two police officers were separately dismissed over allegations they used government vehicles to move a narcotics shipment across Bomi Highway. As recently as this weekend, Boakai ordered a 48-hour investigation into the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency’s own officer-in-charge, Fitzgerald Biago, after Biago recused himself amid allegations he received a vehicle from someone linked to a trafficking organization.

The case has also brushed against the president’s own household. Boakai’s son, Joseph Boakai Jr., issued a public denial in late July after a video circulating on social media sought to tie him to an alleged cartel, insisting he has never trafficked drugs, taken money for influence, or leaned on his father’s office to shield anyone. He invited anyone with evidence to bring it to Liberia’s security institutions rather than social media. The U.S. Department of Justice has since joined the probe, underscoring both its scale and its international dimensions.

Civil society groups have, so far, credited Boakai’s response rather than criticized it. The Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia welcomed his swift order of the Biago investigation, while noting that public trust in security institutions remains thin and urging that the probe be broadened to strengthen its credibility. That reaction captures the peculiar dynamic of this crisis: the scandal itself is corrosive to institutional confidence, but Boakai’s visible willingness to fire his own appointees — including officials tied to agencies under his direct authority — has so far been read as decisive rather than damning. Justice Minister Oswald Tweh has framed the effort as targeting not just individual smugglers but the transnational criminal architecture behind them, a considerably harder and slower undertaking than the arrests and dismissals made so far.

The Border That Won’t Settle

While the narcotics case has unfolded in Monrovia’s courtrooms and press briefings, a quieter but equally persistent crisis has played out nearly 300 kilometers away, at the Sorlumba crossing in Foya District, Lofa County.

The dispute there dates to March 2, when Guinean soldiers confronted road workers at the border and seized equipment. Within a week it had escalated into a sovereignty crisis: Guinean troops allegedly advanced roughly eight kilometers into Liberian territory, tore down a Liberian flag that had flown for decades, and raised their own. A Liberian civilian was shot near the Makona River amid the unrest, schools closed across Foya District, and a subsequent rights commission investigation found that at least 26 towns and villages had been affected by displacement.

Boakai’s government answered with summit diplomacy — an emergency meeting in Conakry on March 17 with Guinean President Mamadi Doumbouya and Sierra Leonean President Julius Maada Bio, witnessed by Côte d’Ivoire, that produced pledges of joint technical commissions on border demarcation. Five months on, those commissions have yet to resolve the underlying line dispute, even as the two sides have proven able to de-escalate specific incidents through local dialogue, as they did again this week when Foya officials mediated a fresh standoff over LIS officers being ordered off their post. That pattern — flare, mediate, calm, repeat — has become the border’s rhythm, and it leaves the core territorial question exactly where it stood in March.

*Two Crises, One Governing Test*

The two situations differ in almost every particular — one is a domestic law-enforcement scandal with international trafficking links, the other a foreign-relations dispute rooted in colonial-era boundary ambiguity. But they share a common test of governance: whether Boakai’s administration can convert crisis management into durable institutional fixes, rather than a string of individually resolved incidents.

On narcotics, that means whether dismissals and prosecutions actually dismantle trafficking networks rather than simply replacing the officials who enabled them. On the border, it means whether the joint technical commissions promised in March produce an actual demarcation agreement, rather than another round of commander rotations and local dialogue sessions each time tensions spike. Both crises have, so far, been contained rather than resolved — a distinction that will matter more the longer either one drags on.

For a president elected in part on promises of reform and stronger institutions, the coming months on both fronts will likely say more about his legacy than either crisis has said so far on its own.

FrontPageAfrica will continue monitoring both the narcotics investigation and the Liberia–Guinea border situation.

World.title: Liberia: At Sorlumba, a Fragile Peace Papers Over an Unresolved Border Crisis
World.content:
Sorlumba may be quiet, but the dispute is far from over. Months after an armed confrontation displaced communities, wounded a Liberian and triggered a presidential summit, Guinean and Liberian officials are still relying on ad hoc talks to prevent fresh clashes at the Makona River. Without a clear demarcation of the border and a permanent joint security mechanism, each new troop rotation, construction project or dispute at the crossing risks reopening a crisis that diplomacy has so far managed only to contain — not resolve.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

FOYA DISTRICT, Lofa County — When Sorlumba Township Commissioner Harris Domah stood between Liberian immigration officers and Guinean soldiers on Monday morning, brokering yet another round of talks at the Makona River crossing, it marked at least the fourth time this year that local officials have had to step in to keep a simmering border dispute from boiling over.

The immediate trigger was small by the standards of what this stretch of border has already witnessed: Guinean troops told Liberia Immigration Service (LIS) officers on Sunday to abandon their post at Sorlumba. The Liberians refused. The Guineans withdrew. By Monday, both sides were sitting down again, this time with a newly rotated Guinean command team hearing, for what officials hope is the last time, the case for peaceful coexistence at the crossing.

But the ease with which this particular episode was resolved should not obscure how far the underlying dispute remains from settled — nor how quickly a routine disagreement over a guard post can escalate at this frontier.

How a Road Project Became a Sovereignty Crisis

The current phase of the crisis traces to March 2, when workers contracted to pave the Foya–Vahun road were confronted by armed Guinean soldiers at Sorlumba. What began as a dispute over sand-mining equipment on the Makona River escalated within a week into something far graver: by March 9–10, Guinean troops had reportedly pushed roughly eight kilometers into land Liberians consider unambiguously theirs, tore down a Liberian flag that had flown at the riverbank for decades, and raised Guinea’s own flag in its place.

Residents describe Guinean reinforcements arriving by helicopter and being ordered off their own posts by foreign troops standing on Liberian soil. When Liberian youths responded by planting a new flag and briefly seizing control of the crossing, the confrontation turned violent — a Liberian civilian, Edward T. Lebbie, was shot in the leg near the river, an injury serious enough that doctors in Foya were unable to fully treat it and referred him for further care in Voinjama.

The human toll extended well beyond one gunshot wound. Schools across Foya District shut their doors. A fact-finding mission by Liberia’s human rights commission later found that at least 26 towns and villages had been affected, with families displaced, livelihoods disrupted, and food insecurity spreading in communities already among the country’s most remote.

Diplomacy Without Demarcation

The response from national governments has, on paper, been swift. On March 17, Guinean President Mamadi Doumbouya convened an emergency summit in Conakry with Liberian President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Sierra Leonean President Julius Maada Bio, with Côte d’Ivoire sitting in as a witness nation. The three Mano River Union governments agreed to route future border incidents through dialogue and pledged joint technical commissions to finally tackle the question that underlies almost every flare-up here: where, exactly, does the border run.

That question is older than any of the current governments. Regional analysts who track conflict along the Mano River basin note that the Guinea–Liberia–Sierra Leone frontier has long suffered from unclear demarcation, thin joint monitoring, and limited state presence — conditions inherited from decades of instability, including Guinea’s 2021 coup, that leave the area vulnerable to exactly the kind of sudden escalation Sorlumba experienced in March. Seen in that light, the summit’s promised technical commissions are less a solution than an acknowledgment of how much work remains undone.

Nearly five months later, that work does not appear finished. Guinean troops have continued to maintain a presence in parts of the contested zone, and residents in some Sorlumba-area communities say they still cannot return home. The commander rotation revealed during Monday’s talks — a changeover local officials only learned about when they arrived to mediate — is itself a reminder of how little continuity or coordination governs day-to-day operations at a crossing that has already produced a shooting, a mass displacement, and a diplomatic summit this year.

A Pattern, Not an Anomaly

What happened at Sorlumba this week fits a broader regional pattern. Border tensions have also flared this year between Guinea and Sierra Leone, prompting comparisons to other unresolved West African boundary disputes, including the long-running maritime dispute between Ghana and Togo. Analysts argue that without durable joint monitoring mechanisms and an agreed demarcation of the Makona River line, the Mano River basin will keep producing these flashpoints — manageable individually, but corrosive cumulatively to the fragile trust between neighbors who all emerged from their own civil conflicts within the past few decades.

For now, Sorlumba is calm. LIS officers remain at their post; Guinean soldiers have returned to theirs. Commissioner Domah’s peaceful dialogue held. But as residents of Foya District have learned since March, calm at this border has a way of being provisional — lasting only until the next command rotation, the next construction crew, or the next unilateral order to stand down.

FrontPageAfrica will continue monitoring developments at the Liberia–Guinea border.

World.title: Liberia: Donors Have Approved Nearly $300 Million More for Climate Adaptation. Can the Boakai Government Bring the Capacity and Commitment Required to Unlock It?
World.content:
Flooding across the country left more than 100,000 people homeless in 2024 Credit: Eric Opa Doue

Summary

Liberia has held its first national coordination meeting to plan implementation of its latest plan to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are causing global warming and help millions of Liberians adapt to floods, heat, and devastation wrought by climate change.

But the plan says only 10 percent of the promised reduction can be financed domestically.

The money is there. Nearly $300 million has already been approved but sits in global coffers. Experts say the question is whether the government can provide the capacity and the co-financing to unlock it.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate correspondent with New Narratives

Last year, the Boakai government made an ambitious promise to its people and the world: Liberia would cut emissions of the so-called “greenhouse” gasses that are causing climate change, by 64 percent by 2035, and make the radical adaptation efforts needed to protect the forests, farmers and coastlines that make the country one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable.

The pledge, contained in Liberia’s third Nationally Determined Contribution, or NDC 3.0, a requirement of the 2016 global Paris Agreement to halt climate change, was validated at a ceremony in Monrovia in September and submitted to the United Nations. This year, the hard part began.

Last week, the Environmental Protection Agency brought together leaders from each of the sectors that are included in the plan along with government ministries, United Nations agencies and development partners to work out how to deliver on the commitments it has made and, importantly, measure it.

“We must move from commitment to implementation, from intention to measurable results,” said Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo, the Agency executive director, in his opening remarks. Liberia’s climate progress, “will not only be measured by our commitment written on paper. It will be measured by our ability to translate those commitments into practical actions that improve the lives of our people.”

But behind those ambitious targets lies a sobering reality: Liberia can afford to finance only ten percent of what it has pledged and will rely on international partners for the rest.

Liberia has been here before. The Sirleaf administration submitted its first NDC in 2015, pledging to reduce emissions by 15 percent. The Weah administration submitted its second in 2021, setting a 64 percent emissions-reduction target by 2030.

But an analysis conducted on the Weah administration’s NDC, led by the Environmental Protection Agency, with support from UNDP, found that Liberia had achieved only 20 percent of its targets by 2024.

That failure has had serious implications for international funding. By 2020 the country had secured $US570 million in international climate-finance commitments from global funders, but less than half of that amount was disbursed in large part because of corruption, a lack of capacity and mismanagement on the part of Liberian bureaucrats. In many cases the EPA was trying to appoint Liberians into position for which they did not have the required skills.

FrontPage Africa/New Narratives has documented suspected corruption and lack of capacity under the Weah administration that led to four-year delays in the US$10 million Climate Information System project which would warn communities about hazardous weather, and the US$27 million Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project which is intended to protect West Point’s coastline from sea-level rise– just two of the many projects that had been approved.

Hundreds of thousands of Liberians were left without rainfall and temperature warnings over four years that may have saved them from crop failure and flooding. On the coast many homes were swept away that would have been saved had the project proceeded as expected.

But there was some progress documented in the report. Between 2021 and 2024, Liberia reported 105 megawatts of hydropower capacity and 5.6 megawatts of solar-energy production. It also recorded 175 electric vehicles contributing to the NDC’s goal of cutting transport emissions Nearly 46,000 hectares of forest were restored through natural regeneration on pace to meet its goal of reforesting an average of 12,285 hectares annually through 2030.

A Plan Liberia Cannot Fund Alone

The gap between ambition and capacity runs through nearly every part of NDC 3.0. Implementing the plan will cost as much as US$3 billion by 2035, according to experts. Of the 64 percent emissions reduction Liberia has pledged, only 10 percent are classified as “unconditional,” meaning they can be achieved using the country’s own resources.

Farmer Rickson Johnson sits on a log on his farm in Nimba County and prays for rain to come down in 2024. Photo credit: Jerome Saye

In an interview Benjamin S. Karmorh, the EPA’s chief technical adviser and Liberia’s national focal point to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change,

said the EPA had not completed its assessment to determine the full cost of its commitments, but he warned it would be big.

“For the next nine to 12 months, we will be able to come up with the real cost of our NDC,” he said, adding that implementing the second NDC alone required more than US$400 million.

Karmorh said the Boakai administration had moved quickly to catch up ground lost under the Weah administration where government failure to provide co-financing and meet the project deadlines required of donors blocked the release of global funds. He cited a 20-megawatt solar facility at the Mount Coffee Hydropower Plant, recently inaugurated to complement the plant’s 88-megawatt hydropower capacity.

He cited President Joseph Boakai’s visit to the Environmental Protection Agency to inaugurate its new headquarters and laboratory as evidence of “the strongest political will on the part of the government in ensuring that the EPA fulfills its mandate.”

A resident affected by flooding makes her way home through standing water on 13th Street, Sinkor, Monrovia, in July.

The 2026 national budget allocated US$2.9 million to the EPA. It includes US$900,000 that the government is required to provide as co-financing for two initiatives backed by the Green Climate Fund. Louis Kuukpen, Deputy Liberia Representative for the United Nations Development Program, which is implementing the coastal defense project, confirmed to FrontPage Africa/New Narratives that the government had disbursed $800,000 co-financing required for the coastal defense project and progress should be seen soon.

Karmorh said the real evidence of the government’s commitment will come in next year’s budget. “We expect that there will be an increase for the EPA,” Karmorh said. “And with that increment, we expect that we’ll be able to do a lot.”

Lack of Data Collection Capacity Also a Handbrake on Global Funding

If money is the headline problem, data is the quieter crisis—and Yarkpawolo devoted much of his address to it.

“We cannot properly manage what we do not measure,” he told the meeting. “We cannot convincingly report progress without credible and consistent data.”

Without reliable data, he said, Liberia cannot determine where resources are most needed, meet its transparency obligations to the United Nations or make a credible case to international climate funders demanding proof of results.

Ongoing solar facility in Voinjama, Lofa County, supporting Liberia’s clean energy and climate goals. Photo credit: RREA

Yarkpawolo said the sectoral officers responsible for gathering data across ministries—from transport and agriculture to energy—are being asked to work without adequate funding, transportation, equipment or reliable internet access.

“This is not sustainable,” he said.

He appealed directly to Liberia’s international donors to establish a dedicated fund for data collection and reporting, separate from project financing. He said such a fund would support field travel, data systems, training and verification—the less visible infrastructure that makes accountability possible and would allow them to employ Liberians to meet the requirements that would unlock funding.“Our partners should not only finance climate projects,” Yarkpawolo said. “They should also invest in institutions and people responsible for measuring and reporting their results.”

A fleet of electric vehicle that are contributing to the Country’s goal of reducing emission by 64 percent. Photo supplied by Spencer Taylor of the Ministry of Transport.

Mobilizing Government Ministries to Meet Climate Targets

Yarkpawolo outlined the EPA’s priorities for the year: finalize a 2026–2027 work plan, validate new coordination tools and reporting templates, and clearly identify which ministry is responsible for providing particular data and when. He said climate reporting is broader than the responsibility of the EPA alone.

“It is not solely an environmental issue,” Yarkpawolo said. “It is a development, economic, social, health, security, and government issue.” Addressing it, he said, will require “a whole-of-government and a whole-of-society approach.”

World.title: Liberia: Auditor General Cites Missing Audit Committee, Non-Competitive Procurement, Unverified Assets, Delayed Projects and Undelivered Digital Lending Platform
World.content:
Monrovia – Liberia’s General Auditing Commission (GAC) has uncovered a series of governance, procurement and project implementation weaknesses in the Smallholder Agriculture Transformation and Agribusiness Revitalization Project (STAR-P), warning that the deficiencies exposed the World Bank and IFAD-supported initiative to weak oversight, poor asset accountability and potential value-for-money risks.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The findings are contained in a Management Letter issued on June 29, 2026, following the audit of STAR-P’s financial statements covering the period ending October 31, 2025.

The audit, addressed to Agriculture Minister J. Alexander Nuetah, identified weaknesses ranging from the absence of a functional audit committee to procurement irregularities, poor asset management, incomplete infrastructure projects and delays in implementing key digital services intended to benefit farmers.

No Functional Audit Committee

The GAC found that the National Project Steering Committee failed to establish an audit committee as required under Liberia’s Public Financial Management (PFM) Act.

Auditors also reported no evidence that the Steering Committee reviewed internal audit reports or monitored the implementation of audit recommendations. According to the report, the committee met only once during the audit period to approve the project’s annual budget and work plan.

The GAC warned that the absence of an audit committee weakens internal oversight and could delay corrective actions on audit findings.

In response, STAR-P management acknowledged the recommendation but said the Ministry of Agriculture has instead established an Audit Recommendation Implementation Committee chaired by the Minister to monitor audit recommendations. The Auditor General, however, maintained that a formal audit committee remains necessary and said implementation would be reviewed during future audits.

Procurement Without Competition

The audit also questioned the procurement process surrounding a US$27,000 consultancy contract awarded to OA & A Consult Limited.

Auditors found no evidence that the consultancy was competitively procured, noting the absence of s, expressions of interest, technical evaluations or financial proposal assessments as required under project procurement rules and World Bank regulations.

The GAC cautioned that bypassing competitive procurement could undermine value for money and increase the risk of procurement fraud.

Management accepted the finding and pledged to ensure future grantees follow competitive procurement procedures consistent with IFAD and World Bank guidelines.

Weak Fixed Asset Controls

The report identified widespread weaknesses in STAR-P’s asset management system.

Among the deficiencies were incomplete fixed asset registers, failure to update newly acquired assets, lack of periodic physical verification, and absence of asset coding.

The audit cited assets valued at US$46,719, including laptops, printers, projectors, office furniture and computers, that were either improperly recorded or omitted from the register.

Although management submitted an updated asset register after the audit, the Auditor General said it still lacked critical information required under public financial management regulations.

Missing and Unverified Beneficiary Assets

Field verification exercises also uncovered concerns regarding assets purchased for beneficiaries under the Liberia Agriculture Commercialization Fund (LACF).

The audit reported that assets worth US$33,500, including cold storage facilities, solar systems, greenhouses and motorcycles, could not be physically verified.

Another US$1,680 solar system procured for a beneficiary had not been put into use, while assets worth US$68,000 supplied to a beneficiary in Grand Bassa County—including trucks, motor tricycles, processing equipment and palm oil machinery—had not been coded for identification.

The GAC concluded that management failed to adequately account for the missing assets or explain why some equipment remained unused.

Management attributed the challenges to decentralized project implementation, incomplete records and logistical difficulties, and said it has begun reconciling assets, strengthening asset tracking and revising its fixed asset management policies.

The Auditor General maintained the findings and called for a joint physical verification exercise with the GAC within one month after submission of the report to the Legislature.

Construction Projects Behind Schedule

The audit further found that US$57,960 had been paid for construction projects that remained incomplete well beyond approved timelines.

The affected projects include a warehouse in Lofa County and a palm oil factory in Grand Bassa County, both of which were still unfinished during GAC’s field verification in May 2026.

Management blamed contractor capacity limitations, adverse weather, rising construction costs and logistical challenges, and said stronger contract monitoring and milestone-based payment systems have since been introduced.

Digital Lending Platform Still Missing

One of the audit’s most significant findings involved an online digital lending platform intended to support farmers through CitiTrust Savings and Loans.

According to the report, US$36,768—representing full payment under the service agreement—was disbursed for the design and implementation of the platform.

However, during physical verification in May 2026, auditors found no evidence that the integrated digital lending system had been deployed or was operational, despite contractual deadlines indicating it should have gone live by May 2025.

Management acknowledged implementation delays, citing software customization requirements, connectivity problems and technical capacity constraints. Officials said the software would be fully integrated before the service agreement expires.

Dashboard and Project Assets Not Handed Over

The GAC also found that the Liberia Agriculture Commercialization Fund’s reporting dashboard and other digital assets were never formally transferred to the Ministry following the expiration of the Fund Manager’s contract.

Auditors warned that the missing dashboard could undermine institutional memory, beneficiary tracking and project reporting.

Management said discussions are underway with the former Fund Manager to complete the handover of databases, user credentials and reporting tools, while committing to strengthen future contractual handover requirements.

Auditor General Maintains Key Findings

While STAR-P management accepted most of the recommendations and outlined corrective measures, the Auditor General maintained several key findings, particularly regarding missing beneficiary assets and incomplete documentation.

The GAC said it will conduct follow-up reviews during subsequent audits to determine whether the Ministry of Agriculture has implemented the recommended reforms aimed at strengthening governance, procurement, financial accountability and project oversight.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Replaces Biago, Taps Ex-Defense Chief Ziankahn to Lead LDEA Amid Cocaine Probe
World.content:
MONROVIA — President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has appointed retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn Jr. as Director General of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA), replacing Deputy Police Commissioner Fitzgerald T. M. Biago, who had been serving as the agency’s officer in charge amid a widening cocaine investigation.

By Jaheim T. Toby

The appointment, announced Monday by the Executive Mansion, is subject to confirmation by the Liberian Senate.

Ziankahn, a former Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia and former Minister of National Defense, most recently served as President Boakai’s Military Advisor. His appointment comes as the government faces mounting pressure over Liberia’s handling of major narcotics seizures, including the interception of nearly four tons of cocaine in Paynesville valued at about US$317 million.

The Executive Mansion said the appointment reflects Boakai’s determination to strengthen Liberia’s response to drug trafficking and transnational organized crime.

“His appointment reflects the President’s confidence in his leadership, integrity, and operational experience, and signals the Administration’s determination to elevate Liberia’s fight against drugs to a new level,” the statement said.

Under the new arrangement, Ziankahn will report directly to the President in consultation with the Minister of Justice.

Boakai also appointed Precious Rue as Deputy Director General for Operations and Prince Mulbah as Deputy Director General for Administration. Both appointments are also subject to Senate confirmation.

The three appointees have been directed to assume their responsibilities immediately in an acting capacity pending legislative confirmation when the Senate returns later this year.

Ernest Tarpeh, who previously served as Deputy Director General of the LDEA, will return to his former assignment at the National Security Agency.

Biago Suspended Amid Ethical Concerns

The leadership change follows the decision by Biago to step aside earlier this week and submit himself to investigation after allegations emerged that he had received a vehicle as a gift from Leroy Harris, a suspect in the US$317 million cocaine case.

Biago has denied the allegation and said he voluntarily stepped aside to allow the investigation to proceed.

According to the Executive Mansion, President Boakai has now indefinitely suspended Biago from the Liberia National Police over what it described as “ethical transgressions” and ordered a more detailed investigation.

The President’s decision followed a review of the Ministry of Justice investigative report.

The report, according to the Executive Mansion, did not establish Biago’s involvement in illegal narcotics trafficking, but raised ethical concerns requiring further scrutiny to determine whether additional administrative or other appropriate action should be taken.

The development comes against the backdrop of a series of high-profile cocaine seizures that have placed Liberia’s law enforcement and security institutions under intense scrutiny.

The government has maintained that the fight against narcotics trafficking is a national security priority, with President Boakai repeatedly describing drug trafficking as one of the gravest threats to Liberia’s security, public health and future development.

‘No Safe Haven’

Following a marathon meeting of the National Security Council on Monday evening, Boakai reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to investigating allegations of misconduct while respecting due process.

The President said allegations should not be treated as proof of wrongdoing, but stressed that public officials must remain accountable when questions about their conduct arise.

“No individual will be condemned without evidence, but no public official will be exempt from accountability where questions of integrity arise,” the Executive Mansion quoted the President as saying.

Boakai directed the new LDEA leadership to work with the Joint Security, the Ministry of Justice and international partners to dismantle drug trafficking networks, strengthen border security and improve intelligence and enforcement capabilities.

He also called for stronger measures to protect Liberian communities, particularly young people, from the impact of illicit drugs.

“Our fight against drugs is a fight for the future of Liberia,” Boakai said.

“We will continue to strengthen our institutions, hold public officials to the highest ethical standards, and pursue those who seek to poison our communities. There will be no safe haven for drug traffickers or those who aid and abet them.”

The appointments mark the latest major shake-up of Liberia’s anti-narcotics apparatus as authorities continue investigations into the country’s increasingly high-profile cocaine cases.

World.title: Kalampa turn to Mopani challenge after Botswana tour
World.content:
Record Super Division champions Nkana FC have returned home after a 12-day pre-season tour of Botswana as preparations for the 2026 Transitional League intensify.

‎

‎Kalampa arrived in the country on Monday after playing six matches in Botswana, recording four wins and two defeats, and finishing as runners-up in the inaugural Tati River Cup.

‎

‎“The Botswana trip provided the environment the technical bench needed to assess the squad, build match fitness and test different combinations ahead of the 2026 Transitional League,” the club said.

‎

‎Nkana opened the tour with dominant displays, beating Tutume Rangers FC 5-1 and 5-0. They then edged Tonota FC 1-0 in a closed-door practice match before suffering a narrow 1-0 defeat to Enesia FC.

‎

‎The Kitwe giants progressed to the Tati River Cup final after a convincing 3-0 semi-final victory over Tafic FC.

‎

‎However, they fell 2-1 to Tonota FC in the final at the Obed Itani Chilume Stadium to finish second in the inaugural tournament.

‎

‎With the Botswana tour concluded, attention now turns to the Mopani Challenge Cup against arch-rivals Mighty Mufulira Wanderers.

‎

‎The 2026 edition will be played over two legs for the third year running. The first leg is scheduled for 22 August at Shinde Stadium, with the return leg set for 29 August at Nkana Stadium.

‎

‎This year’s proceeds will support the Autism School at Kitwe Teaching Hospital and the procurement of physiotherapy equipment for Ronald Ross Hospital in Mufulira.

‎

‎The initiative offers football fans the chance to enjoy one of the Copperbelt’s biggest rivalries while contributing to causes that directly benefit communities in Kitwe and Mufulira.

World.title: Mokambo road works to proceed-DC
World.content:
Mufulira District Commissioner Evaristo Chilumba has assured residents that the $56.7 million Mufulira-Mokambo road project will proceed uninterrupted beyond the upcoming general elections, dismissing claims that the infrastructure initiative is merely a political campaign gimmick.

Speaking during an onsite inspection of the ongoing engineering works, Mr Chilumba emphasised that the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) agreement underpinning the road was established long before the electoral cycle.

He urged members of the public to have faith in President Hakainde Hichilema’s administration, citing its unwavering commitment to delivering critical national infrastructure.

“This project will not stall and it will continue even after the general elections,” Mr Chilumba stated.

He noted that the arrangement was secured independently of political timelines and urged residents to have faith in President Hakainde Hichilema and the government’s commitment to ensuring the road’s completion.

Mr Chilumba pointed out that construction of the road had initially commenced under the Patriotic Front government, stating that money had been spent yet works had not been done.

He explained that when the United Party for National Development government came into power in 2021, they commenced the process of construction from scratch, including having to find a new contractor.

“The contractor is currently on site conducting the road works and the project is moving,” the District Commissioner said.

Mr Chilumba disclosed that graveling works have so far been done on the entire stretch of the road up to the border, while noting that tarring of some patches of the road has already commenced.

He stated that the project is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

Mr. Chilumba stated that the comprehensive infrastructure upgrade includes upgrading the carriageway from Mufulira to Mokambo to bituminous standard, constructing a modern toll plaza, and building a modern border post at Mokambo.

He said that the modern border post will help in speeding up the clearing process of trucks going to the nearby Democratic Republic of Congo.

Highlighting the immediate local impact, Mr Chilumba noted that for many years, residents using the road were subjected to spending about over an hour travelling from Mufulira to Mokambo due to the bad state of the road.

“After the works are done, residents will now spend less than 30 minutes travelling to the border,” he said.

Mr Chilumba said the road will ease access for residents and improve mobility on the road.

He stated that residents suffered, being stuck in mud and potholes, especially during the rainy season for many years, due to the bad state of the road, adding that this will all be a thing of the past thanks to government’s commitment to ensure that the road is completed quickly.

Mr Chilumba noted that the road is of benefit to the entire country as it connects Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) thereby boosting inter-country trade.

World.title: NW UPND calls for re-election of Hichilema
World.content:
United Party for National Development (UPND) Northwestern Provincial Chairperson Adam Sepezo has called on voters to re-elect President Hakainde Hichilema in the August 13 general elections, to enable the government to continue implementing its development agenda.

Mr Sepezo says the UPND administration has recorded significant progress in various sectors of the economy since assuming office in 2021.

He noted that the achievements include investments in education, health, agriculture, social protection and employment creation.

Mr Sepezo was speaking to the Zambia News and Information Services (ZANIS) in Solwezi district, shortly after a stakeholder meeting with the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) at Solwezi College of Education.

He said President Hichilema had delivered on most of the UPND’s 2021 campaign promises, including restoring peace and order and addressing political violence and cadreism.

Mr Sepezo said the re-election of President Hichilema will provide an opportunity for the government to consolidate the gains made and further transform the economy.

He cited sustainable agriculture, mechanisation, social protection programmes and the Constituency Development Funds (CDF) as some of the interventions that have contributed to improving people’s livelihoods.

Mr Sepezo said education remains a key priority for the government, citing the reintroduction of free education, the school feeding programme, increased meal allowances for students and the recruitment of teachers.

He said the government had also recruited health workers, Zambia Police Service officers, Zambia National Service personnel and members of the Zambia Army, among others.

‘‘The recruitment of workers across various sectors demonstrates the government’s commitment to creating employment opportunities for Zambians,’’ he said.

He has, however, urged citizens to maintain peace and unity before, during and after the elections.

Mr Sepezo further called on political players and their supporters to reject political violence and resolve differences through dialogue and lawful channels.

World.title: President Hichilema describes late Mr Liato, as a dedicated public servant
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has described Former Cabinet Minister in the Movement for Multi-Party Democracy (MMD) administration, Austin Liato, as a dedicated public servant who made a significant contribution to the development of Zambia’s labour sector.

President Hichilema notes that the late Mr Liato, distinguished himself through many years of dedicated service to the country, particularly during his time in the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.

ZANIS reports that President Hichilema made the remarks in a speech read on his behalf by Secretary to the Cabinet, Patrick Kangwa, at a Funeral Church Service held at Anglican Cathedral of the Holy Cross in Lusaka today.

President Hichilema said Mr Liato, working as a Cabinet Minister, provided leadership and oversight to one of the most critical sectors of the economy.

He added that the late minister played an important role in maintaining cordial relations between the Government and the labour movement.

President Hichilema said Mr Liato promoted dialogue and an open-door policy, which helped foster harmony in the labour market and contributed to increased investor confidence, job creation and economic development.

He further described the late Mr Liato as a respected trade unionist who laid a strong foundation for improved labour relations between Government, trade unions and other stakeholders.

In his Eulogy, Oasis of Blessings Assembly Bishop, Max Nalumango, said Mr Liato was a man of determination, a family man and cherished his friends, adding that he admired his sense of humor.

And Widow Fatima Liato, in her tribute delivered on her behalf by Aminata Fofana, described her husband as a true friend, kind and star of her story.

Mr Liato who died on August 6, 2026 at the age of 61, at Maina Soko Medical Hospital has since been put to rest at Lusaka’s Leopards Hill Memorial Park.

He is survived by a wife, 13 Children and 12 Grandchildren

World.title: Copper Queens need tactical overhaul – Kaona  ‎
World.content:
Respected sports administrator Mwembe Kaona says the Copper Queens’ early exit from the 2024 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers should force a national reflection on Zambia’s tactical approach.

‎

‎Kaona said while Zambia’s women’s football has grown in talent, ambition and global presence, the tactical system has not kept pace.

‎

‎“Zambia’s women’s football has evolved in talent, ambition, and global presence, yet the tactical system guiding that talent has not kept pace. The result is a widening gap between what the Copper Queens are capable of and what their current tactical identity allows them to achieve,” he noted.

‎

‎Kaona argued that the team must move away from improvisation and emotional football to embrace a modern, structured and intelligent style.

‎

‎He cited the 6–0 victory over Egypt as proof of Zambia’s attacking potential, but said the loss to Nigeria, even after Nigeria went down to 10 players, exposed structural weaknesses.

‎

‎“Zambia’s long‑standing reliance on direct, transition‑heavy football has become predictable. Against disciplined opponents, hopeful long balls are easily neutralised, midfielders are bypassed, and the team loses control of the match tempo,” Kaona said.

‎

‎The administrator proposed that Zambia adopt a clearly defined ‘game model’ covering build-up, pressing, defending and chance creation. He said this would give the Copper Queens predictable patterns, clear roles, and consistency from youth to senior level.

‎

‎Kaona outlined key reforms: modernising build-up play, midfielders who can receive under pressure, full-backs who understand underlaps, using half-spaces as the main attacking corridor, coordinated pressing, controlled transitions, and designed set-piece routines.

‎

‎“Possession is not a luxury; it is a necessity. Against elite teams, Zambia must learn to slow the game down, stretch the pitch, and create chances through structured patterns rather than desperation,” Kaona said.

‎

World.title: State House calls for peace ahead of General Elections
World.content:
State House Chief Communication Specialist, Clayson Hamasaka, has called for peace, tolerance, and honest leadership ahead of this year’s General Elections.

Mr Hamasaka emphasised that peace must be maintained through the final hours following this week’s General Election.

He highlighted that every human life is precious and stressed that any calls for taking of a human life should be treated with the gravity they deserve by all political parties.

Mr Hamasaka expressed concern over a recent incident involving former Nkana Member of Parliament, Binwell Mpundu, and Tonse Alliance President Brian Mundubile, describing them as troubling.

“Zambians are watching a leadership that cannot give straight answers about language touching on human life,” he stated.

Mr Hamasaka condemned the remarks, noting that they were initially blamed on Artificial Intelligence (AI) before an acknowledgment was made.

He urged that this is not a time for political games or contradictory explanations but a moment for political leaders to reject inflammatory language and ensure no citizen is put in danger for political gain.

“The 2026 General election will be peaceful because the Zambian people have chosen peace,” he affirmed.

This is contained in a statement issued to ZANIS today by State House Chief Communications Specialist, Clayson Hamasaka.

World.title: Govt. committed to improving the welfare of public workers
World.content:
Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary Tuesday Bwalya says government will continue to deliver infrastructure development and improve the welfare of public service workers.

Dr Bwalya reaffirmed the critical role of civil servants in policy implementation and national development.

Dr Bwalya made the remarks when he addressed civil servants in Isoka and Mafinga districts.

The Permanent Secretary said as the economy continues to make gains, government will see to it that the welfare of public service workers is improved.

And Dr Bwalya urged civil servants to remain professional, support the government of the day, and not get involved in partisan politics.

In both districts, civil servants commended the government for the achievements so far stating that it is due to the policies implemented in the last five years.

Isoka Town Council Director of Finance Joseph Chanda said the government has introduced and strengthened various programmes aimed at improving the livelihoods of the people

He named some of the programmes as the enhanced Constituency Development Fund (CDF), education and skills development, health infrastructure, social protection and community empowerment.

“As we pledge our full support to government in implementing policies and programmes aimed at bringing development and improving the livelihoods of our people. We remain committed to ensuring that Government programmes are translated into tangible benefits on the ground through effective service delivery, prudent use of public resources, accountability and transparency,” he said

And Mafinga District Director Health Services John Mwiche assured that civil servants in the district will adhere to the Permanent Secretary’s guidance to uphold professionalism and be of good conduct to serve the people better.

World.title: Kabwe magistrate court adjourns case involving NRPUP candidate
World.content:
The Kabwe Magistrate court has adjourned a matter in which National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) Mayoral aspiring candidate for Kabwe, Wilson Pondamali and seven others are facing charges of being in possession of offensive weapons and unlawful assembly contrary to the law, to September 1st, 2026.

Kabwe Resident Magistrate, Gloria Chipasha, adjourned the matter after the accused failed to take plea as they were not present before the court.

The accused are Pondamali aged 53, of House No. H21, Gwembe Street in Highridge, Bright Chileshe 28, of Kamushanga Compound, Mushitu Muhamba 28, of Luansanse Area, Danny Nkhoma, whose age is not known but of Katondo Compound and Daniel Chewe 53, also of Katondo Compound.

Others are Patrick Manson Chimfwembe 22 and Sylvester Kolala 42, both of Katondo Compound in Kabwe District.

The accused persons are charged with unlawful assembly contrary to section 74(1) and 76 and with possession of offensive weapons contrary to section 85(1) of the penal code chapter 87 of the laws of Zambia.

Magistrate Chipasha adjourned the matter after the accused’s legal representative, Changano Changano of Chirwa and Associates informed her that the accused, who were supposed to take plea, were not present before the court and they are all on police bond.

Facts before the court are that in the first count, Pondamali, who is Kabwe Mayoral candidate on the NRPUP ticket in the 13th August general election and others, are alleged to have on 7th June 2026 in Kabwe district, with a common purpose of committing an offence, jointly and whilst acting together, did assemble without lawful authority.

In the second count, it is also alleged that the accused persons on the 7th June 2026 in Kabwe district, jointly and whilst acting together, had in their possession offensive articles namely stones without lawful authority.

State Prosecutor Charity Munyonga informed magistrate Chipasha that instructions from the Director of Public Prosecutions were ready but all the seven accused persons were not present before the court.

The court has since given Pondamali and his co-accused a benefit of doubt, extended their police bond and adjourned the matter to September 1, 2026 for plea.

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Names Retired Army General to Head Anti-Drug Agency
World.content:
The Executive Mansion says Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience."

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has made perhaps his most consequential national security appointment since assuming office, naming former Defense Minister, retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, as Director General of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) in a move that signals a fundamental shift in the government's strategy against transnational narcotics trafficking.

The appointment comes at a defining moment for Liberia's anti-drug campaign -- one marked by record cocaine seizures, allegations of institutional infiltration by organized crime, dismissals of senior security officials, and mounting international scrutiny over whether Liberia has become an emerging transit and storage hub for global narcotics syndicates.

Rather than selecting another career drug enforcement officer, President Boakai has entrusted the agency to one of the country's most experienced military minds, suggesting that the administration increasingly views narcotics trafficking not merely as a law enforcement problem but as a national security emergency.

Ziankahn's appointment follows months of extraordinary anti-narcotics operations that have transformed Liberia's security landscape.



The crisis reached international prominence after authorities intercepted approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine valued at about US$19 million at Roberts International Airport earlier this year. That operation exposed what investigators described as sophisticated trafficking methods involving airport operations and triggered an extensive criminal investigation.

Only weeks later, authorities executed an even more dramatic operation in Duazon, Margibi County, where investigators seized nearly 3.97 metric tons of suspected cocaine with an estimated international street value exceeding US$370 million -- one of the largest narcotics seizures ever recorded in Liberia and among the most significant in West Africa.

The scale of both seizures fundamentally altered perceptions of Liberia's role in international narcotics trafficking.

For years, security analysts had warned that West Africa was increasingly serving as a bridge between cocaine-producing regions in Latin America and lucrative consumer markets in Europe.

The Liberian seizures appeared to reinforce those concerns, suggesting that international trafficking organizations may have established increasingly sophisticated logistical networks within the country.

The investigations that followed produced consequences extending far beyond the drug seizures themselves.

As investigators traced the alleged trafficking operations, allegations emerged suggesting that elements within the security architecture may have been compromised.

President Boakai responded with an unprecedented series of administrative actions, dismissing, suspending and ordering investigations into officials from several security institutions, including the Liberia National Police (LNP), National Security Agency (NSA), Roberts International Airport (RIA), and the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency itself.

Those measures reflected the administration's determination to demonstrate that no institution would be insulated from accountability if credible evidence of misconduct emerged.

The actions also exposed what many analysts consider the greatest institutional threat confronting the country's anti-drug campaign: the possibility that sophisticated international criminal organizations may seek to infiltrate state institutions responsible for combating them.

Such concerns are not unique to Liberia.

Across the world, transnational narcotics organizations have historically relied not only on logistical sophistication but also on corruption, insider facilitation and institutional compromise.

Why Ziankahn?

Against that backdrop, President Boakai's choice of Daniel Dee Ziankahn appears highly strategic.

Unlike many previous leaders of the LDEA, Ziankahn arrives with decades of experience in military command, institutional reform and national security planning.

During his tenure as Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL), he became widely associated with efforts to professionalize Liberia's post-war military following years of civil conflict.

Working alongside international partners, including the United States, he helped oversee reforms aimed at transforming the AFL into a disciplined, professional institution operating under democratic civilian control.

His subsequent service as Minister of National Defense further expanded his experience managing complex security institutions and coordinating with regional and international partners.

More recently, Ziankahn has served as Military Adviser to President Boakai, providing strategic advice on national and regional security matters.

His appointment therefore brings together operational military leadership, institutional reform experience and direct presidential confidence.

Unlike a conventional law enforcement appointment, it places a seasoned strategic commander at the helm of the country's principal anti-narcotics agency.

The Executive Mansion emphasized that Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience," while assigning him direct responsibility for intensifying Liberia's campaign against illicit drugs and organized crime.

The President has also appointed to the LDEA Precious Rue as Deputy Director General for Operations and Prince Mulbah as Deputy Director General for Administration, pending Senate confirmation.

All three officials have been instructed to assume their responsibilities immediately in acting capacities.

The restructuring also returns Ernest Tarpeh to the National Security Agency, while former Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago has been indefinitely suspended from the Liberia National Police over ethical concerns pending further investigation.

Although the Ministry of Justice reportedly found no evidence directly linking Biago to narcotics trafficking, President Boakai concluded that ethical issues identified in the investigation warranted additional scrutiny.

That distinction reflects the administration's emerging message: legal innocence does not necessarily preclude administrative accountability where questions of institutional integrity arise.

Ziankahn's appointment inevitably raises broader questions about the evolving character of Liberia's anti-drug campaign.

Drug enforcement agencies traditionally operate as civilian law enforcement institutions emphasizing criminal investigations, prosecutions and intelligence gathering.

By selecting a retired four-star military officer to lead the LDEA, President Boakai appears to be elevating narcotics trafficking to the level of a national security threat.

That does not necessarily imply militarization of policing.

Rather, it suggests greater emphasis on intelligence coordination, operational discipline, inter-agency cooperation and strategic planning.

The President has directed the new leadership to work closely with the Ministry of Justice, Joint Security and international partners to dismantle trafficking networks, strengthen border controls and improve intelligence capabilities.

Such coordination will likely become increasingly important as investigations continue across multiple jurisdictions.

Liberia's response carries significance beyond its borders.

International partners -- including the United States, the European Union, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), ECOWAS and INTERPOL -- closely monitor countries serving as potential transit points for narcotics trafficking.

Major cocaine seizures often become tests of institutional credibility.

Foreign governments generally assess not only whether drugs are intercepted but also whether investigations reach the criminal networks responsible and whether compromised public officials are held accountable.

Close 

Boakai's successive dismissals, suspensions and institutional reforms therefore appear designed partly to reassure international partners that Liberia remains committed to confronting organized crime despite the scale of recent challenges.

Yet appointments alone cannot dismantle sophisticated international trafficking networks.

Experts note that sustainable success will depend on broader institutional reforms, including stronger financial investigations, improved border surveillance, enhanced intelligence-sharing, witness protection mechanisms, prosecutorial capacity and judicial efficiency.

Liberia must also continue strengthening airport security, maritime surveillance and anti-money laundering systems if it hopes to disrupt the financial infrastructure sustaining organized criminal enterprises.

Equally important will be restoring public confidence in institutions that recent investigations have exposed to allegations of misconduct.

Announcing the appointments, President Boakai reaffirmed that narcotics trafficking represents one of Liberia's gravest threats to national security, public health and national development.

"Our fight against drugs is a fight for the future of Liberia," the President declared. "We will continue to strengthen our institutions, hold public officials to the highest ethical standards, and pursue those who seek to poison our communities. There will be no safe haven for drug traffickers or those who aid and abet them."

Those remarks reinforce an earlier pledge made after the first major cocaine seizure that his administration would dismantle the criminal networks operating within Liberia rather than merely seize narcotics shipments.

The assignment, for Ziankahn, may become the most demanding chapter of a career spanning military leadership, defense policy and national security.

It also represents, for the President, a high-stakes bet that disciplined leadership, institutional credibility and strategic coordination can restore confidence in an agency whose reputation has been shaken by allegations of internal compromise.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Zambia Election Set for Closely Fought Opposition Battle

Zambia's 13 August election has become a closely contested battle between the ruling United Party for National Development and the Tonse-Pamodzi opposition alliance, led by newcomer Brian Mundubile and backed by former Patriotic Front structures. The election is expected to test the opposition's strength and serve as a referendum on President Hakainde Hichilema's record. The government has made progress on debt restructuring, economic growth and inflation. But the high cost of living remains a big concern for voters. The poll is also taking place amid concerns over alleged state interference, restrictions on opposition activity and controversial legislative changes, making it a key test for Zambia's democracy.

WHO Warns DR Congo Ebola Response Falling Behind

More than 1,900 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak. 60-70% of deaths occur in communities before patients reach treatment centres. The WHO said that the concentration of healthcare services in Bunia, Ituri province, is forcing patients to travel long distances and seek care too late. Poor transport systems may also increase transmission. The agency plans to expand treatment facilities closer to communities, add 400 Ebola beds and strengthen public awareness and early referrals. WHO is also looking to the town of Aru, where no new cases have been reported for two weeks after authorities expanded surveillance and response beyond individual patients to surrounding communities.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigeria Lassa Fever Cases Reach 1,000 in 2026

Nigeria has reported 1,000 confirmed cases of Lassa fever and 237 deaths in 2026, with cases reported in 23 states and 116 local government areas. Five states, Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue, account for 86% of confirmed cases. At least 53 healthcare workers have also been infected, prompting the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention to introduce a 30-day protection plan for frontline staff. The agency has said that late presentation, high treatment costs, poor sanitation and limited awareness are contributing to the outbreak and high fatality rate. Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rodents.

Malawi Land Audit Flags Irregular Plot Allocations

Malawi's Ministry of Lands is set to release findings from a pilot land ownership audit in Lilongwe that reportedly uncovered irregularities in the allocation of plots in the affluent Area 3 and Area 10. The audit was launched in February 2026 to improve transparency and accountability in land administration. It is said to have identified politically exposed individuals, including current and former ministers, judges and MPs, among those allegedly linked to irregular land acquisitions. The findings could trigger political controversy, with questions remaining over whether those implicated will be publicly named or face legal or disciplinary action.

UN Somalia Auction Raises Security Concerns

The UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has opened a tender to auction vehicles, generators, IT equipment, medical supplies, construction machinery and other assets. This comes as Washington moves to end funding for the mission's logistical support by the end of 2026. UNSOS provides critical transport, fuel, food and other supplies to about 12,000 African troops and police serving under AUSSOM in the fight against al-Shabab. The auction has raised concerns among civil society groups over transparency and oversight. Regional leaders have warned that any premature reduction in international support could create a security vacuum as al-Shabab continues to operate in parts of Somalia.

Close 

Climate Change Shifts Africa's Malaria Risk

Climate change is reshaping malaria risk across Africa, with rising temperatures making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for transmission, according to a new Nature study. Some parts of West and Central Africa may have become too hot for optimal malaria transmission. The region still bears about 95% of the global malaria burden. But experts warn that climate change is only part of the equation, with funding gaps, drug and insecticide resistance, and weak health systems still major threats. They are urging countries in emerging risk areas to step up malaria prevention and surveillance while maintaining elimination efforts in high-burden areas.

World.title: South Africa: Immigrant Traders See Their Livelihoods Destroyed By March and March
World.content:
Traders with documents and permits chased away, leaving Bellville bus terminus market almost empty

Dozens of immigrant traders who usually traded at the Golden Arrow terminus in Bellville are staying away because of anti-immigrant protests.

When we visited the once bustling site last week, it was quiet with only a handful of traders. Many stalls were deserted.

Some traders we spoke to said they had tried to set up shop in other areas but were stopped. They have not traded at the bus site since the March and March 30 June "deadline" demanding "illegal immigrants" leave South Africa.



"I need to pay rent, put food on the table, and pay the bills," a Zimbabwean man who asked to remain anonymous told GroundUp.

He said he has been selling clothes in Bellville for about five years. He left Zimbabwe in 2008 when its economy collapsed.

While he has not been directly threatened, he has witnessed others being harassed.

"They will take your stuff and throw it on the ground," he said.

"It hurts, but as much as it hurts, it's their country, and they're also marginalised people."

Another trader, who introduced herself as Meye, said she has had a permit to trade since 2010. She fled the DRC in 2003.

"We are legal; everything is correct. But they say we are foreigners and we need to go back to our country."

A single mother of three, she says she is now struggling to feed and school her children.

Another single mother, Safia, says she has been unable to trade despite having refugee status and a trading permit. She came from Somalia in 2010.

She said law enforcement needs to protect the traders better.

"I can't sleep at night because of what is happening. I can't even pay my rent. I can't support my children," she said.

Abdulhakim Husein, Western Cape director of the Somalia Association of South Africa, told GroundUp that he had been assisting traders since the start of July.

He said many asylum seekers and refugees are traders as they have to rely on being self-employed. They came from Somalia, DRC, Zimbabwe, Angola and Burundi.

He said that at a meeting on 13 July (which the City confirmed), it was agreed that traders with valid permits should be allowed to trade. But on 14 July, they received a message warning them about a March and March protest in the area.

Husein said they have approached a legal NGO for assistance.

City spokesperson Luthando Tyhalibongo said foreign nationals whose immigration status has been verified by Home Affairs are permitted to trade with a valid permit. These cost R78 per month.

Close 

"It is a concern whenever permitted traders, whether South African citizens or foreign nationals lawfully permitted to trade, are prevented from engaging in legal economic activity," he said.

He said intimidation and threats should be reported to SAPS.

World.title: South Africa: Gauteng Gets 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications - South African News Briefs - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Gauteng Records Nearly 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications

Almost half a million applications have been submitted for Grade 1 and Grade 8 places in Gauteng for the 2027 academic year since the online application system opened, reports EWN. The Gauteng Department of Education has said that improvements have been made to streamline the process. Education MEC Lebogang Maile has urged parents to apply early. The department also says learners awaiting specialised placement should receive interim support rather than remain on waiting lists, with officials focusing on successful placements and resolving outstanding cases.

Strong Winds Damage Homes in Free State

The South African Red Cross Society is assessing damage caused by strong winds and heavy rainfall in Koppies and other parts of the Free State, reports SABC News. Several homes have reportedly been damaged, including roofs blown off, as severe weather persists. Red Cross volunteers are working with disaster management authorities and municipalities. Assessments continue, with humanitarian assistance being provided to affected households.

Fadiel Adams Unlikely to Testify at Madlanga Commission

National Coloured Congress leader Fadiel Adams is unlikely to testify before the Madlanga Commission, reports EWN. This comes after the commission received his affidavit and supporting documents late. Adams was expected to testify about his involvement in an Investigating Directorate Against Corruption probe into alleged corruption within Crime Intelligence. In 2024, he asked IDAC to investigate claims that the Political Killings Task Team had misused secret service funds for luxury accommodation and vehicles.

World.title: Dangerous drug-resistant fungus spreads across US, reaching 27 states
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Thousands of cases of a potentially deadly, drug-resistant fungus have been reported across 27 states so far this year, according to provisional CDC data.

As of the week ending July 25, a total of 3,437 clinical cases of Candida auris (C. auris) had been documented in the U.S. so far in 2026.

California accounts for 873 cases — roughly one-quarter of the country’s total. Other states with high numbers include Texas (433), Tennessee (283), Ohio (279), Georgia (193), Louisiana (179), Illinois (171), Arizona (171), Michigan (146), Virginia (132) and Pennsylvania (121), per the CDC.

EXPERTS REVEAL HOW TO AVOID DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE AS NYC OUTBREAK KILLS 5

The remaining states have fewer than 100 cases each.

Candida auris is a type of yeast that can cause serious infections, primarily in hospitals, nursing homes and other healthcare settings.

The fungus, which can survive on surfaces for prolonged periods, is "highly transmissible between patients through contact with contaminated surfaces or objects," the CDC states. It can spread through contaminated items such as bedrails, doorknobs and shared medical equipment.

C. auris can also be spread by people who carry the fungus but do not show symptoms, known as "colonization."

California accounts for 873 cases — roughly one-quarter of the country’s total.

Clinical cases do not necessarily represent infections. The CDC defines a clinical case as detection of C. auris in a specimen collected during the normal course of medical care.

Some clinical specimens can come from sites where the presence of C. auris may represent colonization rather than a true infection.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The health effects of the fungus can range from colonization without symptoms to potentially deadly invasive infections, including bloodstream infections.

Those most at risk of infection include patients with severe underlying medical conditions. In particular, those who use breathing tubes, feeding tubes, IVs or catheters are more vulnerable, as are those who are hospitalized frequently or for long periods of time.

People without those risk factors are unlikely to become colonized with C. auris or develop an infection.

Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst and clinical professor of medicine at NYU Langone, said he considers C. auris an "emerging problem of great concern."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"It is resistant to multiple antifungal drugs, and it tends to spread in hospital settings, including on equipment being used on immunocompromised and semi-immunocompromised patients, such as ventilators and catheters," he previously told Fox News Digital.

"Unfortunately, symptoms such as fever, chills and aches may be ubiquitous, and it can be mistaken for other infections."

Invasive C. auris infections have been associated with mortality rates of 30% to 72%, although most affected patients are already seriously ill. This can make it difficult to determine how often the fungus is a direct cause of death.

Candida auris can be difficult to treat because it is often resistant to antifungal medications, leading the CDC to classify the fungus as an "urgent antimicrobial-resistance threat."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

More than 90% of U.S. samples are resistant to fluconazole, a common antifungal treatment. Echinocandins, another family of antifungals, are currently the main treatment option for C. auris, although some strains are resistant to all three main classes of antifungals.

CLICK HERE TO 

"Major research" is ongoing to develop new treatments, according to Siegel.

"This is part of a much larger problem of emerging antibiotic resistance in the U.S. and around the world," the physician previously cautioned. "At the same time, sterilization and disinfection measures in hospitals can be very helpful."

Fox News Digital's Angelica Stabile contributed reporting.

If you've started shopping for a VPN, you've probably come across the terms shared IP and dedicated IP. While they may sound technical, the difference is actually pretty straightforward, and choosing the right one can make your online experience smoother.

Both options encrypt your internet traffic and protect your connection, but they serve different purposes. One prioritizes maximum privacy by blending your activity with thousands of other users. The other gives you your own personal IP address, making it easier to access certain online services without additional verification.

Here's what each option does, and how to decide which one is right for you.

What is a shared VPN IP?

A shared IP is exactly what it sounds like: multiple VPN users connect through the same public IP address. When dozens, or even hundreds, of people are using the same IP at different times, it becomes much harder for websites or other observers to associate online activity with any one individual. That's one reason shared IPs are the default choice for most VPN services.

The trade-off is that shared IPs can sometimes trigger CAPTCHAs, blocked logins or extra verification if a website sees too much activity coming from the same address. That is one reason some people look for ways to fix a VPN that keeps getting blocked.

What is a dedicated VPN IP?

A dedicated IP is reserved exclusively for you. No one else using the VPN service shares that IP address. Because your IP remains consistent every time you connect, websites and online services recognize it as the same connection. That can make certain activities more convenient, especially if you regularly access accounts that use IP-based security checks.

For example, some businesses only allow employees to log in from approved IP addresses. Using a dedicated IP allows your company to "whitelist" this IP so that you can log in smoothly every time.

A dedicated IP can also reduce the number of verification requests you receive when signing in to banking websites, business software, or other accounts that flag unfamiliar locations. If you've ever been annoyed by a CAPTCHA (e.g., "which one of these photos is of a motorcycle?") when trying to log in from a new location, you'll appreciate the consistency of a dedicated IP address.

Some people might argue that letting your VPN provider assign you a dedicated IP inherently makes you less private. This is where your choice of VPN provider is important. A reputable VPN provider distributes IP addresses with a zero-knowledge allocation system, meaning not even the provider can trace it back to you.

With this kind of dedicated IP, you still receive the privacy and encryption benefits of a VPN; the difference is simply that your VPN IP belongs only to you.
