Safe and Beautiful Task Force , despite violent crime being at a 30-year low . While homicides are down this year, violent crime is actually up compared to 2025, according to data from the city .

Sponsor Message

"I worry about these troops standing on street corners fading into the background, and people starting to accept this as just a fact of life," says Joseph Nunn, counsel at the Brennan Center's Liberty and National Security program. "Armed military personnel standing on the street corners in an American city should never be normal."

toggle caption Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America

Nunn says that the U.S. was the first to establish the modern democratic norm of divorcing the military and civilian policing, and points to a line in the Declaration of Independence condemning King George III for keeping standing armies among the population in times of peace.

Multiple studies have since found that the National Guard presence in D.C. has had no effect on violent crime, although there has been a decrease in opportunistic crimes like petty theft and vehicle break-ins.

"They have been deployed to our communities under false pretenses," says Monica Hopkins, Director at the ACLU of D.C. "It's not a genuine emergency as to why these forces were deployed."

All guard members in D.C. have been deputized by the U.S. Marshals Service to temporarily grant them certain law enforcement powers, although they cannot carry out arrests. However they can detain people, and are issued a handgun — which is unusual for a domestic deployment.

"Americans should be concerned about this progression toward the use of the military in situations like the midterms — or in other situations that we may have not even thought about — that will essentially impose the will of the people commanding those forces on our fellow citizens," says Ret. Maj. Gen. Steven Lepper, part of a group of former military lawyers who have sent a report to Congress about their concerns.

The White House did not directly respond to a list of questions NPR asked about such concerns and for clarification about why the extension of the D.C. deployment for another two and a half years was deemed necessary, but instead linked to a press release from the U.S. Marshals Service touting the success of the Joint Task Force, without providing evidence.

Sponsor Message

The Joint Task Force in D.C. did not immediately respond to NPR's request for comment about the one year mark and its mission going forward.

Troop numbers have steadily increased

Throughout the past year, the number of National Guard members deployed to D.C. – which started at around 800 – has steadily increased more than five-fold to around 4,700. The most recent influx came as part of a "summer surge" of law enforcement announced by federal officials ahead of the America 250 events in the city. There has been no indication that the number will decrease significantly in the fall.

Loading...

A vast majority of the guard members in D.C. are part of the mission voluntarily, meaning they raised their hand for the deployment. Such deployments offer extra pay for guard members.

Nunn, of the Brennan Center, points out the consistent and gradual increase of troops is part of what has allowed for their normalization.

"I think there's the risk of people getting used to the troops' presence – period. But there's also the risk of people getting used to the number of troops growing and never decreasing," he says.

Not only have the sheer numbers increased over time, but also the number of states sending them. In the early days of the deployment, the makeup of personnel largely came from the D.C. National Guard and a few Republican-led states.

Loading...

But as the year went on more Republican-led states, as well Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, began contributing. Several Democratic-led states contributed troops as part of the "America 250" celebrations, but they've remained in D.C. and have been counted by the Joint Task Force as part of the "summer surge." Those same states had previously argued in court that the mission was dangerous and illegal.

Still in legal limbo

Like the rest of Trump's controversial domestic deployments of the National Guard, the D.C. deployment has been challenged in court.

Almost immediately, D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued to end the deployment. Nearly two dozen states — all of which are led by Democrats — filed an amicus brief in support of that lawsuit. Several of those states, like Michigan and Hawaii, are now contributing troops to the city.

In November, a judge ruled to end the deployment in the city, calling it "unlawful." But the administration appealed the ruling, and weeks later, a Federal Appeals Court ruled the deployment could continue while the court decides the case.

Sponsor Message

In the ruling, the judges wrote that Washington, D.C.'s unique status as a federal district and not a state allows President Trump to largely control the deployment of troops in the city. For that reason, they said that the Trump administration is likely to win the overall case.

That reasoning has frustrated many local residents and officials, loudening calls for D.C. statehood.

"Not only do we have no recourse, but we cannot hold anyone accountable," says Hopkins of the ACLU of D.C., one of many organizations that have been pushing for statehood. "We deserve to hold our officials accountable, and we can't do that here."

A ballooning cost

All of the troops in D.C. are deployed under Title 32 status, meaning they are federally funded, although they are still technically under the control of their respective governors (or the president, in the case of D.C. guard).

A report last year by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office estimated that this deployment costs about $600 a day per guard member, meaning at the current troop levels, it costs roughly $3 million per day.

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images North America

The Pentagon recently told Congress extending the deployment will cost an additional $1.4 billion. A recent estimate from the nonpartisan, nonprofit watchdog Project on Government Oversight found the total cost of the deployment until 2029 to be around $3 billion.

That steep cost is coming at the expense of other priorities for the National Guard, says retired Gen. Randy Manner, who was once a top official in the National Guard at the Pentagon.

"This is actually negatively impacting readiness because those funds are usually used to pay for fuel, for food, for lodging, and for training exercises for our National Guard. So this is not free money, even though the president views it that way," Manner says. "We're robbing our nation's readiness to be able to pay for the president's deployment."

Sponsor Message

A recent emergency supplemental funding request that the White House submitted to Congress, primarily to cover the cost of the ongoing war in Iran, included around $1 billion earmarked for the National Guard's deployment in D.C.

Concerns about the elections

Trump has repeatedly touted the success of the deployment in D.C., falsely claiming that the city has reached "no crime" or "almost no crime." He has said he would like to replicate the task force elsewhere.

There are already other similar anti-crime National Guard deployments in Memphis and New Orleans, both in states with Republican governors who welcomed them. Many legal and military experts are concerned that there will be more such deployments to come, particularly heading into an election season.

"You don't need to have boots in your streets or in your community, for you to have a stake here. It's something that affects all of us," Beau Tremitiere, counsel at Protect Democracy, a nonprofit legal center that has been tracking the D.C. deployment.

toggle caption Finn Gomez/Getty Images North America

He worries the normalization of a longstanding domestic deployment in a non-emergency situation could allow Americans to accept it as the new norm.

"A normalized, ongoing, years-long deployment in D.C. makes it much easier for the government to attempt to deploy troops in other communities. There are legal nuances as to why it's not an easy copy and paste from the D.C. mission to elsewhere. But the broader point is still very much true," he says.

Ret. Maj. Gen. Lepper has been working with other former military lawyers to cue in lawmakers and other officials about their major worries about these deployments — namely around the midterm elections. There are very clear and strict laws that prevent the military being used around polling places, but Lepper and his colleagues have been tracking various executive orders from the president that could challenge such laws. They recently submitted a report to Congress expressing their concerns.

"We have described how we've connected those dots, and we've sounded the alarm to hopefully wake up our fellow citizens to the idea that we may be seeing something like this in November," Maj. Gen. Lepper says.

Sponsor Message

Republicans have dismissed such concerns as alarmist. In May, Trump announced on social media that he would launch an "Election Integrity Army" this year, but did not offer specifics.

Maj. Gen. Lepper says he worries that Americans are banking on the idea that members of the military will reject illegal orders if such an occasion does arise, but he says that's not something soldiers are trained to do.

"We all sort of cling to the hope that the military will ultimately save us from efforts to use it in illegal ways inside our country. We should abandon that hope," he says.

World.title: Over 29,000 people call for U.S. Ambassador Hoekstra to be removed from Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A petition set to be presented in the House of Commons this fall calls on the federal government to declare U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra persona non grata and remove him from Canada.

The online petition accuses Hoekstra of making statements that undermine the Canada-U.S. relationship and intervening in Canadian political discourse in a manner inconsistent with diplomatic protocol.

It says the Liberal government should also direct a parliamentary committee to review U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian affairs.

More than 29,000 people have signed the petition, which was launched by a woman from Calgary and will be presented in Parliament by Green Party Leader Elizabeth May.

WATCH | Hoekstra on trade talks: U.S ambassador to Canada defends U.S. tariffs, CUSMA negotiation strategy | Duration 16:46 On the eve of his country's 250th birthday, U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra discussed tariffs, CUSMA negotiations and those 51st state jabs with Rebecca Zandbergen, host of CBC's Ottawa Morning.

Hoekstra made headlines in June by saying that Canada's annexation by the United States would be a great topic of discussion for Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump.

A persona non grata declaration is a tool in the UN's Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations that allows a country to strip diplomatic immunity from an individual and force them to leave.

World.title: Canada, U.S. trade officials mapping out potential deal to pitch to Trump next week: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and his American counterpart are aiming to present U.S. President Donald Trump a path to a potential trade deal as early as Monday, CBC News has learned.

Sources who were recently briefed on the matter say the hope is the joint proposal can be presented to Trump at least a day before the president's latest tariff deadline.

That timeline would give Trump the space to make a final decision before new 50 per cent levies on hundreds of Canadian imports are scheduled to take effect on Aug. 19.

CBC News is not naming the sources as they weren't authorized to speak publicly.

Trying to extend the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement

LeBlanc is meeting with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Tuesday, marking the third time in three weeks the pair has met face to face, LeBlanc's office confirmed.

LeBlanc had initially planned to travel to Washington on Monday, but his flight to the U.S. capital was diverted back to Montreal Monday afternoon due to severe weather.

Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, meanwhile, spent all day Monday in Washington meeting with officials from the Office of the United States Trade Representative.

Charette and LeBlanc will not comment on the negotiations before or after the 1:30 p.m. ET meeting, according to the minister's office.

In addition to trying to dissuade Americans from levying new tariffs, LeBlanc and Charette are looking for relief on sectoral tariffs the U.S. has slapped on Canadian steel, aluminum, lumber and autos.

Canada is also hoping the ongoing trade talks between the two countries will result in an extension of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) after the Trump administration declined to renew the deal back in July.

This third meeting between LeBlanc and Greer comes ahead of an Aug. 19 deadline, at which point the U.S. plans to put 50 per cent tariffs on about five per cent of Canadian exports to the country. The targeted goods range from alcohol to hockey sticks to cement.

When announcing the Aug. 19 tariffs, the U.S. raised a number of trade irritants , including Canada's retaliation against U.S. trade policy with the removal of U.S. alcohol from provincial store shelves and alleged Canadian discrimination against U.S. motor vehicles and dairy.

According to U.S. Census Bureau figures, the alcohol bans in every province, save Alberta and Saskatchewan, have resulted in a $360-million US drop in wine exports to Canada in 2025 from the previous year, along with a $150-million US drop in spirit exports.

Conservatives push Carney for results

When negotiating with the White House, Canada should ensure it's in the strongest position possible, Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner said Tuesday.

The Calgary MP also argued Prime Minister Mark Carney has been in office for more than a year, and has yet to secure a trade agreement with the Trump administration.

"The person who needs to be held to account in the domestic capacity in Canada is Mark Carney," Rempel Garner said in Ottawa. "He has to deliver on his promise to Canadians — that's why Canadians lent him their vote."

Her comments come two days after Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wrote to Carney, calling on him to show some "backbone" as trade negotiations ramp up.

Poilievre said Canadians deserve a "good deal" that includes zero tariffs on softwood lumber, an end to sectoral tariffs on steel and aluminum, a tariff-free auto pact and full exemption to Buy America rules on infrastructure projects at all levels of government.

"No more pursuing policies of a managed decline at home. No more caving," Poilievre wrote.

World.title: Alberta widow calls for policy review after Air Canada temporarily loses husband's ashes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Twyla Shannahan says she never should have been separated from her husband’s ashes on a flight from Alberta to Newfoundland.

The Alberta widow is calling for an investigation after Air Canada temporarily lost her late husband’s cremated remains after she was forced to place them in a checked bag, rather than carry them on board.

“This is not luggage … this is a human being,” Shannahan said. “This is my husband, and he wasn’t treated the way he should have been.”

When Shannahan’s husband died in February, she knew she wanted to scatter his ashes in the ocean and made plans to bring his remains back east to his home province.

The couple had spent two decades travelling the world together but Newfoundland always had his heart, she said.

"We had talked about what would happen if something ever happened, and that's what he wanted,” she said.

“He wanted to go back home, so that was my job. I had to get him home."

Shannahan, a resident of Webster, Alta., was eager to honour his wishes. After making arrangements for a memorial with his relatives back east, she booked a June 10 flight from Edmonton to St. John’s.

Shannahan said she had gathered all the required documentation and had called Air Canada weeks before to ensure she met protocol to carry the ashes in her carry-on luggage.

However, when she arrived to check in at Edmonton International Airport, an Air Canada agent told her the remains had to go into a checked bag due to "new rules."

Shannahan said she felt sick but reluctantly followed their orders so she could board her flight.

'Where is my husband?'

When she arrived in St. John’s, one of her bags — the one with the remains inside — was missing.

"My soul just dropped right out of me,” Shannahan recalled. “I said like, 'I failed him. I had one job and I failed him.'"

“I just dropped to my knees instantly. I couldn’t believe this was happening. Like where is my husband?”

After waiting overnight for Air Canada to open, she learned the ashes had been sent to Montreal. When the airline offered to courier them to her, she insisted on collecting them herself.

"I got off that airplane, my husband didn't, and there's a problem with the system,” she said.

“If I can do anything for Lawrence, I'd like to hopefully help make changes to that. This shouldn't happen to another family."

WATCH | Alberta woman calls for accountability after ashes delayed: 'Just regular luggage to them': Widow upset after Air Canada temporarily loses husband’s ashes | Duration 3:18 A Canadian airline temporarily lost the remains of an Alberta woman's late husband. She was travelling to Newfoundland to spread his ashes in the ocean. When she checked in for her flight, Air Canada told her the cremated remains would have to be transported in a checked bag. But when Twyla Shannahan arrived in Newfoundland, the bag containing his ashes was missing. Eventually the remains were recovered, but she continues to seek answers from Air Canada.

In a statement to CBC News, the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority (CATSA) — the federal agency responsible for airport security screening — said that while cremated remains are generally permitted in carry-on luggage, this depends on whether security screening can be successfully carried out.

Because dense materials like metal or stone urns can block X-ray machines, CATSA officials said that unresolved screening alarms may require passengers to check the container with their airline in accordance with Transport Canada regulations.

“We recognize how sensitive and emotional such a situation can be,” CATSA officials said in a statement.

“We are committed to treating passengers and their loved ones with dignity and respect while ensuring compliance with the regulations.”

In a statement to CBC News, officials with Air Canada also confirmed that cremated remains are accepted as carry-on “provided they meet applicable security requirements.”

“We regret that the customer's checked baggage containing the cremated remains was delayed,” the airline wrote.

Documentation provided by Shannahan shows that Air Canada, in its initial email response to her complaint, offered her an apology and a $200 travel voucher as a “gesture of goodwill for the stress caused.”

She said a digital coupon requiring her to spend more money with the airline felt offensive.

She remains dissatisfied with the airline's formal response, which she felt improperly blamed Transport Canada and treated her husband’s remains as merely a piece of replaceable luggage.

She successfully scattered her husband's ashes in the ocean in Newfoundland as she had planned but said she still wants answers.

In a formal complaint she shared with CBC News, Shannahan asked Air Canada to escalate the case to someone with the authority to investigate it properly and provide meaningful compensation.

She is calling for a systemic audit of Air Canada's policies and procedures regarding the transport of human remains, hoping policy changes will prevent this from happening to another grieving family.

She said she has already heard from other travellers who have faced similar mishaps.

“A grieving passenger shouldn’t have to navigate this,” she said. “I am still devastated by it.”

World.title: Europe is getting hit with its 5th heat wave since May — and sunken Nazi warships are resurfacing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nazi German warships scuttled in the Danube River during the Second World War are resurfacing as water levels plunge — a striking sign of the extreme heat and drought gripping Europe this summer.

The fifth heat wave since May is set to scorch western Europe beginning Tuesday, with parts of Spain, France and Italy nearing 40 C before the heat dome pushes temperatures further above average in central and northern Europe.

The European Union's Copernicus climate monitoring service confirmed Monday that June and July were the hottest on record in western Europe. The period saw an estimated 25,000 heat-related deaths.

The sweltering heat has contributed to devastating wildfires and pushed water levels in vital waterways, including the Danube, to record lows.

Climate scientists say the exposed wrecks are a vivid sign of a much broader problem: fossil fuel-driven climate change is intensifying heat and drought, with consequences for wildfires, agriculture, shipping and energy systems across Europe.

"If we keep emitting greenhouse gases at the rate we're doing now, then this is only going to get worse," Richard Allan, a climate scientist at England's University of Reading, told CBC News.

And what we're seeing this summer, he says, is just the "tip of the iceberg" for the effects of global heating.

WATCH | Fossil fuel emissions made Canada's wildfires more likely, study says: Wildfires are more intense, more likely — and humans are to blame: study | Duration 2:05 Climate change caused by fossil fuel use made July's wildfires in parts of Canada twice as likely to occur, researchers say. The new World Weather Attribution study also predicts more frequent — and more intense — wildfires will be the new normal.

What the drying Danube reveals

Historians estimate that the Nazis scuttled up to 200 warships near the Serbian city of Prahovo in September 1944 in an effort to stop advancing Soviet forces.

The New York Times reports that one or two or the wrecks might normally be visible in summer, but residents have counted about a dozen this year.

Elsewhere, the drying Danube has revealed a German military motorcycle in Hungary, an unexploded 700-kilogram British bomb in Slovakia and what are believed to be the ancient remains of a mammoth in Bulgaria.

People view the wreckage of a German warship from the Second World War that emerged from beneath the Danube River, near Prahovo, not far from the Djerdap II dam between the border of Romania and Serbia. (Darko Vojinovic/The Associated Press)

But the extremely low water levels have raised much more urgent concerns for several countries along Europe's second-longest river.

The Danube originates in Germany and runs 2,850 kilometres through nine other countries — Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine — before emptying into the Black Sea. Its tributaries extend into several other countries.

The Romanian government restricted water use for crop irrigation last month and has taken steps to keep its only working nuclear power plant running, including blowing up a rock obstruction to redirect the river's flow.

Hungary switched a turbine back on at its only nuclear power station Monday after citizens and companies voluntarily curbed their power use last week because the river's flow was too low to cool reactors.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said Friday the "succession of unprecedented events," from the extreme heat to the severe water shortage and state of the Danube, has more people realizing "that we must take much better care of our natural resources, our water, our land and our clean air than we have done so far."

PHOTOS | Here's what the Danube River looks like as water levels drop amid record hot summer:

'Clear example' of climate change

In June and July 1944, in the months before German forces sank their warships in the Danube, temperatures in Europe were around average — and perhaps slightly cooler than normal — compared to the 1991-2020 average, according to NASA's National Centers for Environmental Information.

During the same period this year, the average surface air temperature across the western half of the continent was 2.79 C higher, Copernicus reported this week. Much of eastern Europe, including areas of the Danube River basin, was also much warmer than average.

"This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at Copernicus, said in its press release.

By the time a major river system such as the Danube reaches levels this low, Allan said, damage to forests and agriculture has already occurred.

"These big river systems are the last to go," he said. "That's like the end point in the sense that soils have already dried out, vegetation has already dried out and we've seen these massive wildfires."

Allan said next year could be even worse.

He said the emergence of what's been dubbed a super El Niño — a particularly stronger cyclical warming in the southern Pacific Ocean that affects global weather patterns — has not been a factor in the heat that has punished Europe and much of the Northern Hemisphere so far this summer.

Two of the German warship wrecks that have emerged in the stretch of the Danube river in Serbia. Residents of the nearby village of Prahovo say you might normally see one or two of the sunken vessels in summer but there are as many as 12 visible this year. (Darko Vojinovic/The Associated Press)

"Usually ... the planet will be warmer the year following the emergence of El Niño," he said. "So, we can expect very high, unprecedented global temperatures in 2027."

Those effects, Allan said, would come on top of the warming already being driven by climate-harming greenhouse gas emissions.

"If we keep emitting greenhouse gases at the rate we're doing now," he said, "this is only, like, the first signs of what's going to happen in the future."

World.title: Netflix's Love Is Blind is coming to Canada — and Canadians are already tagging their friends
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Is Canada ready to find out if love is truly blind? If you’re single and interested, the pods are soon opening on this side of the border.

Netflix announced Tuesday that its reality dating series Love is Blind — which has been a streaming hit in the U.S. — is on its way to Canada.

If you didn't fall into a deep binge when it launched in February 2020 — here's how it works.

A bunch of single people enter pods. They'll talk, flirt, get to know each other, date one another and, apparently, fall in love. Sight unseen.

That's right. Couples, sitting on opposite sides of a wall, get engaged without seeing each other.

Once they're engaged, they meet face to face and things get real. They jet off on a lavish trip with the other matches, where they put their chemistry to the test.

Then they move in, meet the family and on their expedited wedding day, they'll make the final choice — say "I do" or walk away.

Canadians already tagging their friends

Netflix announced the spinoff on Instagram and Canadian fans of the show were quick to make their feelings heard. Some are even tagging their friends in the comments.

"This is crazy. Should I do it??" one said. "Anticipating all the "No way, eh!'s" convos thru the walls 😜," commented another.

Others took it a step further. "Opening my phone to a text that my friend signed me up for LOVE IS BLIND CANADA?????????????" one wrote on X.

The announcement comes as several other reality shows are getting a Canadian treatment. Big Brother Canada is back this summer on CTV and Crave after it was cancelled by Global in 2024. And Jersey Shore's Canadian counterpart, Canada Shore, just wrapped its second season of filming in Kelowna, B.C.

Casting is open

Think you're up for Love is Blind, too? Casting is open and the show is being produced by Insight Productions, the company behind Big Brother Canada and Canada Shore.

"I'm one of the gazillion Day 1 die-hards who knows how brilliant this format is," Insight co-chief content officer Erin Brock wrote in a media release.

Netflix announced Tuesday that its hit reality dating series Love is Blind is coming to Canada. (Netflix)

"I'm beyond excited to delve into this with a Canadian cast who are genuinely open to finding their soulmates and to share their unique stories and authentic experiences."

To be eligible, you'll have to be at least 19 when you apply and a Canadian citizen or permanent resident of Canada as of January 2027.

Since its launch, Netflix has done 10 seasons of the U.S. version and launched spinoffs in places like Japan, Brazil, Sweden, the U.K., Mexico, Germany, Argentina, Italy and France. It also ran a version called Love is Blind: Habibi featuring singles from from across the Middle East and North Africa.

In the U.S., it's hosted by Vanessa and Nick Lachey. A Canadian host hasn't been announced.

World.title: Wrong bear killed by RCMP after girl attacked in Maple Ridge, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Officials say they are still searching for the black bear that attacked a three-year-old girl in Maple Ridge, B.C., on Sunday, after confirming a bear RCMP killed wasn't the one that did it.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service said the young girl was playing on the deck in her family's back yard when the attack happened. One of her parents intervened and chased the animal away.

Maple Ridge RCMP said what they believed was the bear returned to the area several times that day while police were on site and officers shot it "to protect public safety" after it showed signs of aggression.

Police said it fled into a wooded area after it was hit.

The bear was recovered and a necropsy was performed on it, according to the Ministry of Environment and Parks, which showed it hadn't been the bear responsible for the attack.

The girl was taken to hospital with non-life-altering injuries, according to RCMP.

A B.C. Conservation Officer Service predator attack team is still on site and the public is asked to avoid the area.

RCMP 'aren't bear experts,' says vet

Wildlife veterinarian Ken Macquisten said he wasn't surprised to hear the wrong bear was killed.

"The RCMP definitely aren't bear experts," he said.

He said police officers aren't trained in bear behaviour like conservation officers are, and that the caliber of bullets they use generally won't kill a bear on first shot.

"They are more likely to injure the bear than to kill it," he said. "That presents a real problem in itself because an injured bear, of course, is a more dangerous bear than a bear that's not injured."

WATCH | Bear that attacked girl in Maple Ridge still on the loose: Bear that attacked B.C. girl still on the loose after wrong bear killed | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 6:32 The black bear that attacked a three-year-old girl in Maple Ridge, B.C., is still on the loose after officials confirmed a bear killed by RCMP following the attack was not the same animal.

Lesley Fox, executive director of wildlife conservation group The Fur-Bearers, said while urgency matters in these kinds of situations, so does identification.

"We really need to make good decisions under pressure and having proper evidence, following a scientific method and ensuring that we are dealing with the specific individual animal."

Fox said police are not equipped to tranquilize wild animals, or contain them, long enough for conservation officers to arrive.

Both Macquisten and Fox said more conservation officers are needed so they can be the ones to respond to wildlife calls.

RCMP say decision not 'taken lightly'

Maple Ridge RCMP said in a statement that officers believed they had the correct bear and "made the decision to dispatch the animal to prevent further injury or loss of life."

"The loss of any wildlife is significant, and decisions of this nature are never taken lightly," the statement reads.

First responders at the scene of the bear attack in Maple Ridge on Sunday. (Shane MacKichan)

"Thankfully encounters with bears are not a routine experience for our officers, however, are more common during seasonal bear activity when working in partnership with our [Conservation Officer Service] partners."

The department said it always reviews incidents to determine if there is other training or equipment that could be used to better serve officers and the public.

The Conservation Officer Service said in a statement that predator attacks are the highest priority calls and that it works collaboratively with law enforcement partners across the province.

World.title: A murderer's truck sits in Sask. RCMP cold storage. The Crown says it's time to destroy it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's been 20 years since Curtis Dagenais murdered two Saskatchewan RCMP officers and injured a third, but later this month he will be back in court in Saskatoon.

Why? It's about his truck.

The 1986 blue GMC 1500 is still sitting in cold storage at RCMP headquarters in Regina. The Crown is applying to have it forfeited so it can be destroyed, but Dagenais is opposed.

Dagenais was in the truck on July 6, 2006, when three RCMP constables tried to arrest him in Spiritwood, about 147 kilometres north of Saskatoon. He drove off and led the officers, who were in two separate vehicles, on a chase over rural roads.

RCMP constables Marc Bourdages and Robin Cameron were in one vehicle, which rammed into the side of Dagenais's truck and pushed it up against a tree. Dagenais shot them both in the head and they died of their injuries in hospital.

Const. Michelle Knopp arrived on the scene just moments after her colleagues were shot. Dagenais shot and injured her.

Const. Robin Cameron, left, and Const. Marc Bourdages died in hospital after being shot while on duty on July 7, 2006. (RCMP)

A jury convicted Dagenais in 2009 of two counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder. He received three sentences of life in prison with no chance of parole for 25 years (the parole eligibility date is calculated from the date of his arrest on July 17, 2006).

He appealed the convictions to the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, which dismissed his appeal in a ruling issued in 2012.

Why is the truck issue in court now?

The question of why the forfeiture application wasn't made before was posed in court to Scott Bartlett, the Crown prosecutor who brought the application.

"I really can't answer that, other than it slipped through the cracks," Bartlett said.

Bartlett is one of the two prosecutors who ran the original trial in 2009. He first made the application for forfeiture in 2021, when it was heard by the trial judge, Justice Gerald Allbright, who is now retired.

(Bartlett said he is no longer employed full-time by public prosecutions, but still works under fee-for-service contracts as an agent for the Attorney General.)

Crown prosecutors Al Johnson, centre left, and Scott Bartlett speak to media following the verdict in Curtis Dagenais's trial in 2009 in Saskatoon. (Geoff Howe/The Canadian Press)

At the hearing in 2021, Dagenais said he didn't want the truck destroyed because he maintains he's innocent and the bullet holes in the truck can help prove it.

He said he had asked Innocence Canada — a non-profit organization that advocates for the exoneration of people who are wrongfully convicted — to help him.

Dagenais was on Innocence Canada's waiting list, and Allbright agreed to give Dagenais more time to see whether the organization would take on his case.

Allbright adjourned the Crown's forfeiture application and said it could be renewed any time after Nov. 30, 2022.

"If at that time, no progress has been made in the advancement of Mr. Dagenais's application to Innocence Canada, I am of the view that it would be appropriate for the court to make the forfeiture order which the Crown seeks," Allbright wrote in a fiat.

A court exhibit photo from Curtis Dagenais's trial in 2009 shows the front of an RCMP vehicle after it smashed into the side of Dagenais's blue truck. (Geoff Howe/The Canadian Press)

Crown renews application

The Crown brought the application forward again in May of this year, and a hearing was held in Saskatoon Court of King's Bench on June 25 — this time, in front of Justice Daryl Labach.

Dagenais, 61, attended by video conference from Saskatchewan Penitentiary, wearing a blue T-shirt and glasses. His short-cropped hair is greying at the temples.

Bartlett again represented the Crown, while Dagenais did not have a lawyer and represented himself.

Like he did in 2021, Dagenais said he was opposed to the forfeiture and destruction of the truck.

"I would like to keep it preserved," he said.

"There's a couple holes in that truck that can't be properly re-examined by photograph."

A view from inside the RCMP vehicle that struck Curtis Dagenais's truck on July 7, 2006, and the holes in the windshield from bullets fired that day. (Geoff Howe/Canadian Press)

Labach noted that Innocence Canada had filed a letter with the court indicating they were not representing Dagenais and would not be pursuing any kind of application on his behalf.

Dagenais asked for another adjournment to see if he can get a lawyer to help him oppose the forfeiture application.

"How long are you suggesting it should be adjourned for?" Labach asked.

"I don't know. The wheels seem to roll really slow around here," Dagenais said.

Labach noted that Dagenais's "only opportunity" to reopen his case would be an appeal to the minister of justice. He asked Bartlett for his thoughts.

Bartlett said Saskatchewan Justice has received "numerous requests, submissions" alleging Dagenais was wrongfully convicted and suggesting there was new evidence.

"Nothing of that has ever materialized or come to pass, in our opinion, and of course nothing has changed today," Bartlett said.

Labach said he was prepared to grant Dagenais one more adjournment to give him the chance to get a lawyer.

The forfeiture hearing is scheduled for Aug. 31.

World.title: Ryan Wedding's accused Canadian money launderer agrees to U.S. extradition
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Toronto-area jeweller accused of laundering hundreds of millions of dollars for Ryan Wedding's purported drug-smuggling network has agreed to be extradited to the U.S. to stand trial.

Still, Rolan Sokolovski's lawyer insists his client is presumed innocent and will fight the charges he's facing.

Lawyer Scott K. Fenton confirmed in an email to CBC News that Sokolovski appeared in a downtown Toronto court earlier Tuesday and consented to be extradited several months early. Sokolovski had been scheduled to appear for an extradition hearing in December.

"It should be noted that consenting to extradition is neither an admission of wrongdoing nor an acknowledgement of the strength of the case against him," Fenton wrote.

Ryan Wedding, who was born in Thunder Bay, Ont., is pictured in an undated photo. (U.S. Embassy Mexico)

U.S. prosecutors allege Sokolovski served as a "de facto bank" for Wedding by moving drug money and procuring the longtime fugitive luxury goods, including an ultra-rare $13-million US Mercedes CLK-GTR Roadster.

The Lithuanian-born Sokolovski, 38, was arrested in Toronto last November, as part of the FBI and RCMP's joint takedown of Wedding's network. The former professional poker player was denied bail and has been held in custody at Ontario's Maplehurst jail.

According to court documents, Sokolovski, who went by the aliases Sushi and Applepie, is accused of using cryptocurrency platforms and his Toronto-area business, Diamond Tsar, to launder proceeds for Wedding's transnational criminal enterprise.

Sokolovski faces conspiracy charges related to drug trafficking and money laundering in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles.

WATCH | Sokolovski bought an ultra-rare Mercedes, allegedly for then-fugitive Wedding: We found out who bought a $13M Mercedes now linked to fugitive Ryan Wedding | Duration 2:05 As the FBI continues its hunt for Ryan Wedding, the former Olympian turned alleged cocaine kingpin, CBC News has learned how he may have used a $13-million US Mercedes as part of a global money laundering scheme.

He's also accused of designing a bejewelled necklace for Atna Ohna, a Montreal-based alleged hitman for Wedding's network, as a reward for his purported role in the murder of an FBI witness.

Sokolovski's lawyer, Fenton said his client "is presumed innocent and intends to contest the allegations in the California courts."

The federal justice minister still must decide whether to formally surrender Sokolovski to U.S. authorities.

The U.S. Department of Justice has, since 2024, indicted at least 34 purported members and associates of Wedding's drug ring, which authorities say moved tonnes of cocaine and fentanyl across North America and carried out dozens of killings.

Wedding, a former Team Canada Olympic snowboarder, was captured in Mexico in January and swiftly transferred to California. He remains in U.S. custody, but public prison records do not list Wedding's current whereabouts.

Sokolovski, left, Deepak Paradkar, middle, and Gursewak Singh Bal, right, were arrested on Nov. 18, 2025 in connection with their alleged roles in the transnational criminal network linked to Canadian Ryan Wedding. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California; CBC)

Among the three men arrested in Ontario last fall as part of the investigation dubbed "Operation Giant Slalom" — a nod to Wedding's previous career — Sokolovski is the first to consent to his extradition.

Gursewak Singh Bal, a Canadian crime blogger also facing U.S. federal charges in connection with the sprawling conspiracy, has an extradition hearing set for Dec. 10.

Singh Bal operated the Dirty News, a website that U.S. authorities said was used to set up the murder of Quebec-born Jonathan Acebedo-Garcia, the FBI witness shot in the head while having lunch in Medellín, Colombia.

A court sketch shows Ryan Wedding wearing a tan jumpsuit next to his lawyer Anthony Colombo. U.S. Magistrate Judge John D. Early presided over that January 2026 hearing. (Bill Robles/CBC)

Singh Bal's lawyer Trevin David declined to comment on the case on Tuesday.

Prominent criminal lawyer Deepak Paradkar — who U.S. prosecutors allege accepted "cash drops" and a luxury watch while serving as a high-level fixer in Wedding's network — continues to fight extradition. Paradkar has denied wrongdoing and Ontario's top court rejected a bid to overturn his release on bail.

The prosecutor's office in L.A. has told CBC News that Wedding is scheduled to stand trial twice later this year, for two separate indictments filed in 2024 and 2025, while the Thunder Bay, Ont., native was considered a fugitive.

The first of two trials is currently set to begin Oct. 27.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: De la Espriella sworn in as Colombia’s new president
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in in Colombia’s third largest city, Cali, under extreme security precautions.

De la Espriella was sworn in by the president of Congress, Senator Honorio Henriquez of the far-right Democratic Center party in the theater of the private University of Santiago de Cali.

The first part of the ceremony was attended by the Spanish King Felipe VI, multiple heads of state from Latin America and more than 60 ambassadors.

After being sworn in, De la Espriella went to the nearby Pichincha Battalion to assume the supreme command of the armed forces and hold his first speech as president.

The president vowed the security forces that he would be “an essential part of the miracle country” and vowed that at the end of his four-year mandate “authority will be felt in every corner of the country.”

De la Espriella also promised that “nobody will be persecuted for his opinions” and warned members of the “regime” of former President Gustavo Petro he would cooperate with “other States,” suggesting they could be extradited.

Both ceremonies were boycotted by Petro’s leftist political party, the Historic Pact, which organized political rallies elsewhere in Cali, and in the cities of Bogota and Barranquilla.

In Barranquilla, Senator Ivan Cepeda stressed the left does not recognize the incoming government because of De la Espriella’s US citizenship and his alleged debts with the US Department of Justice.

“De la Espriella, who once acted as an intermediary for drug traffickers and paramilitaries—from whose ill-gotten gains he has profited—has now become a figure who will be pressured by the United States, by his own government, and by its federal agencies to allow all kinds of foreign intervention in Colombia,” said Cepeda.

The leftist senator lost the elections to De la Espriella with a razor-thin margin of less than one percent. His supporters continue to seek a court order to nullify the election.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: Chile’s Municipalities, Senapred Meet Ahead of Storm Forecast
World.content:
SANTIAGO, Chile â As Chile prepares for an approaching winter storm system, the Association of Municipalities of Chile (Amuch) held a high-level coordination meeting with the National Disaster Prevention and Response Service (Senapred) to strengthen municipal emergency response measures.

The discussions focused on improving collaboration among municipalities, national agencies, and private service providers to better protect residents during severe weather events.

Power Companies Face Pressure Over Response Times

A central topic in the meeting was the performance of electric utilities during past emergencies. JosÃ© Manuel Palacios, mayor of La Reina, expressed concern over delayed responses from power companies in recent years.

âWe are exploring ways, together with Senapred and other institutions, to develop more efficient actions and hold the companies accountable to meet the response times our residents need,â Palacios said.

Rural Water Supply Risks Tied to Electricity

For rural municipalities, electrical outages pose a dual threat, as potable water systems often rely on electric power. Paula GÃ¡rate, mayor of Melipilla, emphasized the heightened vulnerability of rural areas during storms.

âLosing electricity also means losing access to potable water. Many rural water systems depend on electricity, and that remains our greatest concern,â GÃ¡rate noted.

Coordinated Municipal Efforts to Mitigate Risks

Senapred Director Alicia CebriÃ¡n highlighted the essential role of municipal governments in both preparation and response phases.

âMunicipalities play a crucial role in coordination, information gathering, and implementing mitigation works to reduce the impact of winter threats on residents,â CebriÃ¡n stated.

She underscored that emergency prevention and mitigation is a shared responsibility across public agencies and institutions. âPublic authorities who are directly involved in disaster management bear this responsibility, and we are committed to fulfilling it,â she added.

Winter System Expected to Test Emergency Readiness

The coordination meeting comes as Chileâs central regions brace for a frontal system expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds. Authorities emphasized that ongoing preparation and inter-agency cooperation will be key to minimizing disruption and protecting vulnerable communities.

World.title: Brian Wilson, Legendary Beach Boys Co-Founder, Dies at 82
World.content:
LOS ANGELES â Brian Wilson, the legendary musician, songwriter and co-founder of The Beach Boys, has died at the age of 82, his family announced.

“We are heartbroken to announce that our beloved father Brian Wilson has passed away,” the family said in a statement. “We are at a loss for words right now. Please respect our privacy at this time as our family is grieving. We realize that we are sharing our grief with the world.”

Born in 1942 in Hawthorne, California, Wilson formed The Beach Boys in 1961 with his younger brothers Carl and Dennis, cousin Mike Love, and friend Al Jardine. The band became one of the most influential and commercially successful acts in music history, selling over 100 million records worldwide.

Wilson was the creative force behind the groupâs distinctive harmonies and groundbreaking studio sound. His 1966 album Pet Sounds is regarded as a masterpiece that reshaped the boundaries of pop music production.

Among The Beach Boys’ many hits, Wilson co-wrote and produced I Get Around, Help Me, Rhonda, and Good Vibrations. Rolling Stone ranked The Beach Boys 12th on its list of the “100 Greatest Artists of All Time.”

Tributes poured in following news of his death. Nancy Sinatra shared a photo with Wilson on Instagram, writing, âHis cherished music will live forever as he travels through the Universe and beyond. God bless you, sweet Brian.â

View this post on Instagram A post shared by ð½ðððð¢ ððððððð (@nancysinatra)

Sean Ono Lennon called Wilson the “American Mozart” and a “one of a kind genius from another world,” adding: âAnyone who really knows me knows how heartbroken I am about Brian Wilson passing. Not many people influenced me as much as he did. I feel very lucky that I was able to meet him and spend some time with him. He was always very kind and generous.”

Throughout his life, Wilson faced significant personal struggles. Diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 1984, his condition was linked by doctors to earlier psychedelic drug use. In early 2024, his family revealed he had developed dementia.

Wilson’s wife, Melinda, with whom he shared 24 years of marriage and five adopted children, died earlier in 2024. He also had two daughters, Carnie and Wendy, from his first marriage.

Despite his health battles, Wilsonâs legacy remains unparalleled. His influence on songwriting, vocal harmony, and studio innovation continues to inspire generations of musicians.

World.title: Chile and Norway Deepen Antarctic Cooperation with New Agreement
World.content:
Chile and Norway signed a memorandum of understanding on Antarctic cooperation Monday, reinforcing their shared commitment to peace, science, and environmental protection in the region.

The agreement, signed by Chilean Foreign Minister Alberto van Klaveren and Norwegian Minister of International Development Ã smund GrÃ¸ver, aims to strengthen bilateral coordination under the Antarctic Treaty System. It outlines enhanced collaboration on scientific research, climate monitoring, and the preservation of marine ecosystems through frameworks such as the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meetings and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR).

The accord includes provisions for regular dialogue between scientific and governmental institutions in both countries and seeks to optimize joint efforts in Antarctic and sub-Antarctic research. Both nations also pledged support for the Polar Codeâs implementation, aiming to improve safety and environmental standards for ships operating in polar waters.

Operational and logistical cooperation between Chileâs and Norwayâs national Antarctic programs will also be explored, particularly in alignment with CCAMLRâs conservation objectives.

This renewed alliance builds on the long-standing historical ties between the two nations and reaffirms their role as active stewards of one of the worldâs most fragile and strategically vital environments.

World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia
World.content:
At least 132 dead in the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:51 UTC Full article

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead

At least 132 people were killed and 570 injured by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday, according to the latest report submitted by the Colombian Association of Capital Cities at 7:00 p.m. local time. Authorities warned the figure is preliminary and that rescue work is continuing.

The quake struck at 07:34, with its epicenter near the municipality of San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, at a depth of more than 80 kilometers, according to the Colombian Geological Service. It is the strongest recorded in the country in the past decade.

Pereira and its metropolitan area account for most of the dead. Departmental tolls released by governors and mayors correspond to different cutoff times and do not match one another: Chocó governor Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi reported 12 dead and 84 injured in that department, while the mayor of Manizales confirmed two deaths. Fatalities were also reported in Valle del Cauca and Antioquia.

| URGENTE: Momento del derrumbe de un edificio de 3 pisos tras el terremoto de magnitud 7,4 en Pereira, Colombia. pic.twitter.com/r3v2lW5pU3 — Alerta News 24 (@AlertaNews24) August 10, 2026

The government put the number of damaged homes at more than 1,500, with 37 destroyed and 61 buildings completely collapsed, along with damage to 18 health centers, 52 schools, 17 community centers and 18 roads. The civil aviation authority suspended operations at seven air terminals: Cali, Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura.

Damage to the hospital network is among the most critical. In Cali, the Hospital Universitario del Valle partially collapsed and seven large health care institutions were closed and evacuated because of structural damage. Valle del Cauca governor Dilian Francisca Toro said at least five intensive care patients were trapped under rubble. Cali mayor Alejandro Eder reported at least twenty collapsed structures with people trapped inside and requested rescue teams from Bogotá and Medellín. The capital's mayor, Carlos Fernando Galán, dispatched a hundred rescue workers.

De la Espriella agreed to declare a national disaster situation and is leading a unified command post at the National Disaster Risk Management Unit, with additional posts in Armenia and Quibdó. The foreign ministry is coordinating international cooperation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was ready to provide assistance.

The Colombian Geological Service reported two aftershocks, of magnitude 2.8 and 4.8. The agency also recorded an emission of ash and gases from the Puracé volcano, in Cauca department, on orange alert since July, coinciding in time with the earthquake.

World.title: Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say
World.content:
Colombia and Venezuela quakes are unconnected despite similar magnitude, experts say

11th Tuesday, August 2026 - 10:11 UTC Full article

“The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” a seismologist stressed

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western and central Colombia on Monday has a different tectonic origin from the earthquakes recorded in Venezuela in June, despite comparable magnitudes, said Viviana Dionisio, a seismologist with Colombia's National Seismological Network.

“It was a tectonic earthquake associated mainly with a subduction mechanism,” the specialist said. That process occurs when the Nazca plate, beneath the Pacific Ocean, slides under the South American plate, on which Colombia's mainland territory sits. Energy accumulated at the contact between the two can be released in large earthquakes, of the kind historically recorded around the Pacific Ring of Fire.

The Venezuelan earthquakes of June 24, of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.4, responded to a different mechanism. According to Dionisio, they originated in the interaction between the Caribbean and South American plates through lateral displacement, known as strike-slip faulting. “The Venezuelan earthquakes are shallower and involve a different mechanism, a strike-slip mechanism. This one is deeper, a subduction earthquake,” she stressed.

Depth is the factor explaining why two earthquakes of similar magnitude can cause very different damage. The focus of the Colombian quake was located at around one hundred kilometers, according to revised data from the Colombian Geological Service, which in its first bulletin had placed it at 82. In shallow earthquakes, waves travel a shorter distance and reach areas near the epicenter with greater intensity; in deep ones they pass through more material and lose energy along the way. The seismologist warned, however, that depth alone does not determine the extent of damage, which also depends on the vulnerability of buildings and ground conditions.

The epicenter was located in San José del Palmar, in Chocó department, on the boundary with Risaralda and Valle del Cauca. Dionisio said it is not unusual for an earthquake of these characteristics to originate in that region, given the tectonic dynamics of western Colombia.

The Colombian Geological Service has recorded more than thirty aftershocks, the strongest of magnitude 4.8. “An earthquake of this magnitude generates a certain number of aftershocks that generally decrease in frequency and magnitude over the following days or weeks,” the seismologist said.

Rodrigo León, of the Geosciences Department at Universidad de los Andes, noted that earthquakes cannot be predicted, nor is it possible to anticipate when an aftershock will occur or to rule out larger movements.
