Claims that “Azerbaijan must give up recognition of Israel to join the agreement” are not supported by specific evidence and remain rumours for now.

Benefits and risks in the context of multi-vector policy

Potential benefits for the South Caucasus and Azerbaijan include stronger collective deterrence, expanded defence industry and technological capabilities, an influx of Saudi capital, synergies with the Middle Corridor, stronger symbolic ties between Turkic and the broader Muslim worlds, and greater strategic autonomy amid questions surrounding external security guarantees.

Azerbaijan could benefit from closer ties among its partners without formally joining the agreement, while retaining room to manoeuvre in its relations with the West, Israel, Central Asia and other partners.

There are also risks. These include the possibility of becoming involved in Middle Eastern conflicts, including tensions involving Iran; potential pressure on relations with Israel and Azerbaijan’s image in the West; and possible negative effects on the peace process with Armenia or ties with Iran and Russia. Another risk is the new format’s institutional immaturity, particularly the absence of a clearly defined commitment to automatically deploy military forces.

Azerbaijan’s tradition of an independent, non-aligned foreign policy makes full membership in the agreement in the near future unlikely.

Likelihood of joining and the limits of Azerbaijan’s multi-vector policy

Azerbaijan’s multi-vector foreign policy does not mean automatically distancing itself from new regional initiatives. Baku seeks to balance the interests of its partners and tends to join new platforms when suitable opportunities arise. Azerbaijan’s decision in 2026 to join the Board of Peace, established at the initiative of US President Donald Trump, as a founding member provides a practical example of this approach. Close ties with Turkey and Pakistan, the trilateral Turkey-Azerbaijan-Pakistan format and the Shusha Declaration could also increase Baku’s interest in the Mecca format.

The 2026 war with Iran demonstrated the practical limits of this balance more clearly. Azerbaijan officially declared neutrality, repeatedly stressed its support for Iran’s sovereignty and said its territory was not being used against third countries. However, several international media outlets, including CNN, reported that Israeli special forces and intelligence structures were allegedly deployed on Azerbaijani territory during the war. Baku called these claims “completely unfounded”.

Several think tanks, including the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), described Azerbaijan’s position as a “carefully maintained balance between its officially declared neutrality and practical rapprochement”. Turkey’s decision not to take part in the war and its advice to Baku to maintain a cautious position also influenced this approach.

This dynamic takes on additional significance in the context of the Mecca agreement. The agreement’s principle that “an attack on one is an attack on all”, along with Saudi Arabia’s response to Iranian strikes during the war, shows how collective defence commitments can operate during periods of real tension. Azerbaijan’s deep strategic partnership with Israel, its allied relations with Turkey and Pakistan, and its expanding ties with Saudi Arabia have led some experts to believe that this rapprochement could increase Baku’s interest in formats similar to the Mecca agreement.

For Azerbaijan, therefore, the main question is not so much whether to join the agreement, but how to benefit from closer ties among its existing partners – Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Israel – without taking on formal commitments. This is precisely the flexibility that its multi-vector policy provides.

Mecca defence agreement and Azerbaijan

World.title: Number of Iranian companies in Georgia up 510% since 2012 – EPRC
World.content:
Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

According to data from the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the number of Iranian companies in Georgia has increased by around 510% since 2012, exceeding 12,800 by 2025–26.

EPRC says the figures are based on data from Geostat and the National Bank of Georgia. The organisation also notes that despite the sharp rise in the number of companies, foreign direct investment from Iran into Georgia has remained relatively low in recent years.

“Between 2013 and 2024, Iranian investment totalled $41 million. Although this is more than in the previous period, the amount per company remains quite small,” EPRC said.

According to the organisation, net foreign direct investment from Iran stood at -$0.65 million in 2024. Preliminary figures for 2025 put the figure at around $0.4 million.

EPRC estimates that Iran’s share of total foreign direct investment in Georgia remains small, according to official statistics.

The centre says Iranian companies registered in Georgia are mainly involved in small-scale trade, real estate transactions, services, construction, logistics and re-export.

“Most of this activity involves small and medium-sized businesses and is less connected to large-scale manufacturing, industrial or technology projects,” EPRC said.

The organisation notes that the activities of these companies have not led to significant job creation. It also says that dozens of companies are often registered at the same address.

According to EPRC, tourism has seen the most notable growth in economic activity linked to Iran. Between 2022 and 2024, tourism revenues from Iran rose from $91.1 million to $151.1 million, an increase of 65%. However, tourism revenues fell by 17.8% in 2025.

Why the number of Iranian companies is growing much faster than investment

The centre believes that the rapid increase in the number of companies, alongside relatively low levels of investment and official financial flows, raises questions about the true scale of their activities.

“Why is the number of Iranian companies growing much faster than investment and official financial inflows overall?” EPRC asks.

The organisation says that, given that a significant part of Iran’s financial sector operates under international sanctions, economic transactions may be taking place through alternative and potentially less transparent financial channels.

EPRC notes that if some economic activity takes place outside the traditional banking system or with limited transparency, this makes it harder for the state to effectively monitor financial flows. It also increases the risks of sanctions evasion and money laundering.

The centre also points to international practice, where such models are sometimes associated with nominal or so-called “paper” companies. These companies are officially registered, but their actual economic activity may be very limited.

According to EPRC, such companies are sometimes used for re-export operations, intermediary financial transactions, or to circumvent sanctions and regulatory requirements in different countries.

“When the number of companies grows rapidly but this is not accompanied by a corresponding increase in investment, production, exports or employment, questions arise about the real economic significance of their activities,” the organisation said.

EPRC also points to the visa-free regime between Georgia and the EU, saying that this could make the country more attractive to Iranian citizens and businesses.

According to the centre, the US sanctions imposed on Shelbit, a cryptocurrency company registered in Georgia and owned by an Iranian citizen, highlight the range of possible ways to circumvent sanctions.

EPRC believes that, in light of this case and the sharp increase in the number of companies opened in Georgia by Iranian citizens, the current figures should be viewed with additional risks in mind.

Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

World.title: Tbilisi’s new zoo ready to welcome visitors – video
World.content:
The new Tbilisi Zoo will open to visitors in August 2026. Construction began after the 2015 floods, and the zoo is opening in stages. Although work is still under way, visitors will soon be able to explore the new site.

One of Tbilisi Zoo’s best-known residents, Shani the lion cub, has already moved to the new zoo.

___________________________________________

___________________________________________

As David Taktakishvili, deputy director of Tbilisi Zoo, explains, the new zoo covers a large area, and the site is being developed in stages. Some animals have already been moved, but construction of the enclosures is still under way. Construction and infrastructure work will therefore continue after the zoo opens.

The zoo administration believes the public should already have the opportunity to see for themselves how a new-generation zoo is taking shape and how much better the animals will live in their new environment.

When the new zoo opens to visitors, the Caucasus biogeographical zone will be accessible to the public. In the future, the zoo will bring together spaces representing different regions of the world. At the first stage, however, the focus will be on the local flora and fauna of the Caucasus. Visitors will see red deer, bison, bears, wolves and other local species in this zone.

Construction of the African zone is currently under way. The new zoo will gradually add other biogeographical zones in the future.

In recent years, the role of zoos has also changed significantly. Today, one of their main functions is nature conservation, including protecting, breeding and caring for endangered species. The new, modern facility will serve this purpose and, in the future, will become not only a place for visitors but also an important wildlife conservation centre.

Admission prices will remain unchanged: free for children under three, 2 lari ($0.76) for children aged three to 12, and 4 lari ($1.53) for visitors aged 12 and over.

Some animals will remain at the old zoo, which will continue to operate as usual.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

New Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgian opposition figure investigated for ‘treason’ over comments on Abkhazia war
World.content:
Giorgi Baramidze case

Georgia‘s Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation into comments by Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, about the war in Abkhazia. The case concerns charges of treason and actions that threaten state interests. The investigation focuses on his account of how prisoners of war were treated during the early stages of the conflict. Baramidze made the comments on a podcast, triggering a political backlash. The de facto authorities in Abkhazia have also reacted to his remarks.

What did Baramidze say?

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, discussed the war in Abkhazia on Yago Khvichia’s “Birth of Georgia” programme.

Speaking about the exchange of prisoners, he said:

“We did not take prisoners, we had no prisoners, we executed them.”

The remark prompted a strong reaction from government officials. Baramidze later clarified several times what he meant.

He said he was referring to the early stages of the war, when the Georgian side did not yet have a regular and organised army. Baramidze later explained that people enraged by the deaths of their relatives in the fighting did not take enemy fighters prisoner.

“At first, the situation was as follows: people who were enraged after their mothers, fathers and relatives had been killed did not take prisoners during the fighting but killed them instead. That is the bitter truth about the early stages of the war. I know this because I personally took part in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze said.

According to him, the situation later changed. The Georgian side began taking prisoners, which made exchanges possible. Baramidze said that around 200 Georgian prisoners were eventually brought home as a result.

“My deputy and I could not have exchanged 200 Georgian prisoners if our side had not taken any prisoners at all,” he added.

Baramidze also denies that his comments were directed against the Georgian army or the state as a whole. He insists that he was referring specifically to the situation during the early stages of the war.

At the same time, he stressed Russia’s responsibility, saying that the Russian Federation acted as an aggressor and occupier in the wars of 1992–93 and 2008.

Why has the prosecutor’s office opened an investigation?

Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office opened the investigation at the request of the State Service of Veterans Affairs.

According to the agency, prosecutors are investigating the case under Articles 307¹ and 318 of the Criminal Code. The first concerns treason, while the second covers actions that threaten Georgia’s state interests.

The prosecutor’s office said:

“The investigation began following an appeal from the State Service of Veterans Affairs concerning comments made by Giorgi Baramidze, a member of the United National Movement. The case concerns his remarks about the war in Abkhazia and the prisoner exchange process, which he made on Yago Khvichia’s programme ‘Birth of Georgia’.”

As part of the investigation, prosecutors also summoned Koba Kobaladze, head of the State Service of Veterans Affairs, for questioning.

Baramidze sees the investigation as political persecution.

“The prosecutor’s office has opened a case against me for ‘betraying Georgia’! I am not afraid of your persecution, let alone your dirty propaganda!” he wrote on social media.

What does the government say?

Members of the Georgian Dream party do not consider Baramidze’s remarks simply an unfortunate choice of words. They argue that such statements could harm Georgia’s national interests and international standing.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze described Baramidze’s comments as morally unacceptable. As for the legal assessment, he said the relevant authorities should make that decision.

“As for the legal aspect, the relevant authorities will determine that, but from a moral standpoint, what this man said is simply disgusting,” Kobakhidze said.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili linked Baramidze’s remarks to a broader political context. He said the opposition had previously promoted what he called a harmful narrative about Georgia’s 2008 war, and that the same was now happening with the war in Abkhazia.

Alexander Tabatadze, chairman of the parliamentary Defence and Security Committee, said Baramidze’s comments could damage Georgia’s international standing.

He argued that such remarks could be used against Georgia. Tabatadze also said the wording insulted veterans of the Abkhazia war and those who were killed in the fighting.

The opposition also criticises the remarks

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Baramidze’s comments were inaccurate. However, he argued that an incorrect statement did not amount to treason.

“What was said is not true… I don’t know where this story came from. In my view, the words got ahead of the meaning, and that is not good. But treason and a crime are different things, and this is not how they are committed,” Gvaramia said.

He said he had no doubts about Baramidze’s patriotism. He described the prosecutor’s investigation as political persecution.

Shalva Kereselidze, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, called Baramidze’s remarks politically inappropriate and unworthy of a statesman.

“This is a statement unworthy of a statesman, and it is inappropriate both politically and from a human standpoint,” Kereselidze said.

The United National Movement, meanwhile, says the investigation is entirely politically motivated. The party also pointed out that Baramidze fought in the wars in Abkhazia and Ukraine.

“While the Kremlin regards Giorgi Baramidze as an enemy and persecutes him, the Georgian Dream government is accusing the same person of treason,” the party said in a statement.

Expert: “Baramidze’s account does not match the facts”

Conflict expert and former state minister Paata Zakareishvili has questioned the factual accuracy of Baramidze’s account.

Zakareishvili himself worked on prisoner exchanges during the Abkhazia war. He said Baramidze’s account differed so sharply from the realities of the time that he initially thought Baramidze was referring to a different war.

He also disputed Baramidze’s claim that he took part in the work of the prisoner exchange commission.

“Baramidze mentions this commission, but to be honest, he did not take part in its work,” Zakareishvili said.

He noted that documents exist detailing the commission’s work, but Baramidze’s name does not appear in them.

At the same time, Zakareishvili questioned the legal grounds for the investigation. In his view, false or exaggerated statements should not provide grounds for criminal prosecution.

“I still believe that Baramidze does not deserve punishment. I will do everything I can to prove that he was not a member of the commission. His comments are simply speculation, nothing more,” Zakareishvili said.

He also said he was ready to provide the prosecutor’s office with the information he has.

How the case moved beyond the domestic political conflict

The de facto Abkhaz foreign ministry has already responded to Baramidze’s remarks.

The ministry used his comments to reinforce its own historical narrative about the conflict. Its statement described the 1992–93 war as Georgia’s armed aggression against Abkhazia.

Sukhumi also criticised the investigation into Baramidze.

“It is clear that this criminal prosecution should serve as a warning to anyone prepared to speak openly about Georgia’s armed aggression and the crimes committed during it,” the statement said.

Giorgi Baramidze case

World.title: ‘Regional stability is main achievement’: assessing Washington peace summit one year on
World.content:
Washington peace summit: one year on

“The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan is visible and tangible to everyone,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in a statement marking the events of 8 August.

A year ago, on this day, Washington hosted a historic peace summit, with US President Donald Trump acting as mediator. Yerevan and Baku initialled a peace agreement, signed a declaration on the TRIPP project – a transit route through Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan (the “Trump Route”) – and signed a number of bilateral documents with the United States.

Pashinyan said the peace agreement “awaits signing and ratification”. He added that practical work on TRIPP would begin in the near future and become a “major regional and international event”.

The prime minister congratulated the people of Armenia and Azerbaijan on the landmark date of 8 August.

“Finally, we have a day that brings peace rather than stirs up our emotions,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also issued a statement, highlighting the “courage and foresight” shown by both countries over the past year.

“We look forward to further progress towards lasting and durable peace in the South Caucasus,” the secretary of state said.

Pashinyan held phone calls with Donald Trump and Ilham Aliyev.

Armenian analysts said the main outcome of the Washington summit was the establishment of stability in the region.

They noted positive developments despite what they described as Baku’s “aggressive agenda”, including its calls for Azerbaijanis to return to what it calls “Western Azerbaijan”. The term refers to almost the entire sovereign territory of Armenia.

Pashinyan on unresolved issues and how to make “peace irreversible”

In his address to the nation, Pashinyan once again said that peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan had been established.

“But this, of course, does not mean that we have already reached the end of the road in implementing the peace agenda,” he added.

According to the prime minister, the following issues remain unresolved:

signing and ratifying the peace agreement,

delimiting the Armenian-Azerbaijani border,

“the continued detention of our compatriots in Azerbaijan” [referring to 19 Armenian prisoners held in Baku].

He also said that 8 August 2025 had marked a turning point, dividing Armenia’s history into the periods “before and after this date”. Pashinyan described the period before 8 August as a dead end, while the period since then has offered “limitless opportunities”.

Pashinyan said the main political and social-psychological result of the Washington summit was that “the wheel of our history has once again fallen into our hands”.

He identified the implementation of the “Trump Route” project as another major outcome:

“It will not only end Armenia’s blockade in the very near future and become the backbone of Armenia’s and the region’s economy, but will also help Armenia and Azerbaijan start seeing each other not as an obstacle, but as a route and as a neighbour.”

The transit route was named the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” after the mediator, as the Armenian and Azerbaijani authorities had been unable to reach an agreement on the issue for several years.

Pashinyan also outlined steps that Armenia and Azerbaijan should take to make the peace between them irreversible:

“We need to put an end to discussions about the ‘right of Armenians to return to Nagorno-Karabakh’ and the ‘return of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan’. Azerbaijan, for its part, needs to end discussions about ‘Western Azerbaijan’ and the ‘right of Western Azerbaijanis to return’. This is an issue that both Armenia and Azerbaijan must resolve in the name of our generations’ right to live together in peace.”

“We hope to see further progress”, Rubio says

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that over the past 12 months, the United States had continued to work with Armenia and Azerbaijan. He highlighted the importance of the TRIPP project. According to Rubio, the transit route is gradually becoming a reality:

“Engineering work on the railway has already begun in Armenia, while construction of the highway and railway linking Azerbaijan with Armenia is nearly complete.”

He stressed that TRIPP is not simply an infrastructure project but also an important link in the Trans-Caspian trade route. It could drive new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries.

“It is a factor that opens up new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries. It is also an example of how economic cooperation can strengthen peace after long-standing disputes have been resolved,” Rubio said.

He added that peace had created an opportunity to deepen relations between the United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan. This, he said, would contribute to the economic prosperity of all three countries.

Thanks to Trump

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan thanked him for organising the peace summit and for signing the peace declaration adopted by the Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders as a testament to the agreement. He also stressed “the significant role of Trump’s personal efforts” in establishing peace.

“The two leaders welcomed the fact that the Washington Peace Summit had led to real peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which people in both countries can see and feel. […] Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Trump reaffirmed their determination to begin work on the construction of TRIPP in the near future. They also discussed other issues on the bilateral Armenian-US and international agendas,” the Armenian prime minister’s office said.

Talks with Aliyev

According to the prime minister’s office, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed progress in normalising relations over the past year. They also focused on the development of trade and economic ties between the two countries.

“In this context, the sides highlighted Azerbaijan’s exports of petroleum products to Armenia, as well as the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and from Armenia to other destinations. They also exchanged views on the implementation of the TRIPP project in line with the agreements reached in Washington. They stressed the importance of continuing efforts to advance the peace process and ensure long-term peace, stability, connectivity and economic cooperation in the region.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“The main result of the Washington summit is that it brought a period of relative stability to the region. For a year now, we have not had to discuss possible escalations or security risks coming from Azerbaijan.

The second positive factor is that the atmosphere has changed to some extent and shifted towards cooperation. “As for Azerbaijan, it continues to promote certain aggressive strategies, such as its ‘Western Azerbaijan’ narrative. But it is also taking steps aimed at establishing peace. Opening its territory for transit is one example, along with other similar measures.

Naturally, it is better for Azerbaijan to open its territory, establish contacts and start trade than for the region to face the risk of escalation.

But, as we have repeatedly pointed out, we will only be able to assess the final results of this process not when the TRIPP project becomes operational, but after we see what else follows TRIPP. Our assessment in the coming years will depend on these developments.

If TRIPP is implemented, and Armenia also gains access to Iran and Russia through Azerbaijani territory, and if the Armenian-Turkish border opens, then we will certainly be able to consider the process a success. If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: A year on, this human skull mystery at Mildura may never be solved
World.content:
A human skull found on the banks of the Murray River in Victoria's north-west more than 12 months ago is being sent for carbon date testing.

In July 2025, a man was walking along the river's edge near the entrance of Apex Riverbeach Holiday park in Mildura when he made the discovery of the partial skull.

NSW Police said the remains were found partially buried and that early indications suggested the remains were not historic.

After the discovery, the skull was sent to Newcastle for special forensic investigation.

NSW Police Detective Inspector Matt Sippel said given authorities were dealing with a partial skull, the tests had come back inconclusive.

"We haven't been able to identify the origin of that skull and the date or the age of the skull," Detective Inspector Sippel said.

"What we'll do [now] is have that sent to the Australian National University where radiocarbon data testing is to occur."

He said a number of inquires had been made including searching through missing person databases.

However, he said there was a lack of evidence.

"We don't know how long this skull had been there and how it got to that location," Detective Inspector Sippel said.

"Obviously, examinations were conducted at the time, nothing further was located and that's pretty much where it sits.

"But, we are very hopeful that we'll be able to get some further answers in relation to the radiocarbon data testing that the partial skull is about to undertake."

He confirmed historic remains were ruled out by an anthropologist.

"Hopefully, we can build a sufficient amount of evidence… [that] can lead to other inquires, our missing persons databases and all those of things and hopefully we will get a result," he said.

"But, ultimately that will all be put before the Coroner. "

The skull will be sent to the Australian National University to undergo carbon dating tests. (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Nethma Dandeniya )

How investigations of this nature unfold

Former Victoria Police homicide detective Charlie Bezzina said the investigation into the mystery skull could take years.

"Your first point of call certainly is missing persons records, given [the length] of the Murray River, [it] makes it quite difficult," he said.

"So, you'd have to really expand it to the whole direction and length of the Murray River and establish any age.

"If you're able to determine any gender, and then any distinguishing factors, more specifically in the teeth … if there is some specific work that's been done on the teeth … they would take X-rays and distribute it to dentists in Victoria and New South Wales [who] may recognise their work if there is something significant in their teeth.

"They may try and extract DNA, depending on the age of it, but that's another avenue of identification."

Former Victoria Police homicide detective Charlie Bezzina says investigations like these could remain a mystery forever. (ABC News: Nicole Asher)

Mr Bezzina said given it was a partial skull, "very little" could be extracted from an identification point of view.

"Because you've only got skull or part of the bone, you might be lucky enough to get some DNA if there's any teeth left there, but it [comes down] to the age of it, how long has it been in the water, has it been buried," he said.

"So it becomes difficult … that's why I say this is a scientific investigation as opposed to a criminal one.

"[You're] dealing with scientific stuff, you're not dealing with door knocks or interviewing witnesses, apart from if the missing persons reports come back as negative," he said.

"Then you're relying on science quite significantly through an anthropologist to try to determine the gender of the skull, the dental records and any DNA."

He said given the circumstances it would not be unusual for the skull to never be identified.

"It may remain a mystery forever and a day but they might be lucky enough to identify the skull and hopefully have some respite for the family," Mr Bezzina said.

World.title: Coalition pushes VIP gambling crackdown in talks with Labor
World.content:
The Coalition is seeking a targeted crackdown on VIP gambling inducements offered to high rollers and a simplified option to curb ads on streaming services amid ongoing "constructive" gambling bill talks with the federal government.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met early Tuesday evening for a second time in as many days to hash out details of an expected agreement to amend Labor’s proposed gambling ad restrictions.

Major changes such as an "opt-in" system for online advertising or a total ban on so-called gambling inducements are not on the table from either side, with Mr Albanese having previously indicated he would not entertain a wholesale rewrite of the draft legislation.

Albanese returns to a gambling debate ready to ignite Drugs, sex and multi-million dollar high rollers are themes more often featured in a Hollywood film than a parliamentary hearing, but this week's gambling inquiry has been the exception.

Instead, the asks put forward by Mr Taylor and Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson have focused on stronger protections for children and vulnerable people from exposure to advertising or predatory industry tactics.

With a modest deal seeming increasingly likely, gambling harm reduction advocates within the Coalition are calling for the bill to include an automatic independent review of the measures in the future.

It is hoped this would eventually expose what they believe are flaws in the legislation and create the case for further changes in the next term of government.

Labor is seeking to pass the legislation through the Senate by the end of the fortnight, which Mr Taylor is understood to be open to though is not in a rush this week as he has committed to take a final proposal back to the full Coalition party room for sign off.

Coalition asks for focus on high-end inducements

Rather than a broader crackdown on so-called gambling inducements, such as bonus bet offers, the Coalition has instead asked Labor for amendments focused on vulnerable and high-spending gamblers.

This included creating some type of cooling period preventing gambling companies from sending any inducements to Australians immediately after they remove themselves from the government’s self-exclusion register Betstop.

Loading...

The Opposition has also suggested targeting VIP offers extended to high rollers, such as access to exclusive events, game day tickets or large bonus-bet offers.

More common inducements pushed out to the average customer, such as deposit or bonus bet deals in the $25 range, are not the focus of the Coalition’s negotiations with Labor.

This is in part due to a view that the Liberals and Nationals must remain the parties of "personal responsibility" where individuals are expected to make their own decisions.

Coalition wants to give streamers option to comply with TV ad laws

The Coalition has also proposed a workaround for concerns among what has been dubbed a "triple lock" requiring all online platforms to restrict gambling ads to logged-in users who are aged over 18, while also giving every adult user a simple way to "opt out".

Harm advocates are unhappy with this proposal, because if a streaming service, social media or other online platform has a triple lock in place, they can show as many gambling ads as they want to over-aged, logged in viewers who have not opted out.

Streamers have also expressed concerns about the complexity of the proposed system.

The Coalition has also proposed a potential workaround for restrictions aimed at targeting gambling advertising loopholes. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

The Coalition has therefore suggested streamers be given the option of either enforcing a triple lock or adopting the far more restrictive advertising rules for TV.

Under the bill, gambling ads are limited to three per hour between 6am and 8:30pm and banned during live sport broadcasts within those hours.

Liberal MP Simon Kennedy used a speech in parliament on Tuesday to attack the "two glaring problems" with Labor’s bill, which he said "did nothing" on inducements and allowed “unlimited advertising online” for adults who had not opted out.

"There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more," he said.

Inducements up for negotiation in ‘unusual’ leader talks

Coalition sources acknowledged it was "unusual" for Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese to meet twice to discuss legislative issues, attributing it to the prime minister's interest in being involved in negotiations.

Both leaders were on annual leave last week when a two-day Senate inquiry heard shocking evidence about the efforts VIP account managers at gambling companies went to strengthen relationships with high-rolling clients.

Gambling companies deny drug claims Sportsbet and TAB have denied explosive claims they offered customers access to illicit drugs.

Allegations of offers to provide access to illicit drugs dominated media coverage of the hearings, but advocates also warned of harmful legal examples of so-called gambling inducements.

This included things like big spending gamblers being offered travel, accommodation and access to exclusive events linked to race days or football games.

Advocates also warned about the targeting of gamblers with inducements such as bonus bets, which the wagering sector described as “promotions”.

Last month Labor members unanimously voted to adopt a pledge to tackle these inducements into the party's 2026 national policy platform.

More than three years ago the You Win Some, You Lose More report into online wagering harms, which was authored by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, recommended a total ban on all inducements.

Multiple Labor backbench MPs have gone public with their push for the party to address inducements since the government’s draft bill did not deal with the issue.

Industry expects 'unscrupulous' VIP account manager crackdown

Sources in the wagering industry said one of the issues discussed between the Coalition and Labor was a crackdown on the "payment" of VIP account managers offering gambling promotions.

At the Senate hearing last week, ACT independent Senator David Pocock was visibly shocked by evidence account managers at some wagering companies were paid on commission based on customers’ losses.

Gambling company offered addict drugs Luke Bateman says gambling company employees unofficially offered him illicit drugs.

A wagering source said they believed Labor's bill could be amended to stop "unscrupulous" account managers being paid in this way.

This would not impact every company however, as the ABC reported last year that Sportsbet and Tabcorp no longer pay commissions to VIP account managers.

Any deal between Mr Taylor and Mr Albanese would still have to be signed off by the Coalition party room, which meets weekly when parliament is sitting.

Five backbenchers using the regular meeting on Tuesday to push for tougher reforms, while four cautioned against over-regulation.

Greens communications spokeswoman Senator Sarah Hanson-Young said Labor always intended to make a deal with the Coalition on the gambling reforms, to get away with doing the "bare minimum" on the issue.

Loading

Senator Hanson-Young said she met yesterday with Communications Minister Anika Wells, who indicated the government was willing to amend the bill to limit inducements.

"Last week, we were told the government wouldn't move at all and now they're saying they're prepared to move. The question is how far?" she said.

"The government has always intended to put this piece of legislation through with the opposition because they want to do the bare minimum.

"I have no faith that Angus Taylor is up to the job of negotiating the best outcome for people here."

World.title: 'It won't fall apart': Leading Liberal says we don't need 'gold-plated' building code
World.content:
The federal opposition wants to demolish Australia's building code, squeezing more than 2,000 pages into just 80.

Speaking at the National Press Club on Wednesday, Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg will say the current rules require "gold-plated houses", which are too expensive.

In a radical overhaul which would require the co-operation of states and territories to deliver, he would turn everything apart from basic safety standards into an "optional extra", including accessibility and energy efficiency requirements.

"It is now illegal to build a cheap house in Australia," the senator will say, according to excerpts from his remarks shared with the ABC.

"We will pare this back."

The National Construction Code, established under a different name in 1988, was initially in the order of eighty pages but has expanded under successive governments.

The real-life Utopia stories blocking new homes A new report from the Productivity Commission calls on governments to embrace a "build mindset" to make housing more affordable.

While some of this is due to expanding scope, the document has also evolved to give builders more detailed guidance on how they can ensure their buildings are compliant.

Another major cause of bloat is the section devoted to explaining variations across each state and territory.

That alone spans more than 700 pages across multiple volumes, resulting in what the Productivity Commission calls a "thicket" of inconsistency.

Regulations add thousands to the cost of a house

Industry groups argue complicated regulations add to the cost of new homes.

Evidence heard by a Senate inquiry into productivity, which Senator Bragg chaired, found the last seven years of code changes have added $3,600 to $33,000 to the cost of a new house.

Senator Bragg says houses under his proposal would not be "gold plated", but they would be safe. (ABC News: John Gunn)

A recent Productivity Commission inquiry into the construction sector found that zoning and the regulatory approvals process was more burdensome than building regulations, but its terms of reference did not include direct consideration of the construction code.

While Senator Bragg's proposal would see much of the existing guidance retained as "optional" and the desired length is informed by New Zealand's approach, such a dramatic reduction could involve risks.

For example, while Senator Bragg has suggested that "essential structural, fire safety, and health-related" standards will be retained, the fire-related sections alone in the existing code run to more than 80 pages.

Senator Bragg's speech suggests houses under the shorter code "won't be gold plated but it won't fall apart. It will be safe."

The proposed new code would be accompanied by a federal "pattern book" with approved templates.

While the code is developed nationally by the Australian Building Codes Board (ABCB), it is implemented in state and territory laws, meaning any changes would require co-operation across jurisdictions.

Expanding scope over time

The total page figure of just over 2,200 pages includes all kinds of buildings, not just homes.

ABCB chief executive Adrian Piani told Senator Bragg's inquiry the section relating to "your standard house" was just 332 pages.

Mr Piani said there were two main reasons the code had expanded. One was the inclusion of guidance.

"It became much more of a document that was trying to give people the answer as well as the performance requirement," he said.

"[The earlier version says] if it's got stairs, those stairs must help people leave the building … [The later version] has all the pictures, all the diagrams about how you design a stair and what a stair looks like."

But the other reason was expanded scope. Recent changes include a mandated seven-star energy efficiency rating and mandatory accessibility standards.

Senator Bragg listed "mandatory ramps" and "flattened shower flooring" as examples.

Factory-built homes could help Australia reindustrialise, report says Factory-built homes could solve Australia's housing crisis and drive reindustrialisation, report says.

The federal government announced a freeze to the code last year, but has since indicated it is taking steps to simplify it in co-ordination with the building industry.

Treasury's Inspector-General of Housing, Ben Rimmer, told Senate estimates earlier this year the complexity of the construction code was "a significant impost on the economy" and a "significant driver of cost", but that much of this was due to states and territories.

"We don't have a National Construction Code … we actually have eight different construction regulatory systems depending on which state and territory you happen to be in on that day of the week," he said.

" If you're a plumber living in Wodonga and you cross the border, you have a different set of regulations … We're working to improve it and to make sure that we get a better system as soon as we can within those constraints. "

In the same estimates hearing, Labor minister Tim Ayres criticised Senator Bragg's longstanding aspiration to slash the code, noting that recent changes included measures to improve waterproofing for balconies.

"I just don't think you can argue — well, you can if you want — [against] stopping people having to spend $2 billion in rectification costs because apartment balconies are leaking," he said.

"I just think that's a sensible proposition … leaking balconies are a bad idea."

Speech to canvas migration

Senator Bragg will also argue the Albanese government has allowed net overseas migration to outpace housing construction, creating a shortfall of 130,000 homes.

The Coalition intends to link migration to housing completions.

"This … can be achieved while benefiting the budget and the economy, including by lifting the skilled share of our permanent migration … and modest reductions in international students, working holiday makers and post-study work visas."

Labor is preparing its own plan to keep net migration closer to Treasury projections, as reported by the ABC last week.

Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says Labor's migration policy needs work. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The details have been the subject of extensive cabinet debate, and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said on Monday there was "work to do".

A National Press Club address by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, cancelled at short notice last week, has not yet been scheduled but is expected as soon as next week.

Labor's proposal is expected to include restrictions on working holiday makers and those who fail in their applications for humanitarian visas, including many graduated students.

Plans for skilled migrants and their families are unclear.

World.title: 'Little Blue Boat' has its 'soul back' ahead of return to water
World.content:
Sporting a fresh shade of blue, Hobart's beloved 'Little Blue Boat' is set to return to the water this morning following a year-and-a-half of restoration works.

The boat has been missing from its long-held spot in Montrose Bay since 2024, when it was ripped from its mooring and battered against rocks during a severe storm.

Hobartians were collectively dismayed when wild weather snapped the chain on the Little Blue Boat's mooring and caused it to run aground. (Supplied: Total Dive Solutions)

The boat had been moored in Montrose Bay for nearly five decades when it was damaged in a storm. (Supplied: Total Dive Solutions)

It's since found a temporary home with the Wooden Boat Centre in Franklin, where boat-building volunteers, students and apprentices have worked to restore the much-loved vessel.

By the time it arrived at Franklin's Wooden Boat Centre, the boat was in need of some TLC. (Facebook: Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

Family's tough decision to let Little Blue Boat go It's been a fixture of Hobart's northern suburbs since the 1970s, but the iconic "little blue boat" could be on the move after its owner makes the tough decision to part ways with his beloved vessel.

Today, the boat will be lifted into the Huon River via crane, marking its first return to the water since restoration works began.

Head shipwright and trainer at the centre, Cody Horgan, said the team was excited to see the boat "regain her energy".

" I think when a boat goes back in the water, it gets its soul back, it's alive again. "

Cody Horgan helped with the restoration in his role as the Wooden Boat Centre's head shipwright and trainer. (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

The boat is constructed of celery-top pine. (Facebook: Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

It took the team about 18 months for the major restoration project. (Facebook: Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

Sold for $1

Over an almost 50-year period, the little blue boat became a ubiquitous feature of the commute south to Hobart down the Brooker Highway.

The boat, officially named Sea Breeze, was built by Robin Attrill in the early 1970s.

It was at Macquarie Wharf in Hobart in the 1970s when the Little Blue Boat was first launched. (Supplied: Colin Attrill)

Constructed of celery-top pine and built in Mr Attrill's backyard in Montrose, his son Colin said it was first launched at Macquarie Wharf in 1976.

While it may feel for many passers-by as if the boat has been moored in Montrose Bay forever, the Attrill family used Sea Breeze for many fishing trips and adventures.

But after being moored in Montrose Bay for almost five decades, like all wooden boats, Sea Breeze needed regular repairs and upkeep.

Loading Instagram content

At least once a year, the Attrill family would put the boat on a slip to make any repairs, as well as clean and antifoul it.

By the time wild weather unmoored the boat in August 2024 — battering it against the foreshore walkway — Mr Attrill was in his early 90s and had already made the decision to sell the beloved vessel to an owner who could give it the time and attention it needed.

The restoration was an opportunity for the centre's students and volunteers to work alongside each other. (Facebook: Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

Mr Attrill sold the Little Blue Boat for a symbolic $1 to the Wooden Boat Centre in Franklin, whose team of volunteers and students, led by Cody Horgan, embarked on an 18-month major restoration project, including the crucial step of finding the correct shade of blue.

The Wooden Boat Centre used a colour chart to determine the correct shade of blue for the top coat of Sea Breeze. (Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

"I didn't want to make the decision personally because I'd get my backside kicked, so we put it out to the world," Mr Horgan said.

The boat centre held an online poll to select the vessel's new look, with 90 per cent opting for 'Bondi Blue'.

Boat in a 'terrible' state, before restoration

Mr Horgan said taking on the boat was a good opportunity for the volunteers and students of the boat school, but it came with "a lot of work".

First, the boat was completely stripped, for the damage to be assessed.

The boat was assessed for damage after being completely stripped. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

"She looked terrible, the poor little girl," Mr Horgan said.

"Overall, there were about 22 ribs that needed replacing, three planks that needed replacing, and a lot of plugs and splines."

A new plywood deck was fitted. (Facebook: Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

Four volunteers worked twice a week on the project, alongside boat school students and boat centre staff.

"The volunteers have done so much work in regard to putting new ribs in; they're putting a new stem on, we've put a new keel on the boat.

"I've also had students assisting; I've taught them how to put a couple of planks in, and they've completed repairing the hull, and volunteers have been doing a lot of painting.

"It's always fun to get students and volunteers working side-by-side," Mr Horgan said.

Nick Whyatt is one of the project's many volunteers. (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

Volunteer Nick Whyatt has volunteered at the centre for six years, and said the project was one of the more difficult he has worked on.

"We've painted it, sanded it, just about everything really.

"We just put some new windows on and managed to salvage all the old brass handmade frames, which are quite quirky, but really add to the character of the boat.

"A lot of the apprentices here have been involved doing some of the more complex work on it,' Mr Whyatt said.

" It's been a great collaboration. "

The beloved Hobart boat is officially named "Sea Breeze". (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

Work being carried out in December 2025. (Facebook: Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

Launch comes two months after passing of boatbuilder

Today's launch is a particularly significant moment for the Attrill family, who will see his beloved boat take to the water two months after his passing.

A notice published at the time of his death in June reads:

"Now sailing into the sunset on the Little Blue Boat together with Mum. Sail peacefully."

Mr Horgan said it was "a great shame" Mr Attrill will not see the boat return to the water but believes the family will get "a lot of delight" in seeing the Sea Breeze restored.

"It's very satisfying to help a family regain a little bit of their history and their maritime culture," Mr Horgan said.

" The volunteers will be really satisfied with their work and what they've achieved over the past year and a half. "

Over the years, the Attrill family used Sea Breeze for many fishing trips and adventures. (Facebook: Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

An online poll was held to select the vessel's new look, with 90 per cent opting for 'Bondi Blue'. (Wooden Boat Centre Tasmania)

Final restoration works to continue, new owner to be found

Although returning to the water today, further works are needed to fully restore the little blue boat to its former state.

Volunteers will complete the remainder of the fit-out, with the mast also to be replaced while the boat is moored behind the boat centre.

The fully restored Sea Breeze will then be unveiled at next year's Wooden Boat Festival.

Nick Whyatt (left) with Sean Guastavino were just two of the boat's repair team. (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

The boat centre is yet to find a long-term custodian for the boat and is currently seeking expressions of interest.

"We're looking for an organisation that can take her on, a not-for-profit who will use it within the community and use it for activities that make people happy," Mr Horgan said.

As for whether the little blue boat will ever return to its traditional mooring, Mr Horgan said it was a possibility.

" I believe there is a group out there who have actually bought the mooring that she used to be on. So there is an opportunity she might go back there, but it all depends on them. "

The centre is currently seeking expressions of interest for the boat's next custodian. (ABC News: Sophie Jaggers)

World.title: Are you really a 'home owner' if you're living at your parents' place?
World.content:
What is the "home ownership rate"?

Most of us assume it refers to the share of Australian adults who own a home.

And we're told that Australia's home ownership rate peaked above 70 per cent in the mid-1960s before declining a bit since then, and it's now sitting around 66 per cent.

Sydney home ownership hits new low Sydney is no longer affordable for most, as new data reveals the number of people who own the home they live in is the lowest it has been in decades.

But what if the real rate of home ownership was much lower? What if it was actually around 52 per cent?

According to economist Karl Fitzgerald, from Grounded Community Land Trust Advocacy, a not-for-profit organisation, there's a major problem with the way we think about the home ownership rate.

He says if more voters knew that only half of Australia's adults actually owned a home, rather than two-thirds as we're led to believe, it would change the politics of housing.

And he says the confusion comes down to a single question in the national census.

A lower home ownership rate in reality

In the graphic below, this is what Mr Fitzgerald says Australia's real home ownership rate looks like (copper-coloured line), compared to the usual rate (black line):

What explains the difference?

The traditional "home ownership rate," which is the one we always talk about, is derived from a question in the census.

Every five years, every household in Australia has to fill out the census, and each household is asked this question: Is the dwelling you're living in owned or rented?

In last night's census, this is what the question looked like:

This was the question about dwelling tenure in the 2026 national census. (Source: 2026 national census)

How did you answer that question last night?

If you own the home you're living (and you're paying off the mortgage) you would have ticked the circle "owned with a mortgage."

But what if you're a young adult and you're living at home with your parents and your parents own their home with a mortgage? How did you answer the question?

Think about it carefully.

Waiting for Goldilocks? 'Affordable' homes sit vacant A Four Corners investigation has found many "affordable" rental homes were unaffordable for those who needed them most, particularly single-income households.

The question was asking you if the dwelling you're living in is owned outright, owned with a mortgage, rented etc. It wasn't asking you if you own the home. It was asking you if the dwelling you're living in is an owner-occupied home or not.

So, if your parents own the home with a mortgage, you should have ticked the circle "owned with a mortgage".

But you're not a home owner, right? You may be 10-15 years away from buying your first property.

So why were all of the adults living in your house counted as owners? Isn't that going to artificially inflate Australia's home ownership rate?

Karl Fitzgerald said every generation has been told a better story about its level of home ownership than the numbers support. (ABC News: Gemma Hall )

The politics of housing

Mr Fitzgerald says that's precisely what's going on.

"Half a million young Australians are living in their parents' spare room, and not one of them appears in their own generation's ownership figure. They are not counted as missing out. They are not counted at all," he argued recently.

He says the statistical quirk explains why Australia's "home ownership rate" has barely moved in 60 years.

Australians have become housing hostages While the government has framed its tax changes as modest tweaks, make no mistake that these are significant for the property market.

"It has sat around two thirds for a generation while the number of adults who actually own their home slid underneath it," he says.

"The people locked out of ownership are propping up the very number that says the market is fine.

"That is a large part of why change has been so hard to win. You cannot build political urgency on a statistic that hides the problem," he says.

He says the same issue is obscuring what's happening in different age cohorts too.

"Every generation has been told a better story about itself than the numbers support," he argues.

In the graphic below, the traditional home ownership rates for different age groups (grey columns) are very different to the more realistic figures (copper columns).

Fitzgerald says the politics of housing would look very different if people were aware of those proper numbers.

“Would voters expect more, and would politicians be more willing to demand answers, on why we are going backwards?” he wonders.

"This makes ownership a razor sharp contest between those who have and those who do not."

Similar findings in the United States

Fitzgerald says a recent paper by researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis found a similar result in the United States.

"The home ownership rate in the United States is reported to be 65 per cent," that report said.

Australia dealing with damage from ideas about housing Do home owners ever complain when house prices rise? A former prime minister said they didn't, but we're now dealing with the fallout.

"But this commonly cited data point on home ownership is actually the owner-occupancy rate, which tells us how many housing units are occupied by an owner. While owner occupancy is an interesting measure, it doesn't tell us how many people own their home.

"As an alternative to better reflect the share of adults who are home owners, we offer the homeowners-to-population ratio, or HPOP, a measure that lends a more nuanced view for important policy considerations and context.

"Using this new measure, the US home ownership rate is 53 per cent," it found.

The paper included this pictograph to show what's going on conceptually, with the two different measures:

(Source: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, 'New homeownership measure puts people first,' July 2026.)

It shows five housing units with different family configurations.

In the first property, elderly parents live with their daughter and her partner who own the home. In the second property, an adult child is living at home. In the third property, a friend is living with a mate who owns the property. In the fourth property, two young children live with their parents. And in the fifth property, three roommates live in a rented home which none of them own.

Then, using the "traditional" measurement, the green rows show that since 4 out of those 5 housing units are occupied by someone who owns the property, it leads to an 80 per cent home ownership rate.

But using the "homeowners-to-population ratio", the blue rows show that only 7 out of 14 adults in those same five housing units are actually home owners, so it produces a 50 per cent home ownership rate.

What's the difference between the two measures?

Fitzgerald says the figure conventionally reported as Australia's "home ownership rate" is the traditional "owner-occupancy rate."

What happened to housing? If you've been wondering how and why Australian house prices spun out of control you're not alone. One filmmaker was so depressed by it he went out and shot a documentary.

The owner-occupancy rate tells us how many housing units in Australia are occupied by an owner.

But a "homeowners-to-population" ratio counts individual adults, rather than buildings.

Under that alternative measure, an adult is considered a home owner if they are the household reference person (or that person's spouse or partner) in an owner-occupied dwelling, but any other adults who live in the dwelling are not counted as home owners because they don't own the home (the denominator for the calculation is all persons aged 18 and over).

The below graph, from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis paper, shows why adjusting for adult children (and other non-owning adults) who live in a home owned by someone else changes the "home ownership rate" in the United States so much:

Note: This figure shows the incremental adjustments in transitioning from the national owner-occupancy rate to the national HPOP (homeowners-to-population ratio). "Adjustment for household size" accounts for the relative difference in the number of adults in owner-occupied units to compared to rental units. Authors' calculations based on 2024 American Community Survey 1-Year microdata. (Source: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, 'New homeownership measure puts people first,' July 2026.)

A request for the ABS

Fitzgerald is now calling on the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) to publish an official homeowners-to-population ratio from person-level census data for Australia.

"The ABS already holds everything it needs. It is a question of deciding the number is worth having," he said.

Big changes for NSW renters as portable bond scheme begins The NSW government's portable rental bond system starts today and will cost renters who want to use the online service $25.

He says the national census records dwelling tenure and, separately, each person's relationship to the household reference person, so both variables exist for every census.

But the cross-tabulation of the two is not published, he says, so the couple share of owner-occupied households is recorded but not released. He says it can be extracted from the ABS's TableBuilder.

He also notes that the census doesn't record ownership of property other than the dwelling in which a person is recording as living in. He says ownership of residential property as an asset is a different and larger question, and an investor who rents where they live is recorded in the census as a non-owner.

World.title: Refugee with disability from Pakistan finds 'dream job' at Sydney airport
World.content:
When Suhail first came to Australia in 2022, the 54-year-old had a tough time trying to get into sustainable work.

The Pakistani refugee's qualifications as an accountant were not recognised, he was unfamiliar with application processes, he had no previous local work history nor social network, and English was his second language.

On top of all that, the situation that forced him to leave his home had also left him with stress and trauma-induced psychosocial issues that sometimes made it hard for him to focus and make decisions.

Each year, Australia takes in about 20,000 refugees who are displaced due to conflict, persecution or human rights abuses.

Suhail asked not to have his full name published, or the reason why he fled Pakistan, due to the nature of his issue.

"The experience, it was quite challenging but if there is a will, there is way," he told the ABC.

Despite the barriers, Suhail is now working in his "dream job".

Suhail first came to Australia in 2022. (Supplied)

Back in Pakistan, Suhail aspired to work in aviation security.

He said that, as a member of the marginalised Christian minority, feeling safe was important to him growing up.

"Providing security to people, just making things go right," he said. "That is my thing."

In March, Suhail started working at Sydney Airport in a baggage screening role.

"It's amazing," he said. "It's just like a heaven to me and I feel so good. I feel so confident."

Suhail got the job after receiving specialised support through the federal government's new employment program for people with disabilities, Inclusive Employment Australia (IEA).

IEA, which replaced the old Disability Employment Services (DES) program in November last year, intends to provide more tailored support and help people "achieve their career goals", Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek said at the time.

Tanya Plibersek says the IEA scheme is designed to provide more specialised support for people with disabilities who want to find work. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Sue Olney, an expert on disability and employment services policy at the University of Melbourne, said the previous DES did not have a good track record of getting people with disability into sustainable work.

During his time with the DES, Suhail drifted in and out of several jobs, including as a hairdresser.

But after being connected with Settlement Services International (SSI), one of the contracted service providers delivering the IEA program, he was provided with a case manager from the same background who spoke the same language.

The non-profit organisation, which specialises in providing support services to diverse communities, worked with Suhail to find a job he genuinely wanted to do.

Getting out of the 'too-hard basket'

SSI executive general manager for service delivery Eric Harper said the barriers to employment for refugees with disabilities were compounded.

Under the DES, he said many had ended up "suspended" by their employment service providers.

"They have often been put in the too-hard basket because of those intersectional and special needs, cultural adjustment, their social isolation, all of those things," he said.

In 2022, an ABS survey found the unemployment rate for Australians with disabilities was 7.5 per cent — double the unemployment rate for people without disabilities at the time which was 3.1 per cent — while the labour force participation rate for the cohort aged 15-64 was about 60.5 per cent compared to 84.9 per cent for those without disabilities.

Refugees' skills still under-recognised a decade on New research shows almost half of refugees previously working as managers and professionals are, 10 years later, still experiencing what's known as an "occupational downgrade".

Dr Olney, who also works with the government's Centre for Inclusive Employment which provides resources and training to IEA service providers, said the unemployment and participation figures for Australians with disabilities remained "pretty consistent" for decades.

"[IEA] is an attempt to to shift something that's been a very intractable problem," she said.

ISS provides staffing at Sydney Airport. (ABC News: Luke Rosen )

Working with employers

Mr Harper said a big part of the approach under IEA was working with employers to determine what skills they needed and where people could fit.

"What happens is you gain trust within the relationship, and those employers then not only spread the word through community and industry, but they're much more willing to take on additional refugees," he said.

Giulia Savio is head of employee experience at facility services company ISS which provides staffing at Sydney Airport and hired Suhail.

Ms Savio said employing people with a disability or from diverse cultural and linguistic backgrounds had a wide range of benefits.

They included having multi-lingual staff to provide better services for customers and helping to create a more inclusive psychologically safe workplace.

"We want our work environments to represent the community as well, and particularly somewhere like an airport, it's important that people see themselves and have that interaction," she said.

Migrant services groups react to Workforce Australia changes Personalised support helped domestic violence survivor and single mother Harsimran get a job, despite significant barriers. It's an approach that could benefit more jobseekers following the federal government's revamp of Workforce Australia.

She also pointed out that finding the right people was difficult and hiring from "non-traditional talent pools" was "broadening that scope to retain and attract really amazing people".

"Partnering with organisations like SSI, where maybe only a small component of either modification or support is required, it's a real no-brainer in getting the right people," she said.

"And when you've met someone like Suhail, who's so passionate and enthusiastic and wants to contribute to the community and wants to give back as well as continually educate himself and develop, it's just such a win-win."

She said Suhail did not require any modifications or amendments to his job responsibilities or environment but multiple layers of support in the team ensured his success in the role and the safety of the airport's passengers.

"In this instance, he was happy just to go in as 'mainstream', for lack of a better word, which is fantastic," she said.

Initial results 'quite impressive'

Mr Harper said most mainstream employment service providers were not equipped to provide tailored support to address the combination of trauma, disability, cultural and language barriers faced by refugees with a disability.

He said the initial results of the IEA approach were "quite impressive".

Of the 1,480 clients who have commenced the program with SSI, 230 had been placed into work in the first eight months

He said only about 35 had left their roles, a conversion rate of about 85 per cent.

The jobs included delivery drivers, age care and disability support workers, commercial cleaners, kitchen hands, factory and process workers.

Mr Harper said the return for taxpayer dollars for getting refugees with disability into work was "enormous".

It took pressure off the NDIS and social security system with workers instead paying tax, he said.

"They are actually contributing to the economy," he said.

Areej has a master's degree, but she's had to 'start from scratch' in Australia Migrant and refugee women often struggle to find employment upon arriving in Australia, even if they have experience and qualifications.

Dr Olney said it was still "early days" for the program.

"I'd say it's an encouraging start regarding outcomes under IEA, and time will tell if those results are sustainable at scale," she said.

"It's a hard road to get these jobs. You've got to find work for people and it has to be the right fit between the employer and the potential employee, and there's a lot of work involved in that.

"So I would say that they have done a good job in a very difficult context."

A Department of Social Security (DSS) spokesperson said under the IEA scheme the number of participants assisted by specialist providers had nearly tripled, increasing to more than 31,000, from around 10,600 under the previous program.

"There are now approximately 51,000 people with disability in a job being supported by an Inclusive Employment Australia provider, including 1,900 refugees," they said.

The DSS is developing a new framework to assess providers' performance and public reporting of outcomes against it will start later this year.

Suhail said he was working hard in his new job and was enjoying being treated like everyone else.

"I don't want to be called disabled in anything," he said.

"I just like to be called as a normal person, you know? When a normal person works in any industry, they're normal, they have their beautiful life, they love, they dance, they eat, they go out and they do everything.

"So, such is my dream."

World.title: The NATO-like defence pact marking a pivot point in the Middle East
World.content:
A NATO-like defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan has landed like a stone thrown into an already swirling Middle East pool.

And the ripples from this deal are spreading as analysts consider its profound implications.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed last Friday in Mecca, is seen as a pivot point in the geopolitics of the region.

It is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and says an armed attack ‌against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, just like Article 5 of the NATO agreement.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan later confirmed the agreement is technically the same as NATO's.

But just what this commitment means in practice in the volatile region is unclear.

In the last 12 months, it has appeared at times as if Israel might emerge as the new hegemonic power in the Middle East.

The unexpected survival of Iran's sphere of influence has also kept open the question of its eventual dominance.

Now a new grouping challenges both of those ideas.

Three powers join forces

Saudi deputy ‌minister for public diplomacy, Rayed Krimly, said in a social media post that the accord "does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc".

"Nor is it linked ⁠to any nuclear ambitions or arms race, rather it is focused on building sustainable capabilities," he said on X.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement commits each country to respond in the event of an attack on the other. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Yet the decision to sign the deal in Islam's holiest city, Mecca, made a point: three of Sunni Muslim's largest and most economically and strategically powerful countries banding together, vowing to come to each other's aid if attacked.

Saudi Arabia is a gulf energy giant, the biggest buyer of US military equipment in the world; and the most strategically located country in the region.

Türkiye is not just a member of NATO but the country with the biggest army in the group apart from the US.

It is also a country that has rapidly become one of the largest defence manufacturers in the world, with ties to Russia and interests lying with the future of both Syria and Lebanon.

And then there is Pakistan: a nuclear-armed power that is not quite in the region, but spending an increasing amount of time this past year finding a role for itself as a mediator between Iran and the United States.

It is an arms manufacturer, with strong ties to China and it is the largest buyer of Türkiye's military exports, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).

There are existing links between the three signatories: Riyadh signed Türkiye's largest ever defence contract in 2023 to buy drones. Pakistan has provided Saudi with fighter jets and other Chinese-made systems.

The pact has been at least expedited by the US-Iran conflict but the complex ties all three countries have in the region means the deal has implications beyond that.

Moving beyond superpower rivalry

There is plenty of agreement that the so-called Mecca Joint Defence Agreement is a reflection of the profound change in the geo-strategic balance in the Middle East that has followed the disastrous US-Israeli war on Iran.

The Iran war has had a far reaching impact on relationships in the Middle East. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

The region can certainly no longer simply be seen as the playground for super power rivalry.

The Mecca pact is the latest response to both the stated intention of the United States to reduce Washington's presence in the region, and to the erratic behaviour of the current incumbent of the White House.

Russia would no doubt like to have more influence in the region, but President Vladamir Putin has his own war to fight just now.
