World.title: Is there a ‘secret death tax’ hidden in Labor’s CGT changes?
World.content:
August 12, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Can I check a recent answer you gave about the CGT impact on inherited shares after July 1, 2027? My understanding is that a death after July 1, 2027 changes how CGT is calculated before and after death, but it does not create an immediate CGT liability for either the estate or the beneficiary. The beneficiary can still inherit the shares in specie and only pay CGT if and when they eventually sell them. However, your answer appeared to say the opposite – that the recent changes rushed through Parliament mean a death after July 1, 2027 creates an immediate CGT liability in the estate before the shares can be passed to the beneficiary. You are the only commentator I have found, whether a real adviser or an AI one, who has taken that view, and I would have expected far more public outcry if this really amounted to a secret death tax. I can only hope I have misunderstood your answer or, heaven forbid, that you are wrong. Perhaps the piece was written before the government walked back its proposal on unrealised capital gains. It’s difficult to believe this tax has been designed without somebody appreciating the consequences for death, divorce and other involuntary transfers. Simon Letch I went back to tax expert Julia Hartman of BAN TACS, who confirms that what I wrote is correct under the legislation as it stands. On August 4, 2026, the Government released draft legislation containing proposed corrections, but unfortunately none of them resolves this particular problem. There are, however, some cryptic remarks in the explanatory memorandum acknowledging problems with rollovers and indicating that they may be dealt with in future amendments. At least that suggests the government is now aware of the issue.



The reason it has received so little media attention is that the legislation is extraordinarily technical, which makes it even more important to keep the issue in the spotlight and put pressure on the government to fix it. It is astonishing that such an important defect was not corrected in this latest round of amendments. Related Article Updated

Federal budget Widows and divorcees protected as Labor reveals details of tax backdown The problem arises because, to preserve the 50 per cent CGT discount on gains accrued up to July 1, 2027, the legislation effectively deems a CGT event to have occurred at that time. The tax is not payable immediately because another provision defers payment until a “realisation event” occurs. Unfortunately, the definition of a realisation event is vast and includes just about any change of ownership. Death is one of those events because, when you die, ownership of your assets passes to your estate. Because you were alive on July 1, 2027, the capital gain accrued before that date has effectively been separated from the rollover provisions that would normally allow assets to pass to your estate and beneficiaries without triggering an immediate tax bill. When death subsequently becomes the realisation event, that deferred pre-July 1, 2027 gain becomes taxable.



It is difficult to believe that the detour away from the normal rollover provisions and into this new concept of a realisation event could have been designed without somebody appreciating the consequences for death, divorce and other involuntary transfers. The good news is that the government now appears to recognise there is a problem. The bad news is that it has not yet fixed it. Given the way this legislation has been handled so far, I would not assume the eventual amendments will automatically restore the position to what it was before. There are no gifting prohibitions between couples. You can give each other as much as you’d like without penalty. We need to keep the pressure on and make sure it is fixed properly. Otherwise, before we know it, July 1, 2027 will be upon us and this extraordinary death, divorce and disaster tax will be part of the law. I turn 67 in April next year and intend to apply for the age pension. I currently have $460,000 in my super accumulation account. My wife will not reach age pension age until September 21, 2028, about 17 months after me. She currently has an account-based pension with a balance of $116,000.



If she were to transfer her account-based pension back into an accumulation account, would I then be able to transfer some of my super into her accumulation account so that my assessable assets fall below the assets test threshold for a single age pension? If this strategy is available, would the transfer be caught by the gifting rules if it were done about eight months before I apply for the age pension? Also, is there a limit on how much I could transfer? You are on the right track. And the good news is, there are no gifting prohibitions between couples. You can give each other as much as you’d like without penalty. Once all the superannuation is in your wife’s name (note that the non-concessional contribution cap will limit how much can be contributed to her account from the withdrawal of your super), and in accumulation mode, not pension mode, the asset will not count until she reaches pensionable age. You will be assessed as a couple, and you will receive 50 per cent of the couple’s pension based on your assets and income. I am 70 and retired, with financial assets of $605,000 in my super pension account and $150,000 in shares. My income is therefore well below the tax threshold. Am I right to understand that from July 2027, any capital gain on my shares will be taxed at 30 per cent, even though my income remains below the threshold? If that is the case, would I be better off invested in an income-producing investment rather than a growth asset? Your understanding is broadly correct, but the key date is June 30, 2027. If, for example, you had owned the shares for three years before that date and sold them one year later, three-quarters of the gain would be taxed under the old rules and one-quarter under the new rules, which impose a minimum tax rate of 30 per cent. However, if you became entitled to the age pension in the income year the shares are sold, the minimum 30 per cent tax would not apply.



You should discuss your circumstances with your accountant, but it may be simpler to sell the shares before June 30, 2027. That way, only 50 per cent of the capital gain would be taxable under the current rules, and any capital losses could be used to offset the gain. You could then contribute the proceeds to super, where you would be in a much more favourable tax environment. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I don’t want to leave an inheritance. How do I spend it all before I die? Paul Benson Money contributor I am 84 and have a SMSF with $1,080,000. If I withdraw $450,000 from my super and use it to pay off my daughter’s mortgage, will that withdrawal be counted for age pension or aged care purposes? Aged care expert Rachel Lane says the short answer is yes – for five years. Under the social security gifting rules, you can give away up to $10,000 in a financial year, with a maximum of $30,000 over five financial years, without affecting your entitlements. Gifts above those limits are treated as “deprived assets”.



Assuming you have not made any previous gifts, $440,000 of the $450,000 would be treated as a deprived asset. It would continue to be counted as one of your assets and deemed to earn income for age pension and aged care purposes for five years from the date of the gift. In effect, it would be treated as though it were still in your SMSF. Based on the figures you’ve provided, you would be unlikely to qualify for the age pension during that five-year period and would continue to pay the maximum means-tested contribution towards your aged care. There is a possibility you could become eligible for a small part age pension during that period if the relevant thresholds increase sufficiently, but that would depend on your circumstances at the time. Once the five years have expired, the deprived asset is no longer counted. Depending on your financial circumstances at that time, you may then qualify for a part age pension, and your aged care contributions could also be reduced. World.title: Half-priced aged care at home sounds like a bargain. Here’s why it isn’t
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementAged care Opinion Half-priced aged care at home sounds like a bargain. Here’s why it isn’t Rachel Lane Money contributor August 12, 2026 — 5:01am

August 12, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For self-funded retirees, Support at Home can offer substantial savings, with government funding ranging from about $11,000 to $78,000 a year, depending on your assessed needs. But the value of that funding depends on how you use it – understanding where the savings are, and where they aren’t. It’s tempting to look at the contribution rates and assume that paying 50 per cent or 80 per cent of a service must be cheaper than paying for it privately. But there’s a simple question you should always ask when someone gives you a percentage: per cent of what? Support at Home services can sound like a good deal on paper but they may end up costing you more. Support at Home divides services into three categories, each with different contribution rates. Clinical care, including nursing and allied health services, attracts no co-contribution regardless of your income or assets. Whether you’re a full pensioner or a self-funded retiree, your contribution is zero. For self-funded retirees, this can make Support at Home particularly valuable. Take a physiotherapy session costing $200. Pay privately and you pay the full $200, although private health insurance may cover some of the cost. Through Support at Home your contribution is $0.



The second category is independence services, which includes personal care such as showering and dressing, transport and social support. Self-funded retirees can pay up to 50 per cent. At first glance, paying half sounds like a bargain. But it is half of the Support at Home price – not necessarily half of what you would pay privately, and there is often a minimum service time. For example, a private provider might charge $65 for 30 minutes of personal care. A Support at Home provider might charge $100 an hour, meaning your 50 per cent contribution is $50 an hour. That looks cheaper until you discover there’s a two-hour minimum visit, making your contribution $100. Shop for the care you need, when you want it, then compare your contribution with the cost of buying the same service privately. The third category is everyday living services like cleaning, gardening and shopping assistance. These attract the highest co-contribution, with self-funded retirees paying up to 80 per cent. For cleaning, a Support at Home provider may charge $105 an hour, with an 80 per cent contribution that means you pay $84 an hour. A private cleaner might charge about $50 an hour; the government-funded service actually costs you more.



Don’t compare provider price lists or hourly rates on My Aged Care. Rates for services outside standard hours can vary widely, and minimum visit times can quickly turn a lower hourly rate into a higher overall cost. Shop for the care you need, when you want it, then compare your Support at Home contribution with the cost of buying the same service privately. Editor's pick Opinion

Aged care Five fees, one room: How aged care costs are actually calculated Rachel Lane Money contributor Many home-care providers offer private services. There are also specialist private-care businesses and platforms such as Mable that can help you arrange your own carers. If you are a self-funded retiree looking at Support at Home, don’t focus on the funding or the contribution rate – focus on what you will actually pay. Support at Home can offer excellent value, particularly for clinical care, but paying 50 or 80 per cent doesn’t automatically make a service cheaper. Ask what you’re really getting out of it, then crunch the numbers.

World.title: I discovered my married boss is cheating with a co-worker. What do I do?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? I discovered my married boss is cheating with a co-worker. What do I do? Kirstin Ferguson August 12, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Each week Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: An office affair, bullying at a community organisation and overreliance on outside consultants. Regarding personal matters at work, it’s important to know when to say something and when to keep it to yourself. Dionne Gain I accidentally discovered my married boss is having an affair with someone at work. My boss handed me his phone during a meeting to look at a document and a message popped up from another employee, leaving little to the imagination. She is not his direct report but a married peer of his. My boss and the woman involved have both always been kind to me but now I feel sick every time I see them together. Do I pretend I never saw it? Yes, I think you should ignore it. Unless what you’ve uncovered involves misconduct that affects the workplace or puts someone at risk, it sounds as if this is something you should leave alone. I don’t think you should share the information. Maintain the confidence you would hope someone else might do for you if they saw something on your phone you hoped no one would see. You didn’t go looking for the information, it came to you – but that doesn’t make you responsible for doing anything about it. Affairs can have devastating personal consequences but they are not automatically workplace matters simply because colleagues, especially if peers, are involved.



Continue to treat both people professionally and resist the temptation to become involved. If either tries to draw you into the situation, politely decline. If the relationship starts affecting decisions, creating conflicts of interest or harming others at work, that’s a different matter. Related Article Got a Minute? I’m a breastfeeding mum. How much should my workplace cater to me? To gain skills while looking for paid employment I became a volunteer with a community organisation. I recently found out that the blokey management had bullied a past female volunteer and she left due to the bad culture. I really love my role but I’m concerned about my legal rights and whether I have any protection. How can I address this with management without creating an awkward scenario? It may lead them to ask me to leave since I’m not being paid anyway. Just because you are a volunteer doesn’t mean it is OK to be bullied. In many organisations volunteers are protected by the same anti-bullying framework that applies to employees, and employers also have duties under work health and safety laws to provide a safe workplace. Don’t assume that because you’re unpaid you have no rights. Rather than confronting management based solely on what happened to someone else, just ask about the organisation’s policies that apply to volunteers, and how concerns are investigated and addressed. You can frame it positively: “As a volunteer, I’d like to understand what protections are in place if issues arise.” The response will tell you a great deal about their culture.



If you later experience or witness bullying, document specific incidents and use the organisation’s internal processes first. A respectful workplace isn’t just a perk for paid employees – every organisation should strive to meet the standard. Whether your community organisation comes within the jurisdiction of the Fair Work Ombudsman will depend on the circumstances but you can always contact the office to be sure and to receive expert advice. Related Article Got a Minute? My holiday was ruined by a redundancy threat. I stayed, but I’m still mad My employer constantly brings in outside consultants who claim major improvements will follow, telling us the changes will improve everyone’s life. The opposite is the case, as most of these new ideas do not work, and cause a wave of disruption. Why does management have so much faith in what is promised but blames everyone else for the often dismal result? I suspect your letter has many readers nodding their heads in agreement. There wouldn’t be many employees who haven’t seen consultants engaged at some point, often by leaders in need of fresh ideas. In principle this is not unreasonable. Where the whole thing becomes unstuck is assuming that an idea that looks good on paper will automatically work in practice. Consultants usually recommend what should happen – but employees at the coal face understand what actually can happen. The only way most initiatives can work is when these align, a fact many leaders overlook in their excitement over the new idea from the latest consultant.

World.title: Why it will take five years, 14 train line closures and $220m to fix a notorious Sydney bottleneck
World.content:
NationalNSWRoads Why it will take five years, 14 train line closures and $220m to fix a notorious Sydney bottleneck Matt O'Sullivan August 12, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Construction of a new seven-lane bridge in Sydney’s north to relieve a notorious road bottleneck is running late due to delays in awarding a major contract for the $220 million project. The planned Epping bridge is regarded as one of the most complex bridge projects in Sydney because the one it is replacing forms part of a major arterial road and passes over a busy train line. The old Epping Bridge passes over a busy train line. Edwina Pickles The state’s transport department is yet to award the contract for the new bridge to replace the existing structure – which was built in the 1930s – despite it previously targeting late last year for a deal. Construction of the single-span bridge is expected to take five years. Transport for NSW terminated an expression-of-interest process for contractors early last year, deciding on an abrupt change in approach for the project’s delivery and procurement. Following the change, the agency said it expected to award the main contract in late 2025.



A promise of joint federal and state funding for the bridge, which is near Epping train station, was first announced in May 2022 by the Perrottet and Morrison governments. Two years later the Minns and Albanese governments each committed $110 million to building the new bridge. Liberal MP for Epping and opposition finance spokeswoman Monica Tudehope said the Labor government had promised more lanes for Epping bridge, but the community was still waiting. An artist’s impression of the new Epping bridge. NSW government “Labor loves a photo op but hates a deadline. And Epping families are the ones stuck paying for it, sitting in traffic every single day,” she said. “They deserve transparency from the government and want to know when this project will get properly under way.”



Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said Epping bridge was a key transport corridor, and Transport for NSW was taking the time to ensure the project delivered the “best outcome for the community, minimises construction impacts and provides value for money”. “The early contractor involvement process is continuing, and the community will be updated as the project progresses,” she said. Epping station neighbours the bridge. Edwina Pickles In a sign of the project’s complexity, a significant amount of construction will have to be undertaken at night or during 14 scheduled shutdowns of the train line. The existing bridge will need to be demolished, and construction will disrupt traffic. Transport for NSW declined to say when it now expects to award the main contract, saying only that the procurement process was “ongoing”.



“Transport for NSW has been undertaking an early contractor involvement procurement process to ensure innovative and value-for-money design and construction solutions are realised, and that impacts to the community are minimised,” it said. Related Article Updated

Roads Tolls cut on Sydney’s motorways after billion-dollar negotiations Under the plans the new bridge will have two more lanes than the existing five-lane structure, including a new westbound traffic lane and an extra right-turn lane southbound onto Blaxland Road. The new bridge is aimed at easing a choke point where Beecroft Road meets Epping Road, which is a major route linking northern Sydney to the lower north shore and the CBD, and is a key access road to the commercial, industrial and university areas of North Ryde and Macquarie Park. Two years ago an environmental review outlined plans for construction to start in mid-2025 and take about five years to complete. A temporary bridge was deemed necessary to enable construction of the new bridge’s northern end, while a significant portion of work would take place at night.



An assessment of the existing bridge in 2022 concluded it was in a “deteriorated condition”. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Adam Liaw’s secret to a great pea and ham soup? Air-fryer croutons
World.content:
A classic pea and ham soup is a masterclass in affordability. A ham hock costs just a few dollars (even if prices are creeping up), and dried peas are among the cheapest items in the supermarket. Put them in a pot, and these budget staples transform into a rich, deeply satisfying soup that is so much more than the sum of its parts.

Blend the soup to your preferred consistency using a stick blender (or in batches using a high-speed upright blender). Taste and adjust the seasoning with salt and black pepper. Return the shredded ham to the soup, stir through, and serve warm, topped with croutons.

While the soup is cooking, make the croutons. If using the oven, preheat it to 180C fan-forced (200C conventional). Toss the sourdough cubes in the olive oil and melted butter, and season well with salt and pepper.

Transfer the ham hock to a plate or cutting board and allow it to cool slightly until safe to handle. Discard the skin, fat and bone, then shred the meat using your hands or two forks.

Simmer the soup for about 1 hour, covered but with the lid slightly ajar, or until the peas are tender. Remove the bouquet garni.

Heat a large saucepan over medium heat and add the butter, onion and celery. Fry for about 8 minutes until softened, then add the garlic and fry for a further minute. Add the ham hock, rinsed peas (no soaking required; see notes), stock and stock powder, and bring to a simmer. Tie the bay leaves, thyme and parsley stalks into a bouquet garni with kitchen string, and add it to the soup.

Masterclass

The split-pea shortcut

A classic pea and ham soup is made with dried green split peas. These are the same species as the fresh or frozen green peas you commonly buy, but a slightly different variety. Split peas come in green and yellow varieties, and both are used across many different cuisines. You don’t need to soak dried split peas. Whole legumes have a skin and take longer to soften, so they are often soaked beforehand, but split legumes cook quickly. Whether you’re making a dhal or this soup, split peas will soften in as little as half an hour. If you want to substitute fresh or frozen green peas into this soup, you’ll need about a kilo, though the colour and flavour of the soup will be vastly different – sweet and bright rather than deep and savoury.

Split peas don’t need to be soaked before going into the pot. Getty Images

The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up

Building the broth

Ham hocks are the lower part of a pig’s leg, and the combination of bone, meat, skin and tendon makes them ideal for soup. Smoked and cured, the ham hock forms the backbone of the broth. While you could make this soup using just water, it will be substantially tastier if you start with a good vegetable or chicken stock. If you don’t have a ham hock, you can use diced bacon or smoked backbone. The bone from a Christmas ham is an ideal base for this soup (adding a bit of the trimmed skin contributes a rich gelatinous texture), along with any leftover meat. For a “pea and chicken” variation, swap the hock for a roast chicken carcass, then stir the stripped meat through at the end.

Baked, not fried

Air-fryers are not fryers. They don’t fry; they bake – and unless you’re reheating frozen food that’s already been deep-fried, they don’t produce results anywhere near frying. However, I am not an air-fryer hater. They’re fantastic for specific jobs, like small batches of food you want baked quickly at high heat. They are perfect for croutons, and a crispy crouton can elevate a good soup to a great one. Let this be your sign to make more soup and more croutons in your air-fryer – though I doubt appliance companies would have sold millions of them if they’d been branded as “crouton-makers”.

Dialling in texture

There are two distinct variables when tweaking the texture of a blended soup – chunky versus smooth, and thick versus thin. Chunky or smooth is determined by how long you run the blender, while thick or thin comes down to your liquid balance. The more you blend, the smoother the soup becomes, but it will also naturally thicken as the broken starches and proteins from the peas swell and bind the liquid. If you prefer a silky, smooth soup that isn’t too thick, simply adjust the consistency by stirring in a little extra stock or water at the end.

Taste the soup after blending and adjust the seasoning. Getty Images

Why blending alters taste

Beyond changing the texture of your soup, blending has a major impact on flavour that often gets overlooked. Whizzing the ingredients releases aromatics, starches, proteins and sugars that were previously bound up in larger chunks of vegetable. Because of this, a smooth puree often tastes significantly more intense and seasoned than a chunky soup. Always give your soup a final taste test after blending to check whether the salt, pepper and savouriness are properly balanced before serving.

World.title: Donald Trump called him America’s worst mayor. Now this Trump target has ideas for Melbourne
World.content:

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Donald Trump once referred to him as “the worst mayor in America”, but Bill de Blasio wears the criticism with pride. The New York mayor frequently clashed with Trump during his two terms in office over his socially progressive policies, including an affordable housing initiative for 300,000 families. De Blasio says that as demand for housing exceeds supply globally, aggressive policies, like those he championed in New York, are needed in cities like Melbourne. “Affordable housing supply has just not kept up with population changes and employment changes, and also just the sheer price reality,” he says. “At this point we have both a climate crisis and an affordable housing crisis, and both of them demand more housing around transit hubs.” Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio backs building more housing around train stations. AP De Blasio’s administration introduced higher-density zoning in New York near major subway and commuter stations, a strategy the Victorian government is pursuing under its framework of 60 activity centres around Melbourne, including in areas such as Camberwell, Brighton, Ringwood and Frankston. De Blasio and Carlos Moreno, the pioneer behind the concept of the 15-minute city, are the headline international speakers joining local experts to discuss Melbourne’s future at a conference to be presented by The Age and the University of Melbourne in October.



Melbourne Assembly will bring together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future as we accelerate towards a population of 9 million people by 2050. It will consider Melbourne’s status as a megacity and the critical tensions that rapid expansion brings, while diving into the debate about whether Melbourne should grow up or grow out. Government has to get involved De Blasio was mayor of New York from 2014 to 2021. He led the city through the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic alongside focusing on affordable housing and homelessness, justice system reform and early childhood education. Related Article City life Vote on 20 ways we could improve Melbourne He believes government intervention is essential to tackling the housing crisis. “Every country, every city is different, but I think there’s some broad commonalities,” de Blasio says over a video call from his home in New York. “If we agree that the market has a crucial role to play, but is clearly not performing sufficiently for a group of people, and I would call those working-class people broadly, by definition, government has to get involved.”



In some places, he says, red tape must be slashed to encourage housing development, and in other areas state action is required, such as the mandatory inclusion zoning policies he introduced in New York. The latter allow private developers to construct higher or denser buildings than would normally be allowed in exchange for a commitment that about 25 per cent of new units will be affordable housing. “Our mandatory inclusionary zoning was a very aggressive policy because we said literally we will not give you a permit to build higher unless you agree to what we need for the public,” de Blasio says. The City of Melbourne has advocated such zoning in the past, but Lord Mayor Nick Reece recently announced plans to abandon these targets, arguing current economic conditions would cause the policy to further constrain housing supply. Lord Mayor Nick Reece says economic conditions are not right for mandatory inclusionary zoning. Eamon Gallagher The Victorian government has drawn criticism for using a limited version of inclusionary zoning on public land, often requiring only 10 per cent affordable housing in deals with private developers. In New York, rezoning efforts in areas such as Manhattan and Brooklyn faced legal battles and furious opposition from some residents worried huge buildings would alter the character of their neighbourhood.



“This upzoning approach of super luxury towers with a small set-aside for affordable units is bad for New York City, bad for our neighbourhoods, and bad for affordability,” Andrew Berman, executive director of the Greenwich Village Society for Historic Preservation, told The New York Times. The Victorian government’s seizure of planning controls, enabling developers to bypass local councils to build high-density apartments of up to 20 storeys, has faced similar opposition locally, sparking protests in Brighton. A formula for disaster De Blasio says planners who want to shake up the system to build more housing must be mindful of history and aesthetics. But maintaining the status quo, he argues, is “a formula for disaster”. In the United States, he points to San Francisco as a cautionary tale where an unwillingness to build taller and denser apartments facilitated massive income inequality and helped create “almost a gilded city for the wealthy”. “We should not underestimate that a healthy city has to have housing for working people, and an environmentally healthy city has to concentrate the housing as close to transit as possible,” he says.



De Blasio also advocates greater regulation of rental increases for young people, who may never be able to afford to buy their own home. In New York, more than 2 million people live in private apartments where the rent increases are decided annually by a public board. A freeze on these increases was central to Zohran Mamdani’s successful mayoral campaign in the city last year. De Blasio is blunt about the impact of this public regulation. “New York City would cease to exist as a viable economy, in my view, if we didn’t have rent regulation for about a quarter of our population,” he says. “We would not be able to house all the people who do the work.” De Blasio says that in New York, residents pay between a third to a half of their income in rent, a similar ratio to Australia, where the typical renter spends about one-third of their household income on rent. Office building conversions

World.title: All Blacks crush Sharks 54-0 in eight-try blitz
World.content:
The All Blacks have thumped the Sharks 54-0 in Durban, overcoming wet conditions to score eight tries and make it two wins from two games on their tour of South Africa.

The Sharks dominated possession and territory in the early stages of the game but it was the All Blacks who scored first in atrocious conditions in Durban with wing Fehi Fineanganofo diving over in the right corner for his first try for the national side.

Ruben Love hit the upright with the conversion but it bounced over to give the All Blacks a 7-0 lead after 20 minutes.

The tourists thought they had scored again with Damian McKenzie latching on to a Quinn Tupaea chip to slide over, but TMO replays showed he had lost the ball just before the line.

McKenzie wasn't to be denied though and scored soon after, sliding over in the right hand corner like Fineanganofo to help put the All Blacks ahead 14-0 going into halftime. McKenzie went off not long after with an injury, and was replaced by Emoni Narawa.

Damian McKenzie scores in wet conditions in Durban. Ron Gaunt/www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks thought they had struck first in the second half when hooker Asafo Aumua barged his way over from close range, but the try was disallowed by the TMO who couldn't see the ball clearly grounded over the line.

However, the tourists would score a couple of phases later with left wing Caleb Clarke dotting down after an easy run to the line following an overlap. Love nailed the sideline conversion to increase the All Blacks lead to 21-0.

Fineanganofo then grabbed his second try of the match after some good play from Love and Clarke and Love continued his perfect record off the kicking tee to put the All Blacks ahead 28-0 with 25 minutes to go.

Fehi Fineanganofo scores a try for the All Blacks. Samuel Shivambu/BackpagePix

Hooker Bradley Slater and prop Siale Lauaki came off the bench to make their All Blacks debuts, as the visitors replaced their entire front row, before midfielder Jordie Barrett scored a great team try where the All Blacks handling skills in the wet were on display.

Love kicked the extras to give the All Blacks a 35-0 lead and then there was a roar from the crowd as former All Blacks centurion Ma'a Nonu came on for the Sharks as a replacement at 44 years old.

The All Blacks were starting to run rampant and halfback Kyle Preston was the next to score after another great piece of interplay between the New Zealand backs, which was sparked by a break from Quinn Tupaea..

Love kicked his sixth straight conversion to put the All Blacks ahead 42-0 and it wasn't long before the All Blacks had their seventh try, with replacement back Timoci Tavatavanawai scoring in the left corner with 10 minutes remaining to extend their lead to 47-0. Love missed the sideline conversion this time to spoil his perfect record, but it was still an impressive night with the boot for the first-five.

Ruben Love kicked well against the Sharks. Ron Gaunt/www.photosport.nz

Lock Sam Darry got his name on the scoreboard with the All Blacks eighth try of the game, using his long arms to reach out and slam the ball down over the tryline and help the tourists push out to a 54-0 lead with five minutes to go and that's how the score would remain, as the All Blacks made it two wins from two games on their tour of South Africa.

'Awesome steps forward' - captain

It was an "awesome game to be a part of," captain Luke Jacobson said in a sideline interview afterwards.

"I think we broke them down well in the first half and we got the fruits of that in the second half and we came away with a good win.

"Against the Stormers (the first game) we weren't where we wanted to be with our set piece around our maul and our scrum, we took awesome steps forward there this week.

"Out there in these wet conditions it's about skill execution and probably didn't start that well there but we started executing really well and we ended up getting points from it.

"It's about trusting your skill sets, trusting your mate, being patient and not being too eager."

The All Blacks next play the Bulls in Pretoria on Sunday morning (NZT).

World.title: Live: Christopher Luxon calls urgent caucus meeting amid leadership speculation
World.content:
RNZ national

National Party MPs have been summoned for an "urgent in-person" caucus meeting in Wellington.

It comes amid renewed pressure on Christopher Luxon's leadership.

Luxon wrote on social media on Tuesday, after postponing various prior arrangements, that it was "clear from various media reports and conversations there is increased speculation about my leadership".

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election.

"I also believe this distraction is unfair to the New Zealand people, and dedicated National Party candidates, supporters and volunteers, when there is so much at stake."

For those reasons, he wrote, the issue "needs to be resolved quickly".

"I am calling an urgent in-person Caucus meeting tomorrow at 9:30am in Wellington to resolve the issue."

World.title: Ali Williams and Anna Mowbray in talks with Netball NZ over new franchise league
World.content:
Former All Black Ali Williams and his wife businesswoman Anna Mowbray are leading a bid to establish a new franchise netball league in 2028, RNZ can reveal.

As reported by RNZ last week, Netball New Zealand is exploring a private ownership model for the ANZ Premiership, as one of several options being considered as it battles to secure the long-term future of the game.

It is understood the national body is in talks with at least one private investor about a proposal to take over the licence to run the ANZ Premiership, in a move that could fundamentally change the way the country's top domestic netball competition is funded and operated.

With the parties understood to have signed non-disclosure agreements while each side carries out its due diligence, details of the proposal remain closely guarded.

However, multiple sources close to the discussions have confirmed to RNZ the project is driven by Williams and Mowbray, who are looking to expand their sports investment portfolio.

The couple are among a group of high-profile investors in A-League club Auckland FC, which has achieved extraordinary success both on and off the field in its first two seasons in the competition.

It is understood Williams and Mowbray want to bring elements of Auckland FC's approach to commercial and fan engagement to netball.

According to a source who asked not to be identified as talks are at a "delicate" stage, the proposal would see the competition run independently of Netball NZ, with private ownership taking responsibility for the commercial and operational arrangements.

Williams, a 77-test All Black, is said to be leading a lot of the behind the scenes work to sound out potential private investors, including key figures from other sports franchises. It is understood he has enlisted the help of several prominent figures from New Zealand netball, including former Silver Ferns Anna Stanley and Adine Wilson.

Despite the ANZ Premiership operating at a deficit of $3.7 million last season, Williams is said to be "bullish" about his prospects of attracting private and commercial partners, and convincing broadcasters to invest.

Williams did not respond to requests for comment.

Ali Williams and Anna Mowbray have a 15 per cent stake in Auckland FC, which this year won the A-League title in its second year. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Netball NZ did not address direct questions about the nature of discussions with private investors, instead issuing a broad-strokes statement.

"Netball NZ is exploring a number of options for the future of the domestic competition for 2027 and beyond," the statement read.

"We are currently in confidential discussions with the [New Zealand Netball Players' Association] and the Zones, and we're not in a position to say any more at this stage."

However, addressing concerns about the future of the domestic competition last month, Netball NZ chair Alastair Carruthers acknowledged private investment was "an area the board is very interested in".

"It's not an obvious possibility for 2027, but I think all forms of investment into our league has to be looked at," he said.

The national body will on Wednesday welcome new chief executive Jennah Wootten, who is expected to front media later this week.

A sport at a crossroads

The talks with private investors come amid increasing concern over the future of the domestic game.

Without a broadcast deal in place for 2027, the national body is yet to commit to running a competition next season. Carruthers last month revealed Netball NZ is facing losses of up to $6 million for the financial year.

The financial strain has fuelled questions over whether the current model is sustainable, with some inside the game increasingly viewing private ownership as the only viable way forward.

But with the privately-backed proposal understood to target a 2028 launch, it leaves New Zealand's top players in limbo over whether they will have a professional contract next year.

Given the ongoing uncertainty the players are facing, Netball NZ last month scrapped the final restrictions preventing Silver Ferns and other leading players from pursuing contracts in Australia and the UK, removing the requirement for athletes to receive a dispensation from Netball NZ before signing with overseas clubs.

One high-profile netball identity told RNZ that Netball NZ was treating next season as a "bridging year" while it works towards a new competition model in 2028.

The source said options under consideration for next season included pausing the ANZ Premiership for a season or reverting to an amateur competition.

But the source warned either option risked accelerating the exodus of New Zealand's best players overseas, leaving little foundation on which to relaunch a professional competition in 2028.

Silver Ferns star Grace Nweke, who has played for the NSW Swifts for the past two seasons, opened the door for other New Zealand players to take up contracts in Australia. Jason McCawley / Getty Images

Not 'dreamed up overnight'

Privatisation is an avenue that has been explored by Netball NZ for some time.

It is understood the origins of Williams and Mowbray's involvement dates back to last year, when the couple was first approached by Netball NZ while former chief executive Jennie Wyllie was still at the helm.

RNZ has learned the approach followed a research project commissioned by the previous board to examine options for improving the sustainability of the elite domestic competition, which has in recent years been operating largely on a year-to-year basis rather than under a long-term commercial model.

"This is not a scheme that's been dreamed up overnight," one netball insider told RNZ.

"It's something Netball NZ has been looking into for a long time, but the change of CEO and the board has complicated matters. We've had fresh sets of eyes come in and examine everything - and rightly so."

The original work was undertaken by former cricket and hockey administrator Anthony Crummy, and examined a range of possible league structures, including the ownership and licensing arrangements for teams.

According to the source the work was later "sharpened" by Australian sports industry expert Shane Mattiske, a former chief executive of the NRL, who now works as a consultant specialising in commercialisation, sponsorship, and media rights.

The model Netball NZ ultimately landed on was for the organisation to sell the licence to run the league, with private investors taking responsibility for its commercial and operational affairs.

The original ambition was to have the new structure in place for the 2027 season, but the process was disrupted by a period of upheaval at Netball NZ.

Despite its financial struggles, the ANZ Premiership attracted strong audience numbers in 2026. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Wyllie left the organisation late last year in the fallout from the drawn-out employment dispute with Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua. Four members of the Netball NZ board also subsequently resigned.

The leadership changes effectively stalled the work on a new league, with the new board and executive team inheriting a process already under way while also developing their own priorities for the organisation.

As a result, any new competition is now being pitched for a 2028 launch.

It remains unclear how committed the current Netball NZ leadership is to the private-ownership model pursued by its predecessors.

The plan would also need the support of the New Zealand Netball Players' Association (NZNPA), which is currently in collective bargaining with the national body.

NZNPA boss Pippa Moore said she was unable to discuss specific plans on the table, but in principle the organisation is open to the idea of privatisation.

"We are open to considering all credible options, including private investment, that can better unlock netball's commercial value," Moore said in a statement.

World.title: More tech projects struggling as govt tries to overhaul 'siloed' system
World.content:
There are major issues with two more big government IT projects, with one having to be revised after a negative rating and the other struggling to be restarted.

The latest problems come after mega-ministry MBIE wasted more than $30m on a failed biometric system that has sparked investigations in parliament.

One of the Justice Ministry's most important digital projects - to expand audio-visual links in courts - last year received a negative 'red' rating, meaning it "appears unachievable".

The ministry says it has revised the project, but is six to eight weeks away from revealing details. It was meant to have completed an early business case by this month.

The second project - to build a new system for people to access records for births, deaths and marriages - is also delayed for years.

The government chief digital officer - the watchdog of all public IT projects - has told ministers there must be more centralisation.

"Agencies' proposed digital investments continue to be siloed, duplicative and deliver little system benefit," the officer said in the latest available Treasury report, for the December 2025 quarter.

"Too many investments are overly large and span multi-years, rather than taking less risky, incremental investment and delivery approaches."

Amber-red second time round

Internal Affairs first attempted its Civil Registration project in 2024 but wrote off $213 million when that project was dumped. It confirmed this week it is still in dispute with the Australian company DWS over that.

After a second attempt, the fledgling new project received an amber/red rating in an independent 'Gateway' review in January, the department told RNZ on Tuesday.

"It received an amber/red rating, noting that the need for system replacement is compelling, but that more work is required before the IBC (indicative business case) to be ready to be submitted to government."

The department has still not decided what is needed and will not lay that out to Cabinet for approval until next year.

"The scope of any future civil registration replacement has not yet been determined. Options are being developed," it said.

Meantime, the old births-and-deaths system continues to limp along.

"While ageing, [it] is stable (although increasingly expensive to modify) and maintenance work continues to be undertaken to ensure secure, functional and legislative compliant systems."

'Continued lower confidence'

The courts and births-deaths projects are examples of chronic and persistent tech-building problems for the government, as it tries to both speed up and save on billions of dollars of demand for new digital systems.

Progress appeared to be slow.

"Investment initiatives submitted by agencies over the past six quarters point to continued lower confidence about their capacity and capability to deploy the internal expertise needed to support their projects," the government chief data steward told ministers, according to the latest available Treasury report, dated December 2025.

"Agencies are investing in modernisation, but underlying capability, standards adoption and lifecycle funding discipline remain uneven.

"Without sustained focus in these areas, the system risks increasing technical debt and cost pressures over time."

The government chief digital officer told chief executives last year to start pooling resources to build IT and stick to its standards under Cabinet's 'Back-Office Transformation' initiative.

The top IT officials and ministers had to get an early look at IT plans.

"This is critical to... the development of digital system assets that can be re-used by multiple agencies."

Revised approach

The Justice Ministry told RNZ that after it got the red rating in a Gateway review in May 2025, it revised the programme to strengthen its approach to delivering it.

Out of 10 high-risk big investments reviewed in the June 2025 quarter across public agencies, the ministry's remote participation project was the only one rated red.

"The next steps in the programme are currently under active consideration, and the ministry is not in a position to provide further detail."

The ministry and the government have expressed high hopes for several years that standardising use of AVL in courts would get many more cases heard on time and help fix the backlog. "Remote participation was invaluable during the pandemic," the ministry said on its website.

The project has now created its own backlog: The choice of tech was meant to have been finalised in early 2025. It requires a secure and reliable network and devices across many courts and tribunals.

Law changes in 2024 - and again this year -were designed to pave a path to more remote participation.

The Justice Ministry's wider digitisation programme Te Au Reka has been forecast to cost $170m.

'Largely delivered'

Internal Affairs said it was learning. "In developing options, we will be informed by the issues that arose through the phase 1 approach."

All current civil registration services remained operational, and customers continued to receive "the same service".

Civil registration had been split out from its wider $300m Te Ara Manaaki digital change programme, which closed at the end of June.

Te Ara Manaaki "largely delivered the majority of its scope", Internal Affairs told RNZ.

It received an amber-green rating on completion.

World.title: 'Perfect storm': Irish passport demand, UK border rules create travel woes
World.content:
Irish New Zealanders say they are struggling to get passports after a surge in applications caused by new British border rules and Brexit.

Dual citizens are reporting long waits, lack of updates, and sometimes heartbreaking consequences when passports do not land in time.

Among them is Dara Shearer, who applied in February for her Irish passport but did not get it until last Friday. The retired dentist and researcher, who has lived in New Zealand for 40 years, wants action to speed up the process to help overseas-based Irish citizens trying to fly to the UK.

When Britain ordered its own dual citizens to use UK passports to return there, it also meant dual Irish citizens all over the world had to travel on an Irish passport to get into Britain, too.

That's because the UK and Ireland operate a Common Travel Area, allowing each other's citizens work and residence rights.

Shearer said the rush of applications when people found out they were no longer able to use New Zealand passports at the British border from February coincided with a resurgent demand for the Irish passport and its EU work and travel rights, in the wake of Brexit.

"This created a perfect storm of a massive number of passport applications and subsequent backlogs," said Shearer, from Oamaru. "It's a bit of a shambles really. Some more clarity about the timeframe would be helpful - on their website, they still say 20 days turnaround for a first-time applicant. I mean, that's laughable, obviously. That's a month.

"In reality, the timeframe is anywhere between four to six months - longer when you factor in the time for posted documents to get from NZ to Dublin."

Social media is awash with similar - and dissimilar - stories. One Wellington man had his first-time Irish passport in 11 weeks, while other families had to get emergency documents or miss family events after their passport did not arrive in time.

When Britain ordered its own dual citizens to use UK passports to return there, it also meant dual Irish citizens all over the world had to travel on an Irish passport to get into Britain, too. RNZ / Gill Bonnett

'Panicking'

Shearer said she felt sorry for others with urgent reasons to travel to Britain, such as family illness, weddings or bereavement, or who just had trips planned.

She also discovered applications expired once they had been in the passport processing system for six months - just as she was approaching that time.

She filled out an online complaint form and her passport was approved within days. But she and her husband Nick Shearer had already missed out on a trip to Britain, where they first met.

"We have actually just come back from six weeks in Europe, we got back at the beginning of June. But we avoided the UK obviously, because neither of us had valid Irish passports so we couldn't enter."

Shearer said because her previous Irish passport expired in 2015 her application was not treated as a renewal, leading to a slower process and document request.

"I'd like maybe for them to get more staff, too. I feel quite sorry for the staff at the office, they probably are dealing with a lot of flak with people who are panicking."

Foreign Affairs sees rise in applications

Ireland's population is similar to New Zealand's, but millions more people have Irish ancestry and live overseas. Estimates of diaspora numbers differ wildly - between 50 million and 100m+.

According to official Stats NZ data, 21,261 people identified as Irish in the last census. However, the Irish in Aotearoa report from 2020 estimated one in six New Zealanders had Irish links - and it's possible the number could be far higher.

The UK and Ireland operate a Common Travel Area, allowing each other's citizens work and residence rights. Unsplash

The Irish Foreign Office, which runs passport services, told RNZ it had seen an increase in first-time and renewal applications from New Zealand.

It said its advertised passport approval time remained 20 working days (four weeks), although that excluded postage times and requests for further documents.

"The Passport Service endeavours to process all applications within the advertised turnaround times, however these turnaround times are not a service delivery guarantee. Processing begins on the date that the Passport Service receives any supporting documentation required."

Applications with incorrect photos or a missing document took longer, it said.

It acknowledged that passport applications expired after six months, citing reasons including International Civil Aviation Organisation regulations on the requirement for a recent photograph.

The Passport Service did not detail the increase in application volumes it is dealing with. UK Home Office figures show overseas passport applications almost tripled to more than 300,000 in the first quarter of 2026.

Shearer questioned whether Irish embassies could check birth and marriage certificates rather than having to post them to Dublin, to save time and money.

The Irish Embassy in Wellington said it had only a small part to play as the Irish Passport Office processed applications.

World.title: Renters 'could end up $700,000 better off' than first-home buyers, economist calculates
World.content:
An Auckland first-home buyer who decided to rent instead could end up more than $700,000 better off in 30 years' time, one economist says.

First-home buyers have been taking advantage of flat house prices and strong investment markets, which have allowed many to accumulate significant amounts in KiwiSaver to use as a deposit.

But with growth in property values expected to be slower from here, does buying pay off?

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub has produced example scenarios for RNZ that indicate that the answer is "it depends".

Why have Ooshies taken over my house? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

His calculation showed the likely outcome of someone buying a house for $900,000 now, which is a typical Auckland first-home buyer amount.

The scenario assumed a 10 percent deposit, annual house price growth of 3 percent, which Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson said was reasonable, and a mortgage rate of 5 percent, with the loan paid off over 30 years.

It includes house insurance costs of $2500 in the first year, increasing at a rate of 7.3 percent a year, council rates of 0.4 percent of the house value in the first year, increasing at a rate of 5.6 percent a year, and maintenance costs of 1 percent of the house value, increasing at 2.7 percent a year.

Rates and insurance have been increasing at a faster rate than that in recent times.

The calculation also includes buying and selling costs.

He compared this to a renter starting with weekly rent of $619 and rent growth of 3.2 percent a year, who could invest the difference between rent and their mortgage payments in a managed fund with a net after-tax return of 5.4 percent a year.

It also includes inflation at 2.5 percent a year.

He calculated that after 30 years, the homeowner would have wealth of $2.1 million and the renter would have investment funds of $2.83 million, leaving the renter $724,530 better off.

But at that point, the homeowner would have a freehold house, while the tenant would need to use some of their wealth to continue to fund their rent through retirement.

Eaqub said it highlighted that there were many aspects that people could think about when they were weighing up a house-buying decision.

Whereas in the past, people expected capital gains to make it worth spending money on rates and insurance, that was not always going to be the case in future, he said.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. Supplied

"There are some pretty big costs of ownership that are coming down with the pipe. It doesn't mean one thing or the other, it's just, I think, that you should do this with your eyes wide open.

"Just being really clear about the cost of ownership and the cost of renting. They're both real it's about the tradeoff… People's circumstances are different.

"For the average homeowner now, rates insurance and maintenance are probably running at $10,000 a year. That's a lot. If you're a fixed income person, a retiree, have you budgeted for $10,000 a year for those things?"

Many buyers are making their choice based on more than the financial calculation.

Eaqub said home ownership would give people connection to community and stability, which were harder to access when renting.

"Security of tenure is a legitimate concern for people both young and old, nobody likes to move house because somebody else wants you to move."

He said people also tended to rent houses that were more expensive than those they might buy. "You have to do an apples with apples comparison."

Davidson said it was reasonable to assume that the growth in house prices over the coming years would not be as strong as it had been over the past decades. He said it was also true that buying a house would not be right for everyone.

Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson. SUPPLIED

"Renting has never been dead money or a waste of time or a huge problem in your life. Renting is a perfectly legitimate way of living and a choice a lot of people around the world make so I don't think it's ever been a slam dunk.

"Even putting aside all the ins and outs of running these numbers, I think it's becoming a more common view that house price growth will be lower in the next 10 or 20 years all else being equal. That will reduce the appeal of being a homeowner. It might not necessarily tip things fully in favour of renting but it shifts the balance a bit.

"We might look over the next 30 years and go well clearly it was a time to not worry so much about owning a house. We're only going to know if things have truly changed in hindsight but it does feel like we're at a bit of a junction now where people are starting to question the long run assumption of capital growth."

He said owners would have the benefit of forced savings. Renters were relying on being disciplined enough to save the difference to build up their wealth to the same extent.

Ed McKnight, of Opes Partners, said the outcome was heavily reliant on the assumptions used, and house prices could rise faster than 3 percent.

"The whole benefit of buying your own home is that eventually payments stop after year 30."

World.title: Kiwi firefighters head to US to help tackle unprecedented wildfires
World.content:
New Zealand firefighters have answered a call for help from the United States.

A convoy of 57 firefighters, chainsaw crews and forestry experts depart this week to help their counterparts fight wildfires in America's north-west.

It's senior firefighter Cameron Grylls' first deployment overseas.

"It's going to be pretty different for us given the scale and the size of what they're dealing with over there," Grylls said.

"It's just that next level so we're expecting some long hot days and a lot of strenuous exercise, but we're going to to help our teammates out over there and do our best."

He's Fire and Emergency's assistant district commander for Waikato and would be leading a crew of boots on the ground - they could be deployed to any of the neighbouring states of Oregon, Washington State or Idaho.

They would spend 28 days firefighting.

The team is made up of 43 personnel from Fire and Emergency, four from the Department of Conservation (DOC), five from the Defence Force and five from the forestry industry.

They would be taking on multiple roles, ranging from firefighters and fire engine crews to chainsaw specialists, and including incident management roles such as helibase managers, logistics and liaison officers.

"They could be blacking out, that's extinguishing, dampening down where fires have gone through so that they don't reignite, could be clearing access for other crews, cutting down trees," Grylls said.

"We go over with a fairly open mind and know that we're going over to help them in whatever task they might need doing. So we're pretty flexible."

Cameron Grylls. RNZ / Amy Williams

The scale of wildfires in America's north-west and Canada is unprecedented.

In western Canada, over 20,000 people were forced to flee communities in British Columbia over the weekend and in the US, crews in Washington have been fighting three wildfires that began burning in the Spokane area.

The New Zealand firefighters are experienced working in arduous conditions, including steep terrain and high temperatures, and living in fire camps in remote areas.

It's not just the scale of the wildfires that would be challenging for the Kiwi crews - they've been told to keep an eye out for local wildlife.

"Bears, scorpions, rattlesnakes any of those sorts of things that we typically don't have over here that are out to hurt us. It's a different environment for us...we just have to keep our wits about us."

Blair Calder is a DOC ranger in Dunedin and his team is likely to be focused on making fire breaks.

"There'll be a lot of walking onto the fire ground then there'll be a lot of using hand tools and not a lot of water, possibly, where we're going. We've got chainsaw operators with us," Calder said.

"It's crucial and it can be very time consuming and physically demanding."

This was his sixth deployment overseas, he'd been to Canada and Australia to join firefighting efforts.

"I really enjoy the challenge. I enjoy working with other people from around New Zealand who you don't always get to work with.

"When you get over there, the upskilling you get from 28 days of firefighting is pretty intense and it's a really good way to learn."

The Bald Range wildfire near Summerland in Canada's western British Columbia province on August 7, 2026. Handout / BC Wildfire Service / AFP

Forestry-trained firefighters have worked with Fire and Emergency in overseas deployments for decades, bringing specialised chainsaw skills and expertise.

Forestry worker Jarron McInnes is going to the US as a leader for a chainsaw crew and had previously fought wildfires in Canada and Australia.

"It's their chainsaw skills where they really shine - tree felling, cutting fire breaks and fire lines," he said.

Defence force Staff Sergeant Matthew Anker is a Fire Master based in Waiouru and he said it was the type of deployment soldiers train for.

"They are experienced in wildfire response and accustomed to operating in demanding environments as part of a coordinated multi-agency team," he said.

"It is an opportunity for them to apply those skills in support of our international partners, while gaining further experience that will strengthen our response capability at home."

Cameron Grylls said they would come back home to New Zealand with news skills to tackle an expected dry spring and summer...something crews were already preparing for.

"Some brigades are looking at going out and starting up training around working with helicopters and all of that rural aspect that we do...our crews are very much aware of that and looking to start building that into their training now as we move forward into that season."

Some of the fire fighters departed for the US on Tuesday and the remainder leave Wednesday.

World.title: What happens to your KiwiSaver if you die?
World.content:
What happens to your KiwiSaver money if you die?

Australians might be being warned to make sure they've organised who will get their superannuation savings when they die - but New Zealanders don't have as much to worry about.

ABC reported this week that 15.5 million Australians might not have made a binding death nomination for their superannuation accounts, to direct their fund on who to pay the money to.

In Australia, superannuation does not automatically become part of a person's estate if they die.

In New Zealand, the situation was quite different - and simpler.

Why have Ooshies taken over my house? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

KiwiSaver formed part of a person's estate when they died and became another asset that was dealt with by their will if they had one.

"New Zealanders don't generally need the equivalent of Australia's binding death benefit nomination to make sure their KiwiSaver follows their estate wishes," Pie Funds chief executive Ana-Marie Lockyer said.

"There are still good reasons to have an up-to-date will and make things easy for your executor, but there isn't the same additional layer of superannuation estate planning that Australians face."

If they did not have a will, there were rules that determined how the estate was distributed.

If they had a spouse or partner and children, the spouse or partner would get all personal possessions, $155,000 and a third of anything remaining. The other two-thirds would be divided among the children.

Kernel founder Dean Anderson said the main thing for New Zealanders to be aware of was that the limit at which probate was required had increased.

It was now the case that most estates under $40,000 could be handled without the need to apply to the court.

It was increased from $15,000 because many KiwiSaver balances had grown past that level.

World.title: Cats confirm Kolodjashnij unavailable to play amid concussion waiver saga
World.content:
The player at the centre of a concussion waiver controversy, Geelong's Jake Kolodjashnij, will not play this weekend as the club prepares to find out whether it will face sanctions.

It emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with a player, who had had a history of concussions.

Kolodjashnij went public confirming he was the player involved.

The waiver has since been removed from his contract.

"Geelong Cats defender Jake Kolodjashnij will be unavailable for selection at AFL or VFL level this weekend," the club said a statement late on Tuesday.

"The care and wellbeing of Jake remains the club's priority, and the club will continue to support him and his family through this period."

The Cats had until the end of Tuesday to respond to the "please explain" from the AFL over the concussion waiver that Kolodjashnij signed but which was never seen by the AFL or the AFLPA.

Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's please explain as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board had held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Media reports on Tuesday said that the AFL Commission had hired independent legal counsel to help determine whether the Cats should face sanctions over the issue.

The 31-year-old Kolodjashnij was drafted by the club in 2013 and he has played 209 games for Geelong.

He last played at AFL level for the Cats against GWS a month ago.

His twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, was forced to retire in 2020 due to concussion issues.

World.title: Veteran Manly prop Nathan Brown outlines NRL exit plan
World.content:
Manly prop Nathan Brown has revealed he decided at the start of the season this would be his last in the NRL, as the veteran forward eyes a move to the Super League.

Off contract at the end of 2026, Brown has confirmed he will finish up at Manly this year as the Sea Eagles begin a changing of the guard in the forward pack.

Brown's final month at Manly will take on even more importance on Friday night, after he was called in to start for the first time in two years against the Dolphins amid the Sea Eagles' forwards shortage.

The 33-year-old is still hoping to exit the NRL in a finals series, with Manly likely needing to win their last four games to return to the top eight.

Munster free to play Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster avoids suspension after the NRL match review committee downgrades his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

"I just knew it was my time to call it quits in the NRL … I made my debut in 2013, so it's my 14th year. When your time's up, your time is up," Brown told AAP.

"The last thing I wanted to do was sit on the fence with whether I want to stay or go overseas.

"It's just made everything a lot easier to go all in this year and enjoy every moment, every training session and every game."

Brown was regarded as one of the most aggressive forwards in the game when he debuted at Wests Tigers in 2013, as well as during a two-year stint at South Sydney.

Nathan Brown played six seasons at the Eels, making his Origin debut while at the club. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yeung)

He came into his own at Parramatta, playing two State of Origins for NSW in 2020 and the 2022 grand final for the Eels before reviving his career with a train-and-trial deal at Manly in 2024.

"I find it funny [looking back at old footage)]" said Brown, who is on track to reach 200 games this month.

"When I started, I was a lot bigger. I wasn't really that fit. I was a bit overweight for my size and my position. And I had a different attitude back then.

"But at the same time, you learn a lot from it. You feel grateful that you had to go through those things."

Brown's NRL retirement comes with fellow veteran Manly prop Siua Taukeiaho off contract after breaking his leg in two places in May.

The Sea Eagles have signed props Davvy Moale and Toni Mataele for next year, while Kayliss Fatialofa will arrive as a highly-heralded second rower.

Teenage prop Simi Laiafi has also shown promise starting this year alongside Taniela Paseka, and looms as a long-term prospect.

Brown said he was proud of the impact he was able to have off the bench this year, still hitting the line with gusto.

"You don't want to be finishing by just clutching at the straws and hanging on by a thread," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I feel like I can probably still physically play another year in the NRL. But in the mental side of things, I'm just ready."

Manly expect to be without prop Paseka for at least a fortnight after he injured his knee against Melbourne last week, in a seismic blow to their finals chances.

Ethan Bullemor (concussion) remains sidelined, while Kobe Hetherington (biceps) last week joined Taukeiaho in being out for the season.

Second-rower Ben Trbojevic (concussion) is also still out, while his superstar brother Tom has been kept on ice for another week in his return from a hamstring injury.
